topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Numerical Processes (1): Indices and Logarithms
topics.overview: Indices are a shorthand for repeated multiplication. This chapter builds the laws of indices, extends them to zero, negative and fractional indices, uses them to write very large and very small numbers in standard form, and then introduces logarithms as another way of writing indices, culminating in calculations with logarithm tables.

concepts.title: Index notation: base, index and power
learningObjectives: Explain what a^n means and name the base and the index
Write repeated multiplication in index form and expand index form
Evaluate numbers with positive whole-number indices, including negative bases and fractional bases
Tell the difference between (-3)^2 and -3^2
prerequisiteNotes: Rules of signs for multiplying negative numbers

keyTerms.definition: The number (or letter) that is being multiplied by itself. In 2^5 the base is 2.
The small raised number that tells how many times the base is used as a factor. In 2^5 the index is 5.
The whole expression or its value. 2^5 is 'the fifth power of 2', and its value is 32.
The plural of index.

concepts.definition: Index notation is a short way of writing repeated multiplication. If a is any number and n is a positive whole number, then a^n (read 'a to the power n') means a multiplied by itself n times: a^n = a x a x a x ... x a (n factors).
explanation: Suppose you have to write 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2. It is tiring to write, and easy to miscount. Mathematicians therefore write it as 2^5. The big number 2 is the base, because it is what everything is built on. The small raised number 5 is the index. It does not tell you to multiply 2 by 5. It tells you to use 2 as a factor five times. So 2^5 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32, and not 2 x 5 = 10. This is the single most common beginner error, so remember it from the start.

Special names exist for the first two indices. a^2 is read 'a squared' because the area of a square of side a is a x a. a^3 is read 'a cubed' because the volume of a cube of side a is a x a x a. For all other indices we say 'to the power of': 2^5 is 'two to the power five'. And a^1 is simply a, because the base is used just one time.
Order matters in the sense that base and index cannot be swapped. 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, but 3^2 = 3 x 3 = 9. They are different numbers.

Negative bases need care with brackets. When the base is a negative number you must put it in brackets, so that the minus sign is part of the base. (-3)^2 means (-3) x (-3) = +9. But -3^2 (no brackets) means -(3 x 3) = -9, because the index acts only on the 3 and the minus sign is applied afterwards. The pattern for a negative base is: an even index gives a positive answer (two negatives multiply to a positive, four negatives multiply to a positive, and so on) while an odd index gives a negative answer.

Fractions as bases also need brackets. (2/3)^3 means (2/3) x (2/3) x (2/3) = (2 x 2 x 2)/(3 x 3 x 3) = 8/27. The index applies to both the numerator and the denominator. Note that 2/3^3 would mean something different (2 divided by 27).

Powers of ten deserve special attention because our number system is built on them. 10^1 = 10, 10^2 = 100, 10^3 = 1 000, 10^4 = 10 000 and so on. The index tells you the number of zeros after the 1. This is the foundation for standard form, which you will meet later in this chapter.

rows: number of times the base is a factor

illustrations.caption: Powers of 2 and 10 worth knowing
illustrations.description: Memorise these; they appear again and again.

workedExamples.problem: Write 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 in index form.
steps: Identify the repeated factor: it is 7.
Count how many times it appears: 4 times.
(b) (-2)^5 = (-2)(-2)(-2)(-2)(-2). Pairs of negatives give positives: (-2)(-2) = 4, then 4 x (-2) = -8, then -8 x (-2) = 16, then 16 x (-2) = -32. An odd index gives a negative answer.
(c) (-2)^4 = (-2)(-2)(-2)(-2) = 4 x 4 = 16. An even index gives a positive answer.
(d) -2^4 has no bracket, so only the 2 is raised to the power: -(2 x 2 x 2 x 2) = -16.

workedExamples.problem: A single bacterium splits into two every hour. Assuming none die, how many bacteria are there after 10 hours?
steps: After 1 hour: 2 = 2^1. After 2 hours: 2 x 2 = 2^2 = 4. After 3 hours: 2^3 = 8.
The pattern is that after n hours there are 2^n bacteria.

realWorldApplications: Area and volume: square metres (m^2) and cubic metres (m^3) are index notation in units.
Population and bacteria growth: quantities that double or triple at regular intervals follow powers of 2 or 3.
Computing: memory is measured in powers of 2 (1 kilobyte is 2^10 = 1 024 bytes).
Money: compound interest uses a power, for example an amount growing by 10% a year is multiplied by 1.1 each year, giving 1.1^n after n years.
Science: very large and very small measurements (distance to the Sun, the size of a cell) are written with powers of 10.
commonMistakes: Treating a^n as a x n. For example, thinking 2^5 = 10. The correct value is 32.
Forgetting brackets: writing -3^2 and getting +9. Without brackets the answer is -9.
Mixing up 2^3 and 3^2 (8 versus 9).
Thinking (2/3)^2 = 2/9 (the index must apply to both top and bottom: 4/9).
summary: a^n means a multiplied by itself n times; a is the base and n is the index.
a^1 = a. a^2 is 'squared' and a^3 is 'cubed'.
Negative base: even index gives a positive answer, odd index gives a negative answer, and brackets are essential.
10^n is a 1 followed by n zeros.

concepts.title: Multiplication and division laws of indices
learningObjectives: State and explain the multiplication law x^a * x^b = x^(a+b)
State and explain the division law x^a / x^b = x^(a-b)
Simplify expressions with coefficients and more than one letter
Know that the laws apply only to the SAME base

keyTerms.definition: The number multiplying a letter or term. In 5y^3 the coefficient is 5.
Bases that are exactly the same, such as 2 and 2, or x and x.

concepts.definition: Law 1 (multiplication): when multiplying powers with the same base, add the indices: x^a x x^b = x^(a+b). Law 2 (division): when dividing powers with the same base, subtract the indices: x^a / x^b = x^(a-b). Both laws hold for any x that is not 0.
explanation: Why does Law 1 work? Expand it. 2^3 x 2^4 = (2 x 2 x 2) x (2 x 2 x 2 x 2). Counting every 2, there are 3 + 4 = 7 of them. So 2^3 x 2^4 = 2^7. In general, x^a has a factors of x and x^b has b factors of x. Multiplying them gives a + b factors of x altogether, which is x^(a+b). Never multiply the indices here. You add them.

Why does Law 2 work? Expand and cancel. 2^5 / 2^2 = (2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2)/(2 x 2). Two of the 2s on top cancel with the two on the bottom, leaving 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3. The number of factors left is 5 - 2 = 3. In general, x^a / x^b = x^(a-b). The index of the bottom is subtracted from the index of the top, and the order matters: top minus bottom.

When there are numbers in front (coefficients), treat them separately from the letters. Multiply or divide the coefficients in the usual way, then apply the index law to each letter. For example 3x^2 x 4x^5: coefficients 3 x 4 = 12, letters x^2 x x^5 = x^(2+5) = x^7, giving 12x^7. A letter written without an index has index 1, so x = x^1. This matters: a x a^3 = a^1 x a^3 = a^4.

When an expression contains different letters, apply the law to each letter independently. (a^5 b^2)(a^2 b^3) = a^(5+2) b^(2+3) = a^7 b^5. The a-terms combine with the a-terms and the b-terms with the b-terms.

The laws only work if the bases are the same. 2^3 x 3^4 cannot be combined by adding indices, because the bases 2 and 3 are different. You would have to calculate 8 x 81 = 648. Likewise x^2 x y^3 stays as x^2 y^3.
The division law can give an index of zero or a negative index. For example x^3 / x^3 = x^(3-3) = x^0, and x^2 / x^5 = x^(-3). These cases are explained fully in the next two lessons.

illustrations.caption: Seeing the law by counting
illustrations.description: Expanded forms show why the indices add (multiplication) or subtract (division).

rows: (x x x) x (x x x x x x)

steps: (b) Coefficients: 3 x 4 = 12. Letters: x^(2+5) = x^7. Answer 12x^7.

workedExamples.problem: Simplify 24a^8 b^3 / 6a^5 b.

steps: Top: coefficients 2 x 5 = 10; a: a^(3+2) = a^5; b: b^(1+4) = b^5. So the top is 10a^5 b^5.
Divide by 10a^4 b^2: coefficients 10/10 = 1; a: a^(5-4) = a; b: b^(5-2) = b^3.

realWorldApplications: Scientific calculation: multiplying large quantities written as powers of ten (for example 10^3 x 10^5 = 10^8).
Computing: combining storage units, for example 2^10 x 2^10 = 2^20 bytes, which is how a megabyte relates to a kilobyte.
Algebra and physics formulas: simplifying expressions such as area x height or speed x time when the quantities carry powers.
Compound growth: multiplying growth over two periods adds the number of periods (1.05^3 x 1.05^2 = 1.05^5).
commonMistakes: Multiplying the indices instead of adding in x^2 x x^3 (the answer is x^5, not x^6).
Adding the coefficients when multiplying: 3x^2 x 4x^5 is 12x^7, not 7x^7.
Trying to combine different bases: 2^3 x 3^2 is not 6^5.
Subtracting in the wrong order in division (top index minus bottom index).
Forgetting that a letter alone has index 1.
summary: Same base, multiply: add indices. x^a x x^b = x^(a+b).
Same base, divide: subtract indices. x^a / x^b = x^(a-b).
Handle coefficients and each different letter separately.
The laws do not work for different bases.

concepts.title: Zero index and negative indices
learningObjectives: Explain why x^0 = 1 for every x not equal to 0
Explain that x^(-n) means 1/x^n (the reciprocal of x^n)
Evaluate and simplify expressions with zero and negative indices
Rewrite expressions so that all indices are positive

keyTerms.definition: The reciprocal of a number is 1 divided by that number. The reciprocal of 5 is 1/5; the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.
An index of 0. Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1.
An index below zero. It tells you to take the reciprocal of the positive power.

concepts.definition: Law 3: x^0 = 1 (x not equal to 0). Law 4: x^(-a) = 1 / x^a. Also, 1 / x^(-a) = x^a, and (a/b)^(-n) = (b/a)^n.
explanation: Where does x^0 = 1 come from? Use the division law on something that is obviously 1. Any non-zero number divided by itself is 1, so 5^3 / 5^3 = 1. By the division law, 5^3 / 5^3 = 5^(3-3) = 5^0. Therefore 5^0 must equal 1. The same reasoning works for any base, so x^0 = 1 for every x except 0 (0^0 is left undefined). Notice that 19^0 = 1, (-4)^0 = 1 and even (3/7)^0 = 1. And be careful: 6x^0 = 6 x 1 = 6 because the index 0 applies only to x, but (6x)^0 = 1.

Where do negative indices come from? Look at 2^3 / 2^5. Expanding, (2 x 2 x 2)/(2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2) = 1/(2 x 2) = 1/2^2. The division law says the same quantity is 2^(3-5) = 2^(-2). So 2^(-2) must equal 1/2^2 = 1/4. In general x^(-a) = 1/x^a. A negative index does NOT make the answer negative. It flips the base into the denominator. So 5^(-2) = 1/25, which is positive.

Here is a pattern that makes it feel natural. Read down the list: 2^3 = 8, 2^2 = 4, 2^1 = 2, 2^0 = 1, 2^(-1) = 1/2, 2^(-2) = 1/4, 2^(-3) = 1/8. Each time the index drops by 1, the value is divided by 2. The pattern continues smoothly through 0 into negative indices.

The reverse also holds: 1/x^(-a) = x^a. A negative index in the denominator moves up to the numerator and becomes positive. So 1/2^(-3) = 2^3 = 8. A simple memory aid: a negative index means 'move to the other side of the fraction bar and change the sign of the index'.
Fractions to a negative power: flip the fraction, then use the positive index. (2/3)^(-2) = (3/2)^2 = 9/4. Check: (2/3)^(-2) = 1/(2/3)^2 = 1/(4/9) = 9/4. Same answer.

Brackets decide what the negative index applies to. 3x^(-2) means 3 x (1/x^2) = 3/x^2, so only the x is moved. But (3x)^(-2) = 1/(3x)^2 = 1/(9x^2). Always check whether the index belongs to the whole bracket or just to the letter next to it.

illustrations.caption: The pattern that continues past zero
illustrations.description: Each step down in the index divides the value by the base.

illustrations.caption: Quick-reference for zero and negative indices

rows: any non-zero base to the power 0

steps: (a) Anything non-zero to the power 0 is 1, so 8^0 = 1.
(c) Flip the fraction and use the positive index: (1/2)^-3 = 2^3 = 8.

workedExamples.problem: Simplify and give the answer with positive indices: (a) r x r^0 x r^-5 (b) x^3 / x^-5 (c) 4a^-3 x 3a^5.

steps: 2^-2 = 1/4, so dividing by 2^-2 means multiplying by 4.

realWorldApplications: Metric prefixes: 1 millimetre = 10^-3 metres, 1 micrometre = 10^-6 metres, 1 nanometre = 10^-9 metres. Negative indices describe very small quantities.
Science: the mass of an electron is about 9.1 x 10^-31 kg; the thickness of a cell membrane is about 7 x 10^-9 m.
Chemistry: concentrations such as 10^-7 mol/dm^3 for pure water, which underlies the pH scale.
Finance and decay: a value that falls by half each period can be written with negative powers, like 100 x 2^-n.
commonMistakes: Believing a negative index gives a negative answer: 2^-3 is 1/8, not -8.
Believing x^0 = 0. It is 1.
Treating 3x^-2 as 1/(3x^2). Only x is flipped, so it is 3/x^2.
Forgetting to subtract a negative index correctly: x^3 / x^-5 = x^(3+5) = x^8.
Flipping only the numerator or only the denominator of a fraction raised to a negative power.
summary: x^0 = 1 for any x not equal to 0.
x^-a = 1/x^a, and 1/x^-a = x^a.
(a/b)^-n = (b/a)^n: flip the fraction.
A negative index means reciprocal, not a negative number.

concepts.title: Power of a power, power of a product and power of a quotient
learningObjectives: State and use (x^a)^b = x^(ab)
State and use (xy)^n = x^n y^n and (x/y)^n = x^n / y^n
Simplify expressions that combine several index laws

keyTerms.definition: A power that is itself raised to another power, such as (x^2)^3.

concepts.definition: Law 5: (x^a)^b = x^(a x b). Also (xy)^n = x^n y^n, and (x/y)^n = x^n / y^n.
explanation: Consider (x^2)^3. The outer index 3 says 'use x^2 three times': (x^2)^3 = x^2 x x^2 x x^2. By the multiplication law, add the indices: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, which equals 2 x 3. So (x^2)^3 = x^6. In general (x^a)^b = x^(ab): when you raise a power to a power, you multiply the indices. Compare this carefully with Law 1 where you add. Add when multiplying powers (x^2 x x^3 = x^5). Multiply the indices when raising a power to a power ((x^2)^3 = x^6).

When the bracket contains a product, the outer index applies to every factor inside, including the number. (2a^2)^3 = 2^3 x (a^2)^3 = 8 x a^6 = 8a^6. A common error is to cube only the letter and forget to cube the 2. Think of it as 2a^2 written three times and multiplied: (2a^2)(2a^2)(2a^2) = 8a^6.
When the bracket contains a quotient, the outer index applies to both the top and the bottom. (x/y)^3 = x^3 / y^3. For numbers, (2/3)^2 = 4/9.

The laws combine freely with negative and zero indices. (3x^-2)^2 = 3^2 x (x^-2)^2 = 9 x x^-4 = 9/x^4. And (2^3)^-2 = 2^-6 = 1/2^6 = 1/64. A bracket raised to the power 0 is always 1, as in (5a^3 b)^0 = 1.

Strategy for harder expressions: first remove brackets using the power laws, then collect each base separately with the multiplication and division laws, and finally rewrite negative indices if the question asks for positive indices.

illustrations.caption: Which law do I use?
illustrations.description: A decision table for index laws.

steps: (b) Apply the 3 to the 2 and to a^2: 2^3 = 8 and (a^2)^3 = a^6. Result 8a^6.

workedExamples.problem: Simplify (x^2 y)^3 / (x y^2)^2.
Evaluate (2^3)^-2 x 4^2.

realWorldApplications: Geometry: if a cube's side is multiplied by k, the volume is multiplied by k^3 (a power of a power appears when the side itself is a power).
Physics: formulas like kinetic energy (1/2)mv^2 involve squaring a quantity that may itself carry a power, such as v = 3 x 10^4 m/s, giving v^2 = 9 x 10^8.
Scientific notation: (3 x 10^4)^2 = 9 x 10^8.
Compound interest over multiple blocks of years uses (1 + r)^(n x m) = ((1 + r)^n)^m.
commonMistakes: Adding indices in (x^2)^3 and getting x^5. The correct answer is x^6.
Forgetting to raise the coefficient: (2a^2)^3 = 8a^6, not 2a^6.
Applying the outer index to only the first factor of a product.
Making sign errors with negative indices inside brackets.
summary: (x^a)^b = x^(ab).
(xy)^n = x^n y^n and (x/y)^n = x^n/y^n.
Apply the outer index to every factor in the bracket, including numbers.
Remove brackets first, then collect like bases.

concepts.title: Fractional indices (roots as powers)
learningObjectives: Explain that x^(1/n) is the nth root of x
Evaluate x^(m/n) as the nth root of x raised to the power m
Evaluate expressions with negative fractional indices
Simplify expressions combining fractional indices with the other laws
prerequisiteNotes: All index laws so far (1.1 to 1.4)

keyTerms.definition: A number which, multiplied by itself, gives the original number. The square root of 25 is 5, because 5 x 5 = 25.
A number which, used as a factor three times, gives the original. The cube root of 27 is 3.
A number which, used as a factor n times, gives the original number.

concepts.definition: x^(1/n) is the nth root of x. More generally, x^(m/n) = (nth root of x)^m = nth root of (x^m). For example 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4.
explanation: What could the index 1/2 mean? Apply Law 5. (x^(1/2))^2 = x^((1/2) x 2) = x^1 = x. So x^(1/2) is a number which, when squared, gives x. That is exactly the definition of the square root. So x^(1/2) is the square root of x, written sqrt(x). For example 25^(1/2) = 5. In the same way x^(1/3) is the cube root and x^(1/n) is the nth root.

Now the general case x^(m/n). Write m/n as m x (1/n), so x^(m/n) = (x^(1/n))^m. This means: take the nth root first, then raise to the power m. For 8^(2/3): the cube root of 8 is 2, then 2^2 = 4. Taking the root FIRST keeps the numbers small and is the recommended order. You will get the same answer if you compute 8^2 = 64 first and then take the cube root (4), but that is harder.
The denominator of the fractional index is the root; the numerator is the power. Read x^(3/4) as 'fourth root, then cubed'.

Negative fractional indices combine both ideas: a negative index means reciprocal, and the fraction means a root and a power. 81^(-1/4) = 1/81^(1/4) = 1/3 because the fourth root of 81 is 3 (3 x 3 x 3 x 3 = 81). For fractions as bases, flip first: (1/4)^(-1/2) = 4^(1/2) = 2.

Fractional indices only give a nice answer when the base is a perfect power of the required root. For example 16^(3/4) works because 16 is a perfect fourth power (2^4). Learn the common perfect powers: squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144), cubes (1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 1 000), fourth powers (1, 16, 81, 256, 625) and fifth powers (1, 32, 243).

steps: (b) The cube root of 27 is 3. Then 3^2 = 9.
(c) The fourth root of 16 is 2 (since 2^4 = 16). Then 2^3 = 8.
(d) 81^(-1/4) = 1/81^(1/4). The fourth root of 81 is 3. So the answer is 1/3.
Apply the root to top and bottom: cube root of 27 = 3 and cube root of 8 = 2, giving 3/2.

workedExamples.problem: Simplify (x^4)^(1/2) x x^(-3).

realWorldApplications: Geometry: the side of a square with area A is A^(1/2); the edge of a cube with volume V is V^(1/3).
Physics: the period of a pendulum is proportional to L^(1/2); speed formulas often involve square roots.
Finance: finding the yearly growth rate from total growth over n years uses the nth root, written as a power of 1/n.
Engineering and science: scaling laws, such as how animal metabolism scales with body mass, use fractional powers.
commonMistakes: Reading x^(1/2) as x divided by 2.
Mixing up numerator and denominator: in x^(2/3) the 3 is the root and the 2 is the power.
Ignoring the negative sign in a negative fractional index (it gives a reciprocal).
Doing the power before the root and ending up with huge numbers, which causes arithmetic slips.
summary: x^(1/n) = nth root of x.
x^(m/n) = (nth root of x)^m: root first, then power.
A negative sign gives a reciprocal.
Memorise perfect squares, cubes and fourth powers.

concepts.title: Solving simple equations involving indices
learningObjectives: Solve equations of the form a^x = b by writing both sides with the same base
Equate indices when the bases are equal
Solve equations in which the unknown is the base, such as x^(3/2) = 8
Check solutions by substitution

keyTerms.definition: An equation in which the unknown appears in an index (for example 2^x = 32).
If a^m = a^n (with a > 0, a not 1) then m = n.

concepts.definition: Key principle: if two powers with the same base are equal, then their indices are equal. That is, if a^m = a^n then m = n (for a positive and not equal to 1).
explanation: Suppose 2^x = 32. Ask: what power of 2 is 32? Writing 32 = 2^5 gives 2^x = 2^5. Both sides now have the same base, so the indices must be equal: x = 5. This is the whole method: express both sides as powers of the same base, then equate indices.

To use the method you must be able to rewrite numbers as powers of small bases. Powers of 2: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Powers of 3: 3, 9, 27, 81, 243. Powers of 5: 5, 25, 125, 625. Powers of 10: 10, 100, 1 000. Fractions are handled with negative indices: 1/8 = 2^-3 and 1/25 = 5^-2.

When the bases are different but related, convert to a common base. For 4^x = 8, note 4 = 2^2 and 8 = 2^3. So (2^2)^x = 2^3, giving 2^(2x) = 2^3, therefore 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. For 9^x = 27, note 9 = 3^2 and 27 = 3^3, so 3^(2x) = 3^3 and x = 3/2.
When the index is an expression such as x + 1 or 2x - 1, equate the indices to form an ordinary linear equation and solve it. For 3^(x+1) = 81: 81 = 3^4, so x + 1 = 4 and x = 3.

A second type has the unknown as the base, such as x^(3/2) = 8. Here raise both sides to the reciprocal of the index: (x^(3/2))^(2/3) = 8^(2/3). The left side becomes x^1 = x. The right side is 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 4. So x = 4.
Always check your answer by substituting back. For x = 4 in x^(3/2): 4^(3/2) = (square root of 4)^3 = 2^3 = 8, correct.

illustrations.caption: Common bases cheat-sheet
illustrations.description: Rewrite numbers as powers of a small base before solving.

workedExamples.problem: Solve x^(3/2) = 8.
steps: Raise both sides to the power 2/3 (the reciprocal of 3/2).
The cube root of 8 is 2, and 2^2 = 4.

realWorldApplications: Finance: how many years does it take money to reach a target? For doubling at a fixed rate you solve equations like 2^x = 16.
Biology: how many hours until bacteria reach a target count when the population doubles each hour.
Computing: how many bits are needed to represent a number of values (2^n = number of values).
Physics and chemistry: radioactive decay and half-life reasoning (how many half-lives until only 1/32 remains: (1/2)^n = 1/32 gives n = 5).
commonMistakes: Trying to solve 2^x = 32 by dividing 32 by 2. Instead write 32 as 2^5.
Equating indices when the bases are different.
Forgetting to convert 1/25 into 5^-2 and getting stuck.
Forgetting to multiply the index when the base itself is a power: 4^x = (2^2)^x = 2^(2x), not 2^(x+2).
Not checking the answer.
summary: Make the bases the same, then equate the indices.
Rewrite fractions with negative indices.
For x^(m/n) = k, raise both sides to the power n/m.
Check by substitution.

concepts.title: Standard form (scientific notation)
learningObjectives: Write large and small numbers in standard form A x 10^n
Convert numbers in standard form back to ordinary numbers
Multiply and divide numbers in standard form
Add and subtract numbers in standard form
Interpret standard form in real measurements
prerequisiteNotes: Powers of ten and negative indices (1.1, 1.3)

keyTerms.definition: A number written as A x 10^n where 1 <= A < 10 and n is an integer (positive, negative or zero).
The meaningful digits of a number, counted from the first non-zero digit.

concepts.definition: A number is in standard form when it is written as A x 10^n, where A is at least 1 but less than 10, and n is a whole number (an integer). For example 45 000 = 4.5 x 10^4 and 0.00032 = 3.2 x 10^-4.
explanation: Very large and very small numbers are awkward. The distance from the Earth to the Sun is about 150 000 000 000 m, and the mass of a hydrogen atom is about 0.00000000000000000000000000167 kg. Standard form removes the long strings of zeros. The distance becomes 1.5 x 10^11 m and the mass 1.67 x 10^-27 kg.

The two conditions are strict. The first part A must lie from 1 up to (but not including) 10, so it has exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point. 4.5 is fine, but 45 x 10^3 and 0.45 x 10^5 are not in standard form. The second part is a power of ten with an integer index.

To convert a large number: place the decimal point after the first non-zero digit, count how many places the point moved to the left, and that count is the positive index. 45 000: the point (after the last zero) moves 4 places left to get 4.5, so 4.5 x 10^4.

To convert a small number: the point moves to the right, so the index is negative. 0.00032: move the point 4 places right to get 3.2, so 3.2 x 10^-4. A handy check: numbers less than 1 always have a negative index; numbers 10 or more have a positive index; numbers from 1 up to 10 have index 0.

To convert back to an ordinary number, move the decimal point the number of places shown by the index: right for a positive index, left for a negative index, filling with zeros as needed. 3.2 x 10^-3 = 0.0032 and 6.5 x 10^4 = 65 000.
Multiplication: multiply the A-parts and add the indices (Law 1). (3 x 10^4)(2 x 10^3) = 6 x 10^7. If the A-part of the answer is 10 or more, adjust: (6 x 10^5)(5 x 10^3) = 30 x 10^8 = 3 x 10^9.
Division: divide the A-parts and subtract the indices (Law 2). (8 x 10^6)/(2 x 10^2) = 4 x 10^4. If the A-part comes out below 1, adjust: (2 x 10^5)/(5 x 10^2) = 0.4 x 10^3 = 4 x 10^2.

Addition and subtraction: first make the powers of ten the same, then add or subtract the A-parts. 3.5 x 10^3 + 4 x 10^2 = 3.5 x 10^3 + 0.4 x 10^3 = 3.9 x 10^3. You cannot add the indices here; that is only for multiplication.

rows: Speed of light in a vacuum

illustrations.caption: Moving the decimal point
illustrations.description: Show 45 000 becoming 4.5 with an arrow of 4 jumps left (index +4), and 0.00032 becoming 3.2 with 4 jumps right (index -4).

workedExamples.problem: Write in standard form (a) 560 000 (b) 0.0075 (c) 38.4 x 10^3.
steps: (a) Move the point 5 places left: 5.6, so 5.6 x 10^5.
(b) Move the point 3 places right: 7.5, so 7.5 x 10^-3.

workedExamples.problem: Calculate (a) (2.5 x 10^3) x (4 x 10^5) (b) (9 x 10^7) / (3 x 10^-2), giving answers in standard form.
Light takes about 500 seconds to travel from the Sun to the Earth at 3 x 10^8 m/s. Find the distance in standard form.

realWorldApplications: Astronomy: distances between planets, stars and galaxies.
Physics and chemistry: atomic masses and sizes, Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23 particles per mole).
Calculators: the screen shows '3E8' or '3 x10^8' for 3 x 10^8.
Engineering and medicine: dosage and measurement of tiny quantities such as micrograms.
Data: file sizes and internet traffic are written in standard form to compare very large values.
commonMistakes: Leaving A outside the range 1 to 10, such as 45 x 10^3 or 0.45 x 10^5.
Using a positive index for numbers smaller than 1.
Adding the indices when adding numbers (only multiplication adds indices).
Forgetting to adjust when the A-part of a product reaches 10 or more.
Counting the decimal places wrongly: count carefully.
summary: Standard form: A x 10^n with 1 <= A < 10 and n an integer.
Large numbers have positive n, small numbers have negative n.
Multiply: multiply A-parts, add indices. Divide: divide A-parts, subtract indices.
To add or subtract, first make the powers of ten equal.

concepts.title: Meaning of a logarithm: connecting logs and indices
learningObjectives: Explain that a logarithm is a power (an index)
Convert between index form and logarithmic form
Evaluate simple logarithms in any base by inspection
Know that log of a number means log to base 10 in this course

keyTerms.definition: The logarithm of a number N to base a is the index x such that a^x = N.
The number being raised to a power (here a in a^x = N).
A logarithm to base 10. Written log N or log10 N.

concepts.definition: If a^x = N (with a > 0 and a not equal to 1), then x is called the logarithm of N to base a, written log_a N = x. The two statements a^x = N and log_a N = x say exactly the same thing in two different forms. When no base is shown, log N means log to base 10.
explanation: Logarithm is just another word for 'power' or 'index'. Look at 10^3 = 1 000. We say '3 is the logarithm of 1 000 to base 10', and write log 1 000 = 3. It answers the question: to what power must the base be raised to get this number?

Think of it as a translation between two languages. Index form: 10^3 = 1 000. Logarithmic form: log10 1 000 = 3. The base stays the base, the index becomes the answer of the log, and the number stays the number. Other examples: 2^5 = 32 means log2 32 = 5; 3^4 = 81 means log3 81 = 4; 5^0 = 1 means log5 1 = 0.

In SS1 the most important base is 10, because our number system uses it. Log means base 10 unless stated. The key values: log 1 = 0 (because 10^0 = 1), log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1 000 = 3, log 10 000 = 4. For numbers less than 1: log 0.1 = -1, log 0.01 = -2, log 0.001 = -3, because 10^-1 = 0.1, 10^-2 = 0.01 and so on.

What about numbers that are not exact powers of 10, such as 450? Since 100 < 450 < 1 000, its logarithm lies between 2 and 3. The exact value, 2.6532 (to 4 decimal places), is read from tables or a calculator. So log of a number is always a whole number plus a decimal, which leads to the idea of characteristic and mantissa (next lesson).
Two facts to know: you cannot take the log of zero or a negative number, because no power of 10 gives zero or a negative result. And log of 1 is 0 in every base, since any base to the power 0 is 1.

To find a logarithm in any base, convert to index form and use your knowledge of indices. log2 8 = x means 2^x = 8, so x = 3. log5 25 = 2 since 5^2 = 25. log10 0.001 = -3 since 10^-3 = 0.001. log3 (1/9) = -2 since 3^-2 = 1/9. log4 2 = 1/2 since 4^(1/2) = 2.

illustrations.caption: Translating between forms
illustrations.description: Index form and logarithmic form say the same thing.

illustrations.caption: Powers of ten and their logarithms
illustrations.description: Logs of powers of ten are whole numbers.

workedExamples.problem: Write in logarithmic form (a) 10^4 = 10 000 (b) 2^6 = 64 (c) 5^-2 = 1/25.
Find (a) log2 8 (b) log5 25 (c) log10 0.001 (d) log4 2.
steps: (a) Let log2 8 = x. Then 2^x = 8 = 2^3, so x = 3.

workedExamples.problem: Between which two consecutive whole numbers does log 450 lie?
steps: Find the powers of 10 on each side of 450: 100 = 10^2 and 1 000 = 10^3.
Since 100 < 450 < 1 000, log 450 lies between log 100 = 2 and log 1 000 = 3.

realWorldApplications: Earthquakes: the Richter scale is logarithmic, so each whole-number increase means about 10 times more ground motion.
Sound: decibels are logarithmic; 10 dB more is about 10 times the sound intensity.
Chemistry: pH = -log of hydrogen-ion concentration, which is how acidity is measured.
Finance and population growth: logs are used to find how long growth takes.
Before calculators: logarithm tables turned hard multiplications into easy additions.
commonMistakes: Reading log 100 as 10 rather than 2.
Mixing up which number is the base and which is the answer: in log2 8 = 3, the base is 2.
Trying to find the log of zero or a negative number.
Thinking log (a + b) equals log a + log b. It does not.
summary: A logarithm is an index: a^x = N is the same as log_a N = x.
log means base 10 unless stated.
Logs exist only for positive numbers.

concepts.title: Characteristic and mantissa; reading logarithm tables
learningObjectives: Split a logarithm into its characteristic and mantissa
Find the characteristic of the log of any number greater than 1 from standard form
Use 4-figure tables (or a calculator) to find the mantissa
Find the logarithm of a number greater than 1

keyTerms.definition: The whole-number part of a logarithm. For a number N greater than 1 it is one less than the number of digits before the decimal point; equivalently it is the index of 10 when N is written in standard form.
The decimal-fraction part of a logarithm (between 0 and 1), read from tables or a calculator. It depends only on the digits of the number, not on the position of the decimal point.

concepts.definition: Every logarithm can be written as log N = characteristic + mantissa. For a number greater than 1, the characteristic is the power of 10 in standard form (the number of digits before the decimal point, minus 1), and the mantissa is a decimal between 0 and 1.
explanation: Take a number such as 5 230. In standard form it is 5.23 x 10^3. Take logs of both sides using the multiplication idea (logs of products add): log 5 230 = log 5.23 + log 10^3 = log 5.23 + 3. Now log 5.23 = 0.7185 (found in tables) and log 10^3 = 3. So log 5 230 = 3.7185. The whole-number 3 is the characteristic; the decimal 0.7185 is the mantissa.

Finding the characteristic is easy: write the number in standard form and read the power of 10. 5.23 x 10^3 has characteristic 3. A quick rule for numbers greater than 1: count the digits before the decimal point and subtract 1. 5 230 has 4 digits, so the characteristic is 3. 62.3 has 2 digits before the point, so the characteristic is 1. 4.7 has 1 digit, so the characteristic is 0.

The mantissa depends only on the digits, not on where the decimal point is. The digits 5, 2, 3 always give the mantissa 0.7185. So log 5.23 = 0.7185, log 52.3 = 1.7185, log 523 = 2.7185, log 5 230 = 3.7185, and log 52 300 = 4.7185. The decimal part never changes. Only the whole-number part (characteristic) tells you the size of the number. This is because multiplying by 10 just adds 1 to the log.

To read the mantissa from 4-figure logarithm tables: ignore the decimal point and use the first two digits to choose the row, the third digit to choose the column, and (if there is a fourth digit) use the 'mean differences' columns on the right to add a small correction. For 5.23, row 52, column 3 gives 0.7185. If you use a scientific calculator, press log and type the number; the calculator gives characteristic and mantissa together. You should be able to do both, since examinations may require tables.
Some mantissas are worth remembering: log 2 = 0.3010, log 3 = 0.4771, log 5 = 0.6990, log 7 = 0.8451. From these, log 20 = 1.3010, log 200 = 2.3010, log 30 = 1.4771 and log 5 000 = 3.6990.

A reverse reasoning check: if log N = 4.8325, the characteristic is 4, so N has 5 digits before the decimal point (4 + 1 = 5), and the digits come from the mantissa 0.8325. Finding those digits is the job of antilogarithms (next lesson).

Looking ahead (not required for all SS1 syllabuses): numbers less than 1 have negative logs. For example log 0.045 = log 4.5 + log 10^-2 = 0.6532 - 2 = -1.3468. In tables this is written with a bar over the characteristic as 2-bar.6532, which keeps the mantissa positive.

illustrations.caption: The mantissa stays the same; only the characteristic changes
illustrations.description: Digits 5 2 3 give mantissa 0.7185 wherever the decimal point is.

workedExamples.problem: State the characteristic of (a) log 4 560 (b) log 62.3 (c) log 4.7.
steps: (a) 4 560 has 4 digits before the point, so the characteristic is 4 - 1 = 3.
(b) 62.3 has 2 digits before the point, so the characteristic is 1.
(c) 4.7 has 1 digit before the point, so the characteristic is 0.

workedExamples.problem: Given log 2.5 = 0.3979, write down log 25, log 250 and log 25 000.
steps: The mantissa stays 0.3979. Only the characteristic changes.

workedExamples.problem: Find log 47.8 using tables and write it as characteristic + mantissa.
steps: Characteristic: 47.8 has 2 digits before the point, so it is 1.
Mantissa for the digits 4 7 8: row 47, column 8 gives 0.6794.

realWorldApplications: Slide rules and log tables were the standard calculating tools for engineers and scientists for over 300 years before calculators.
Estimating the size of a number quickly: the characteristic tells you the number of digits.
Science: pH, decibels and magnitude scales all use logarithms whose whole-number part gives the order of magnitude.
Computing: logs describe how many digits or bits are needed to store a number.
commonMistakes: Using the number of digits (instead of digits minus 1) as the characteristic.
Changing the mantissa when the decimal point moves. It must stay the same.
Reading the wrong row or column in the tables, or forgetting the mean-difference correction.
Treating log 450 as 'about 450' instead of about 2.65.
summary: log N = characteristic + mantissa.
Characteristic (N > 1): digits before the decimal point minus 1, which equals the power of 10 in standard form.
Mantissa: from tables or calculator; same for all numbers with the same digits.
Moving the decimal point only changes the characteristic.

concepts.title: Antilogarithms: finding a number from its logarithm
learningObjectives: Explain an antilogarithm as the reverse of taking a logarithm
Use antilogarithm tables (or a calculator) to find a number from its log
Place the decimal point correctly using the characteristic

keyTerms.definition: The number whose logarithm is given. If log N = x then N = antilog x = 10^x.

concepts.definition: If log N = x, then N is called the antilogarithm of x, written N = antilog x = 10^x. Finding an antilog undoes finding a log.
explanation: Taking a log answers: 'what is the power of 10 for this number?' The antilog is the reverse: 'which number has this power of 10?' If log 1 000 = 3 then antilog 3 = 1 000. If log 5.23 = 0.7185 then antilog 0.7185 = 5.23.

Method with tables: (1) Write down the logarithm and separate the characteristic from the mantissa. (2) Look up the mantissa in the antilogarithm table, using the first two decimal digits to choose the row, the third digit for the column, and the fourth digit for the mean-difference correction. The table gives the digits of the number. (3) Use the characteristic to place the decimal point: the number has (characteristic + 1) digits before the decimal point.

Example: find antilog 2.7634. The characteristic is 2, so the number has 2 + 1 = 3 digits before the decimal point. The mantissa 0.7634 gives the digits 5800 (approximately 5.800), so the number is about 580. With 4-figure tables the answer is reliable to 3 significant figures: antilog 2.7634 is approximately 580.

Example: find antilog 3.2. Mantissa 0.2000 gives the digits 1.585, and the characteristic 3 means 4 digits before the decimal point, so the number is about 1 585. To 3 significant figures that is 1 580, so always state the accuracy you are working to. For exact powers like antilog 3 = 1 000 the mantissa is 0, whose antilog is 1.000.
Using a calculator: press the 10^x function (often shift + log) and type the logarithm. 10^2.7634 = 579.96, close to 580.
Check your answer using the characteristic: if the log has characteristic 2, the answer must lie between 100 and 1 000. If it does not, you have misplaced the decimal point.

illustrations.caption: From log back to number
illustrations.description: The mantissa gives the digits; the characteristic places the decimal point.

workedExamples.problem: Find the antilogarithm of (a) 1.5 (b) 2.8 (c) 0.9. Give 3 significant figures.
steps: (a) Characteristic 1 means 2 digits before the point. Mantissa 0.5 gives digits 3.162. Number = 31.6.
(b) Characteristic 2 means 3 digits before the point. Mantissa 0.8 gives 6.310. Number = 631.
(c) Characteristic 0 means 1 digit before the point. Mantissa 0.9 gives 7.943. Number = 7.94.

workedExamples.problem: Find the number whose logarithm is 1.7782.
steps: Characteristic 1 means 2 digits before the decimal point.
Mantissa 0.7782 is the log of 6 (log 6 = 0.7782), so the digits are 6.00.

workedExamples.problem: If log N = 3.3010, find N.
steps: Mantissa 0.3010 is log 2, so the digits are 2.00.
Characteristic 3 means 4 digits before the decimal point.

realWorldApplications: Finishing any log calculation: the last step always converts the answer back into an ordinary number.
Chemistry: pH = 3 means the hydrogen-ion concentration is antilog(-3) = 10^-3 mol/dm^3.
Seismology: converting a magnitude back into the size of the ground motion.
Sound engineering: converting decibel values back to intensity ratios.
commonMistakes: Misplacing the decimal point (forgetting to use characteristic + 1 digits before the point).
Using the log table instead of the antilog table for this step.
Rounding too early and losing accuracy.
Forgetting that a mantissa of 0 means the digits are 1.000.
summary: antilog x = 10^x, the reverse of log.
Mantissa gives the digits (from the antilog table); characteristic positions the decimal point.
Number of digits before the point = characteristic + 1.
Always sanity-check size with the characteristic.

concepts.title: Calculations using logarithms
learningObjectives: State the laws: log(ab) = log a + log b, log(a/b) = log a - log b, log(a^n) = n log a
Multiply and divide numbers using logarithms
Find powers and roots using logarithms
Set out log calculations neatly in a table
Apply logs to real calculations such as compound interest

keyTerms.definition: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a - log b; log(a^n) = n log a.
A neat table with columns Number and Logarithm, so the working can be followed and checked.

concepts.definition: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, division into subtraction, powers into multiplication and roots into division: log(ab) = log a + log b, log(a/b) = log a - log b, log(a^n) = n x log a, and log of the nth root of a = (1/n) log a.
explanation: These laws come straight from the index laws. Let a = 10^x and b = 10^y, so log a = x and log b = y. Then ab = 10^x x 10^y = 10^(x+y), so log(ab) = x + y = log a + log b. Similarly a/b = 10^(x-y), so log(a/b) = log a - log b. And a^n = (10^x)^n = 10^(nx), so log(a^n) = n log a. Roots are powers with fractional index, so log of the nth root of a = (1/n) log a.

This is why logs were so valuable before calculators: adding 4-digit numbers is far easier than multiplying large ones. The procedure is always the same. Step 1: write the calculation. Step 2: set out a table with the numbers and their logs (from tables). Step 3: add, subtract, or multiply/divide the logs as the calculation requires. Step 4: take the antilog of the result to get the answer.

Neat setting out is essential. Use two columns: 'Number' and 'Log'. Put a + sign or a - sign in front of each log to show whether it is added or subtracted, draw a line, and write the total underneath. Show the antilog step clearly. Examination markers give marks for method.
Accuracy: 4-figure tables give three significant figures reliably, so give the final answer to 3 significant figures. Do not round the logs too early; use all four decimal places from the table.
For powers, multiply the log by the index: log(1.8^4) = 4 x log 1.8 = 4 x 0.2553 = 1.0212. For roots, divide the log by the root: log(sqrt(500)) = (1/2) x log 500 = (1/2) x 2.6990 = 1.3495.
Always estimate first. 23.4 x 5.67 is roughly 20 x 6 = 120, so an answer near 133 is sensible, while 13.3 or 1 330 would signal a decimal-point error. Estimation catches most mistakes.
A final warning about the laws. There is no law for log(a + b) or log(a - b). log(10 + 100) is not log 10 + log 100. You must work out 10 + 100 = 110 first, then take its log.

illustrations.caption: Summary of how operations change under logs
illustrations.description: Each operation becomes a simpler one.

workedExamples.problem: Use logarithms to calculate 23.4 x 5.67.
steps: Antilog of 2.1228: characteristic 2 gives 3 digits before the point; mantissa 0.1228 gives 1.327. Number = 132.7.
To 3 s.f. the answer is 133. (Check by direct multiplication: 132.678, which agrees.)

workedExamples.problem: Use logarithms to calculate 845 / 3.6.
steps: Antilog of 2.3706 = 234.7 (3 digits before the point).

workedExamples.problem: Use logarithms to find (a) 1.8^4 (b) square root of 500.
steps: (a) log 1.8 = 0.2553. Multiply by 4: 4 x 0.2553 = 1.0212. Antilog of 1.0212 = 10.50 (2 digits before the point). So 1.8^4 is about 10.5. (Check: 1.8^4 = 10.4976.)
(b) log 500 = 2.6990. Divide by 2: 1.3495. Antilog of 1.3495 = 22.36, so the square root is 22.4 (3 s.f.).

workedExamples.problem: Calculate (6.28 x 14.5) / 3.2 using logs.

realWorldApplications: Compound interest: an amount P growing at rate r per year for n years becomes P(1 + r)^n. Logs make it easy to compute large powers, for example 50 000 at 8% for 6 years gives about 79 300 naira (3 s.f.).
Science: pH, decibel and magnitude calculations all combine logarithm laws.
Engineering and surveying: before calculators, long chains of multiplications were done with logs.
Population and growth models: logs convert growth into straight-line addition so that doubling times can be found.
Computing: the number of steps in efficient search algorithms is described using logarithms.
commonMistakes: Adding the numbers instead of their logs.
Subtracting in the wrong order when dividing (top log minus bottom log).
Forgetting to multiply or divide the log by n for powers and roots.
Misplacing the decimal point after taking the antilog (always estimate first).
Believing log(a + b) = log a + log b.
Rounding logs too early.
summary: Multiply: add logs. Divide: subtract logs.
Power n: multiply the log by n. Root n: divide the log by n.
Set out in a neat table and finish with antilog.
Estimate first to guard against decimal-point errors; give answers to 3 s.f.
There is no rule for the log of a sum or difference.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Formal Geometry: Triangles and Polygons
topics.overview: Moves from measuring and drawing to proving. You learn the angle sums of triangles and polygons, the four tests for congruent triangles, the properties of isosceles and equilateral triangles and parallelograms, the equal intercept theorem, and how to write proofs and solve riders.

concepts.title: Angle sum of a triangle (Theorem 1)
learningObjectives: Recall the angle facts needed for proofs: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles
State and prove that the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees
Use the theorem to find unknown angles, including problems that need algebra
prerequisiteNotes: Basic angle measurement and naming angles with three letters

keyTerms.definition: A mathematical fact that has been proved from earlier facts by logical argument.
Equal angles on opposite sides of a transversal between two parallel lines (the 'Z' shape).
Equal angles in matching positions at two parallel lines cut by a transversal (the 'F' shape).
A straight line that crosses two or more other lines.

concepts.definition: Theorem 1: The sum of the three interior angles of any triangle is 180 degrees (two right angles).
explanation: In JSS you may have found this by tearing the corners off a paper triangle and placing them side by side on a straight line. That is a fine experiment, but experiments only test particular triangles. Formal geometry proves the fact for EVERY triangle at once, using earlier facts and logical steps.

Facts we are allowed to use. (1) Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees. (2) Angles around a point add up to 360 degrees. (3) Vertically opposite angles are equal. (4) When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, alternate angles are equal, corresponding angles are equal, and co-interior (allied) angles add up to 180 degrees. Memorise these. Every proof in this chapter is built from them.

The proof. Let ABC be any triangle. Extend side BC to a point X, so that BCX is a straight line. Through C draw the line CP parallel to BA. Label the interior angles of the triangle a (at A), b (at B) and c (at C). Now CP is parallel to BA and AC is a transversal, so the angle between AC and CP equals angle a (alternate angles). Also CP is parallel to BA and BX is a transversal, so the angle between CP and CX equals angle b (corresponding angles). The three angles c, a and b now sit side by side along the straight line BX. Since angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees, a + b + c = 180 degrees. Because the triangle ABC was arbitrary, this holds for every triangle.

Consequences you will use constantly. A triangle cannot have two right angles or two obtuse angles (their sum would already reach 180 degrees). In a right-angled triangle the other two angles add up to 90 degrees. In an equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees. If two angles are known, the third is 180 degrees minus their sum.

When the angles are given as algebraic expressions, form an equation. For example, if the angles are x, 2x and 3x, then x + 2x + 3x = 180, so 6x = 180 and x = 30. The angles are 30, 60 and 90 degrees.
Always give a reason beside each step in a proof or a riders question, such as 'angle sum of a triangle' or 'alternate angles, CP parallel to BA'. Markers award marks for the reasons.

illustrations.caption: Proof of Theorem 1
illustrations.description: Triangle ABC with BC extended to X and CP drawn parallel to BA. Angles a, b and c are marked along the straight line BX.

illustrations.caption: Angle facts used in proofs
illustrations.description: Know each fact and its reason name.

rows: angles on a straight line = 180 degrees
co-interior angles add to 180 degrees (parallel lines)
angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees

workedExamples.problem: Find the missing angle in a triangle with angles 48 degrees and 75 degrees.
The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find them.
steps: The angles are 40, 60 and 80 degrees. Check: 40 + 60 + 80 = 180.

workedExamples.problem: In triangle ABC, angle A = (2x + 10) degrees, angle B = (3x - 20) degrees and angle C = x degrees. Find x and the three angles.
workedExamples.answer: x = 31 2/3 degrees; A = 73 1/3, B = 75, C = 31 2/3 degrees

realWorldApplications: Structural engineering: triangles are rigid, and engineers use angle sums to design roof trusses and bridge frames.
Surveying and navigation: triangulation finds an unknown angle when two angles are measured.
Carpentry and tailoring: cutting pieces to fit a triangular corner or panel.
Computer graphics: every 3D surface is built from triangles whose angles must add up correctly.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the 180 and using 360 (that is for quadrilaterals).
Arithmetic slips when subtracting from 180.
Writing a proof without reasons.
Assuming a triangle is isosceles or right-angled just because the diagram looks that way. Only use what is stated.
summary: Angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
Proof: extend a side, draw a parallel line, use alternate and corresponding angles.
Third angle = 180 minus the sum of the other two.
Always state a reason.

concepts.title: Exterior angle of a triangle (Theorem 2)
learningObjectives: Define an exterior angle and its adjacent and opposite interior angles
State and prove that an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles
Use the theorem to solve problems with numbers and algebra

keyTerms.definition: The angle formed outside a triangle when one side is extended (produced).
The two interior angles that are NOT next to the chosen exterior angle.
Extend a line beyond one end.

concepts.definition: Theorem 2: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
explanation: Take triangle ABC and produce side BC to a point X. The angle ACX outside the triangle is an exterior angle at C. The interior angle at C (angle ACB) is its neighbour. The other two interior angles, at A and at B, are the 'interior opposite' angles.

Proof. Let the interior angles at A, B and C be a, b and c. Angles on a straight line BCX add to 180 degrees, so the exterior angle ACX = 180 - c. By the angle sum of a triangle, a + b + c = 180, so a + b = 180 - c. Therefore the exterior angle ACX = a + b. This completes the proof.

Why is the theorem useful? It saves a step. Instead of finding the third interior angle and subtracting from 180, you can add the two opposite interior angles directly. It also immediately tells you that the exterior angle is bigger than either of the opposite interior angles.

Using it in algebra: if the exterior angle is 120 degrees and the interior opposite angles are x and 2x, then x + 2x = 120, so x = 40. The angles are 40 and 80 degrees, and the interior angle next to the exterior angle is 180 - 120 = 60 degrees. Check: 40 + 80 + 60 = 180.
Make sure you pick the right pair. The two angles to add are the ones away from the exterior angle, not the one touching it.

illustrations.caption: Exterior angle
illustrations.description: Triangle ABC, side BC produced to X, exterior angle ACX equal to angle A plus angle B.

illustrations.caption: Which angles to add
illustrations.description: For the exterior angle at C.

rows: angle ACB (add to exterior to make 180)
angle A and angle B (add to get the exterior angle)

workedExamples.problem: An exterior angle of a triangle is 115 degrees. One interior opposite angle is 65 degrees. Find the other interior opposite angle.
steps: Exterior = sum of the opposite interior angles.

workedExamples.problem: In triangle ABC, BC is produced to D. Angle A = 50 degrees and angle B = 60 degrees. Find angle ACD and angle ACB.
steps: Angle ACD = A + B = 110 degrees (exterior angle theorem).
Angle ACB = 180 - 110 = 70 degrees (angles on a straight line). Check: 50 + 60 + 70 = 180.

workedExamples.problem: The exterior angle at C is (5x - 10) degrees and the interior opposite angles are (2x + 5) degrees and (x + 15) degrees. Find x.

realWorldApplications: Roof and ramp design: finding the outside angle at a joint.
Navigation: when a ship changes direction, the turn angle is an exterior angle.
Machine and bridge frames: checking angles at joints.
Photography and architecture: sight-line angles at a corner.
commonMistakes: Adding the adjacent interior angle instead of the two opposite angles.
Forgetting that the exterior angle plus its adjacent interior angle is 180.
Not producing the side before naming the exterior angle.
summary: Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.
Exterior angle + adjacent interior angle = 180.
Exterior angle is greater than each opposite interior angle.

concepts.title: Interior angles of a polygon (Theorem 3)
learningObjectives: Name polygons and distinguish convex from re-entrant polygons
State and prove that the angle sum of an n-sided convex polygon is (2n - 4) right angles
Find interior angles of regular and irregular polygons and the number of sides from the angle sum

keyTerms.definition: A closed shape bounded by straight sides.
A polygon in which every interior angle is less than 180 degrees (no corner points inwards).
A polygon with at least one interior angle greater than 180 degrees.
A polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal.

concepts.definition: Theorem 3: The sum of the interior angles of any convex polygon with n sides is (2n - 4) right angles, that is (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
explanation: A polygon with 3 sides is a triangle, 4 a quadrilateral, 5 a pentagon, 6 a hexagon, 7 a heptagon, 8 an octagon, 9 a nonagon, 10 a decagon and 12 a dodecagon. A convex polygon has no corner pointing inwards; every straight line joining two points inside it stays inside it.

Proof. Take a convex polygon ABCDE... with n sides. Choose a point O inside it and join O to every vertex. This splits the polygon into n triangles. Each triangle has angle sum 2 right angles, so the n triangles have a total of 2n right angles. But this total includes the angles around O, which add up to 4 right angles and are not part of the polygon's interior angles. So the sum of the interior angles = 2n right angles - 4 right angles = (2n - 4) right angles. Since a right angle is 90 degrees, the sum is (2n - 4) x 90 = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
Check with known shapes. For a triangle n = 3: (6 - 4) = 2 right angles = 180 degrees. For a quadrilateral n = 4: 4 right angles = 360 degrees. For a pentagon n = 5: 6 right angles = 540 degrees.
For a REGULAR polygon all n interior angles are equal, so each interior angle = (2n - 4) x 90 / n degrees. For a regular hexagon: (12 - 4) x 90 / 6 = 8 x 90 / 6 = 120 degrees.

To find the number of sides from the angle sum, set (n - 2) x 180 equal to the given sum. If the sum is 1 440 degrees, n - 2 = 8, so n = 10. A sum that is not a multiple of 180 means the question has an error or the polygon is not what you think.
For irregular polygons, subtract the known angles from the total to find the missing one, or form an equation if the angles are algebraic.

illustrations.caption: Angle sum and regular-polygon angle
illustrations.description: Angle sum = (n - 2) x 180. Each interior angle of a regular polygon = sum / n.

illustrations.caption: Splitting a polygon into triangles
illustrations.description: A pentagon with an interior point joined to each vertex forming five triangles.

workedExamples.problem: Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon.
Four angles of a pentagon are 100, 110, 120 and 95 degrees. Find the fifth.

Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.

realWorldApplications: Floor tiling and paving: only polygons whose angles fit around a point (such as hexagons) tile a surface neatly.
Architecture and design: stadiums, nuts and bolts (hexagons) and stop signs (octagons).
Computer graphics and CAD drawings.
Honeycombs in nature use regular hexagons.
commonMistakes: Using n x 180 instead of (n - 2) x 180.
Forgetting to divide by n for a regular polygon.
Applying the formula to a re-entrant polygon.
Mixing up the sum of angles (grows with n) with a single angle.
summary: Angle sum = (2n - 4) right angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
Regular polygon: each interior angle = (n - 2) x 180 / n.
To find n, solve (n - 2) x 180 = sum.

concepts.title: Exterior angles of a polygon (Theorem 4)
learningObjectives: Define an exterior angle of a polygon
State that the exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to 4 right angles (360 degrees)
Use exterior angles to find the number of sides and the angles of regular polygons

keyTerms.definition: The angle between one side of the polygon and the extension of the adjacent side, measured outside the polygon.

concepts.definition: Theorem 4: The sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon (one at each vertex) is 4 right angles, that is 360 degrees.
explanation: Walk once around a convex polygon, turning at every corner. At each corner you turn through the exterior angle. After the last corner you face your starting direction again, having turned through a complete rotation of 360 degrees. That is the idea behind the theorem.

Formal proof. At each vertex the interior angle and the exterior angle lie on a straight line, so interior + exterior = 180 degrees. For n vertices the sum of all (interior + exterior) angles = 180n. The interior angles add to (n - 2) x 180 = 180n - 360 (Theorem 3). So the exterior angles add to 180n - (180n - 360) = 360 degrees.
Remarkably the answer does not depend on n. A triangle, a square and a 100-sided polygon all have exterior angles that sum to 360 degrees.

For a regular polygon with n sides all exterior angles are equal, so each exterior angle = 360 / n degrees. And each interior angle = 180 - 360/n degrees. For a regular hexagon: exterior = 60 degrees, interior = 120 degrees.

This gives the fastest way to find the number of sides of a regular polygon: n = 360 / exterior angle. If each exterior angle is 40 degrees, then n = 9. If each interior angle is 150 degrees, the exterior angle is 30 degrees, so n = 12.

illustrations.caption: Walking round a polygon
illustrations.description: Arrows show turning through each exterior angle; the turns add up to a full circle.

workedExamples.problem: Find each exterior and interior angle of a regular pentagon.
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 40 degrees. How many sides has it?
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 156 degrees. Find the number of sides.
Four exterior angles of a pentagon are 80, 70, 90 and 60 degrees. Find the fifth.

realWorldApplications: Robot and vehicle turning: the total turning around a closed path is 360 degrees.
Drawing regular shapes in programming (turtle graphics): turn by 360/n at each corner.
Road design and surveying closed traverses.
Garden and track layouts.
commonMistakes: Using the interior-angle sum formula by mistake.
Giving interior instead of exterior angle (or the reverse).
Believing the exterior-angle sum grows with n.
summary: Exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360 degrees.
Regular polygon: exterior = 360/n; interior = 180 - 360/n.
Number of sides n = 360 / exterior angle.

concepts.title: Congruent triangles and the four conditions
learningObjectives: Define congruent triangles and use the symbol
State the four conditions for congruence: SAS, ASA/AAS, SSS and RHS
Choose the correct condition and write a congruence statement with matching vertices
Use congruence to deduce unknown sides and angles

keyTerms.definition: Exactly the same shape and size. One figure can be placed exactly on top of the other (turned over if necessary).
The angle between two given sides.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
Sides or angles that match each other in congruent figures.

concepts.definition: Two triangles are congruent if they satisfy any one of these: (1) SAS two sides and the included angle equal; (2) ASA or AAS two angles and a corresponding side equal; (3) SSS three sides equal; (4) RHS a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal.
explanation: If two triangles are congruent, every pair of matching sides is equal and every pair of matching angles is equal. We write ABC congruent to PQR with the symbol, meaning A matches P, B matches Q and C matches R. The ORDER of letters matters: it tells which vertices correspond.
Condition 1, SAS: two sides and the ANGLE BETWEEN THEM. If |AB| = |PQ|, |AC| = |PR| and the angle at A equals the angle at P, the triangles are congruent. The angle must be the included one.

Condition 2, ASA or AAS: two angles and a side that corresponds. Since the angles of a triangle add up to 180, knowing two angles fixes the third, so it does not matter whether the equal side is between the angles (ASA) or not (AAS), as long as it is in the corresponding position.
Condition 3, SSS: all three sides equal. The three side lengths fix the shape of a triangle completely.

Condition 4, RHS: both triangles have a right angle, equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides. This is a special case of the 'two sides and a non-included angle' idea that works only because the angle is 90 degrees.

What does NOT work. AAA (three equal angles) only guarantees the same shape (similar triangles), not the same size. SSA (two sides and an angle that is NOT between them) can give two different triangles, so it is not a test, except in the RHS case.

A good habit: write the equal parts in matching order, mark them on the diagram, state the condition, then write the congruence statement. For example: |AB| = |PQ| (given); |AC| = |PR| (given); angle A = angle P (given); so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR (SAS).

illustrations.caption: The four congruence tests
illustrations.description: Each needs three matching parts, but the right three.

rows: two sides and the angle between them
angle must be between the sides
two angles and one corresponding side
right angle, hypotenuse, one other side

illustrations.caption: The four tests
illustrations.description: Four small paired-triangle sketches with equal parts marked.

Angle B is the angle between AB and BC, and angle Q is between PQ and QR, so the equal angle is included.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR (SAS).

Equal side BC is opposite angle A and equal side YZ is opposite angle X, so the sides correspond.
Two angles and a corresponding side are equal.

steps: Equal angles show the triangles have the same shape.
No side lengths are given, so size may differ (for example a large and a small triangle).

realWorldApplications: Construction and manufacturing: identical parts (roof trusses, window frames) must be congruent.
Surveying: congruent triangles let a surveyor measure an inaccessible distance, such as across a river.
Design and tiling: repeated congruent tiles.
Proofs in geometry: showing two sides or angles are equal by showing the triangles containing them are congruent.
commonMistakes: Using AAA or SSA as a test.
Writing the congruence statement with the wrong order of letters.
Using SAS when the angle is not between the two sides.
Assuming parts are equal because they look equal.
summary: Congruent triangles are identical in shape and size.
Tests: SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, RHS.
AAA and SSA are not valid tests (except RHS).
Write corresponding vertices in matching order.

concepts.title: Isosceles and equilateral triangles (Theorem 5)
learningObjectives: Define isosceles and equilateral triangles
Prove that base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal
Use the converse, and the angle properties of equilateral triangles
Solve numerical and algebraic problems on isosceles and equilateral triangles

keyTerms.definition: A triangle with two equal sides. The angles opposite the equal sides are the base angles.
A triangle with all three sides equal.
The vertex between the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle.
The reverse of a statement: if the base angles are equal, then the opposite sides are equal.

concepts.definition: Theorem 5: The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal. Converse: if two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite them are equal. An equilateral triangle has all angles equal to 60 degrees.
explanation: Let triangle ABC have |AB| = |AC|. Then angles B and C are the base angles, opposite the equal sides. We want to show angle B = angle C.

Proof. Draw the bisector of angle A, meeting BC at D, so angle BAD = angle CAD. In triangles ABD and ACD: |AB| = |AC| (given); angle BAD = angle CAD (AD bisects angle A); AD is common to both. So triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD (SAS). Matching angles are equal, so angle B = angle C. Because the triangles are congruent, |BD| = |DC| and angle ADB = angle ADC. These two angles lie on a straight line so each is 90 degrees. So the bisector of the apex angle also bisects the base at right angles.

Finding angles: if the apex angle is 40 degrees, the base angles share the remaining 140 degrees, so each is 70. If a base angle is 50 degrees, the other base angle is also 50, and the apex is 180 - 100 = 80 degrees. Notice that you only need one angle to find the other two.

The converse. If two angles of a triangle are equal then the sides opposite them are equal. So a triangle with angles 50, 50 and 80 is isosceles, and the sides opposite the 50-degree angles are equal.

Equilateral triangles. All three sides are equal, so every pair is isosceles, hence all three angles are equal. Each angle is 180/3 = 60 degrees. Conversely, a triangle with all angles equal to 60 degrees is equilateral.
Tip for problems: when you see 'isosceles' or 'equal sides', mark the equal sides, identify the angles opposite them and mark those equal. Then use the angle sum or exterior angle theorem.

illustrations.caption: Isosceles triangle
illustrations.description: Triangle ABC with AB = AC, bisector AD meeting BC at D, tick marks on equal sides and arcs on equal base angles.

illustrations.caption: Triangle types by sides and angles

steps: In triangles ABD and ACD: |AB| = |AC| (given); |BD| = |DC| (given); AD is common.
These angles lie on a straight line, so each is 90 degrees: AD is perpendicular to BC.

realWorldApplications: Architecture: gable roofs and A-frames are isosceles triangles, so the beams meet the walls at equal angles.
Design and logos: flags, road signs (triangular warning signs are equilateral).
Engineering: truss designs rely on isosceles and equilateral triangles for balance.
Navigation: the line from the apex to the midpoint of the base is a line of symmetry.
commonMistakes: Assuming the unequal angle is a base angle.
Forgetting that the base angles are opposite the EQUAL sides.
Using 60 degrees for any isosceles triangle (only for equilateral).
Skipping the reason (base angles of an isosceles triangle).
summary: Isosceles triangle: base angles equal; converse also true.
Equilateral triangle: all sides equal, all angles 60 degrees.
The apex bisector of an isosceles triangle meets the base at 90 degrees and bisects it.

concepts.title: Parallelograms and related quadrilaterals (Theorems 6 and 7)
learningObjectives: Define a parallelogram and prove that opposite sides and opposite angles are equal (Theorem 6)
Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other (Theorem 7)
List the properties of the rectangle, rhombus, square, trapezium and kite
Apply the properties to find unknown lengths and angles

keyTerms.definition: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
A line joining two non-adjacent vertices.
Divide into two equal parts.
A parallelogram with all four sides equal.
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.

concepts.definition: Theorem 6: In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal and the opposite angles are equal. Theorem 7: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect one another.
explanation: Let ABCD be a parallelogram, so AB is parallel to DC and AD is parallel to BC. Draw the diagonal AC. It splits the parallelogram into triangles ABC and CDA.

Proof of Theorem 6. In triangles ABC and CDA: angle BAC = angle DCA (alternate angles, AB parallel to DC); angle BCA = angle DAC (alternate angles, AD parallel to BC); AC is common. So the triangles are congruent (ASA). Hence |AB| = |CD| and |BC| = |DA|, so opposite sides are equal. Also angle B = angle D (matching angles of congruent triangles). Adding the equal pairs of angles, angle A = angle BAC + angle CAD = angle DCA + angle ACB = angle C, so opposite angles are equal too.

Proof of Theorem 7. Let the diagonals AC and BD meet at O. In triangles AOB and COD: angle OAB = angle OCD (alternate angles, AB parallel to DC); angle OBA = angle ODC (alternate angles); |AB| = |CD| (Theorem 6). So the triangles are congruent (ASA). Hence |AO| = |OC| and |BO| = |OD|. Each diagonal is cut in half by the other.

Useful extras. Adjacent angles (angles next to each other along a side) of a parallelogram add up to 180 degrees (co-interior angles). Each diagonal splits a parallelogram into two congruent triangles, so the diagonal bisects the area.

Special quadrilaterals. Rectangle: a parallelogram with four right angles; its diagonals are equal. Rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides; its diagonals bisect at right angles and bisect the angles of the rhombus. Square: both a rectangle and a rhombus (four equal sides and four right angles). Trapezium: exactly one pair of parallel sides. Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides; its diagonals meet at right angles.

Converses are also true and useful for proofs. A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its opposite sides are equal, or if its opposite angles are equal, or if its diagonals bisect each other, or if one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel.

realWorldApplications: Machines and linkages: parallelogram linkages (scissor lifts, car jacks, folding gates, tool boxes) keep one part parallel to another.
Architecture and tiling: floor tiles, bricks and windows use these shapes.
Engineering: rhombus-shaped scissor jacks use the equal-sides property.
Cutting and sewing: rectangular and parallelogram panels.
commonMistakes: Saying the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal (only true for a rectangle).
Saying all parallelograms have perpendicular diagonals (only rhombus and square).
Confusing adjacent angles (add to 180) with opposite angles (equal).
Calling a trapezium a parallelogram.
summary: Parallelogram: opposite sides equal and parallel; opposite angles equal; adjacent angles add to 180; diagonals bisect each other.
Rectangle: equal diagonals. Rhombus: perpendicular diagonals. Square: both.
Trapezium: one pair of parallel sides.

concepts.title: Equal intercept theorem (Theorem 8)
learningObjectives: State the equal intercept theorem
Use it to find unknown lengths on transversals
Use it to divide a line into equal parts
Recognise the midpoint property as a consequence

keyTerms.definition: The segment of a transversal that lies between two parallel lines.
A straight line cutting a set of parallel lines.

concepts.definition: Theorem 8: If three or more parallel lines cut off equal intercepts on one transversal, then they cut off equal intercepts on any other transversal.
explanation: Picture three parallel lines like the rungs of a ladder tilted on its side. A transversal crosses them at A, B and C. Suppose |AB| = |BC|. A second transversal crosses the same lines at X, Y and Z. The theorem says |XY| = |YZ|. Equal spacing on one line forces equal spacing on any other.

Proof. From X draw a line parallel to the first transversal ABC, meeting the second parallel line at P. From Y draw a line parallel to ABC meeting the third parallel line at Q. Now XPBA is a parallelogram, so |XP| = |AB|. Similarly YQCB is a parallelogram so |YQ| = |BC|. Since |AB| = |BC|, |XP| = |YQ|. In triangles XPY and YQZ: |XP| = |YQ|; angle PXY = angle QYZ (corresponding angles, XP parallel to YQ); angle XPY = angle YQZ (corresponding angles, since XP is parallel to YQ and PY is parallel to QZ, both lying along parallel lines). So the triangles are congruent (AAS) and |XY| = |YZ|.
Practical use 1: finding lengths. If |AB| = |BC| = 4 cm and |XY| = 3.5 cm, then |YZ| = 3.5 cm.

Practical use 2: dividing a line into equal parts without measuring. To divide a line AB into 5 equal parts, draw any line AC at an angle, mark off five equal steps along it with compasses, join the last mark to B, and draw lines parallel to this through the other four marks. They cut AB into five equal parts.

Consequence: the midpoint theorem. In a triangle, a line drawn through the midpoint of one side parallel to a second side bisects the third side. In a trapezium, a line through the midpoint of one non-parallel side, parallel to the bases, bisects the other non-parallel side.

Warning: the equal-intercept theorem requires the lines to be parallel and to cut off EQUAL intercepts on the first transversal. If the intercepts are not equal, you cannot say the second set is equal.

steps: Equal intercepts on one transversal give equal intercepts on the other, so |YZ| = |XY| = 3.5 cm.

steps: The line DE is parallel to BC through the midpoint of AB.
By the consequence of the theorem, E is the midpoint of AC.

Mark three equal steps along the ray with compasses.
Join the last mark to the other end of the 9 cm line.

realWorldApplications: Surveying and mapping: dividing plots of land into equal strips.
Technical drawing: splitting a line into equal parts without a ruler.
Carpentry: equally spacing slats, steps or shelves along a sloping side.
Art and architecture: equal divisions in perspective drawings.
commonMistakes: Using the theorem when the lines are not parallel.
Assuming equal intercepts when only one intercept is known to be equal.
Mixing up the transversals and measuring on the wrong line.
summary: Parallel lines with equal intercepts on one transversal give equal intercepts on every transversal.
A line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.
Used to divide lines into equal parts.

concepts.title: Writing proofs and solving riders
learningObjectives: Set out a theorem proof with Given, To prove, Construction and Proof
Choose suitable reasons and theorems for each step
Solve riders (applications of theorems) with clear logic
Avoid common errors in geometrical reasoning
prerequisiteNotes: All theorems in this chapter (2.1 to 2.8)

keyTerms.definition: A problem that asks you to prove a result by using the theorems you already know.
The facts stated in the question.
The result you must show.
Extra lines you draw to help the proof.

concepts.definition: A geometrical proof is a chain of statements, each justified by a given fact or an already proved theorem, leading from what is given to what is to be proved.
explanation: Every proof has four parts. (1) Given: write down what is known, in terms of the diagram. (2) To prove: write the result you want, using the same letters. (3) Construction: describe any extra lines. (4) Proof: a numbered list of statements, each with a reason.

Typical reasons to quote: angle sum of a triangle; exterior angle of a triangle; angles on a straight line; angles at a point; vertically opposite angles; alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles (parallel lines); base angles of an isosceles triangle; congruent triangles (SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, RHS); opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram; diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other; equal intercept theorem.

Strategy for riders. (a) Read carefully and mark everything on a neat diagram (equal sides with tick marks, equal angles with arcs). (b) Look at what you are asked to prove. Equal sides or angles often come from congruent triangles; angle sums from the angle sum or exterior angle theorems. (c) Work backwards: what would be enough to prove the result? (d) Write the proof forwards with a reason on every line. (e) End with the statement of the result.

Example: prove that the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles. Let ABCD be a rhombus with diagonals meeting at O. Given: |AB| = |BC| = |CD| = |DA|. A rhombus is a parallelogram, so |AO| = |OC| (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other). In triangles AOB and COB: |AB| = |CB| (given); |AO| = |CO| (shown); OB is common. So they are congruent (SSS), hence angle AOB = angle COB. These angles lie on a straight line AOC, so each is 90 degrees.

Example using an exterior angle: in triangle ABC with BC produced to D, prove that angle ACD is greater than angle A. Proof: angle ACD = angle A + angle B (exterior angle of a triangle). Angle B is positive, so angle ACD is greater than angle A.

Common errors: assuming something because it looks true in the drawing; using a theorem without its conditions (for example 'alternate angles' when the lines are not given parallel); skipping reasons; proving the converse instead of the statement.

illustrations.description: Use this layout in tests and examinations.
