State the seven fundamental quantities with their SI units and symbols
Name instruments used to measure the common base quantities
Explain that all other quantities are built from the fundamental ones

keyTerms.definition: A quantity that is defined independently and cannot be written in terms of other quantities.
The SI unit of a fundamental quantity.
The SI unit of length.
The SI unit of mass.
The SI unit of time.

concepts.definition: Fundamental quantities are the basic quantities from which all others are derived. The SI has seven: length (metre), mass (kilogram), time (second), electric current (ampere), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin), amount of substance (mole) and luminous intensity (candela).
explanation: Imagine building a language from a small alphabet. In the same way, physics builds all measurements from a small set of basic quantities. These are called fundamental or base quantities. There are seven of them in the SI. Every other quantity (speed, force, pressure, power, ...) is a combination of these seven and is called a derived quantity.

The seven. (1) Length, unit metre (m). (2) Mass, unit kilogram (kg). (3) Time, unit second (s). (4) Electric current, unit ampere (A). (5) Thermodynamic temperature, unit kelvin (K). (6) Amount of substance, unit mole (mol). (7) Luminous intensity, unit candela (cd). At SS1 level, length, mass and time are used the most, with temperature and current appearing later in heat and electricity.

What the units mean (in simple terms). The metre is a standard length; the original idea was a ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole, but today it is defined using the speed of light so that it is exactly the same everywhere. The kilogram is a standard mass, now defined through a fundamental constant of nature (Planck's constant) rather than by a metal cylinder. The second is defined by the very regular vibrations of atoms of caesium-133, which is why atomic clocks are extremely accurate. The kelvin measures temperature from absolute zero. The ampere measures electric current. The mole counts amount of substance in a very large fixed number of particles (6.02 × 10^23). The candela measures how bright a light source is in a given direction.

Instruments. Length: metre rule, measuring tape, vernier calipers, micrometer screw gauge. Mass: beam balance, electronic balance. Time: stop clock, stopwatch, ticker-tape timer. Temperature: thermometer. Current: ammeter. Amount of substance: counted indirectly using mass and the mole. Luminous intensity: photometer.

Kelvin and Celsius. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero (0 K), the lowest possible temperature. A change of 1 K equals a change of 1 degree Celsius, so T(K) = T(°C) + 273 (approximately). Water freezes at 273 K (0 °C) and boils at 373 K (100 °C).

Not every well-known unit is a base unit. The newton (force), joule (energy), watt (power), pascal (pressure), hertz (frequency), coulomb (charge), volt (potential difference), ohm (resistance) and weber (magnetic flux) are DERIVED units built from the base units. The litre is a convenient everyday unit of volume, not an SI base unit.
Another tip: the kilogram is the only base unit that carries a prefix (kilo) in its name. Prefixes are always applied to the gram when forming other units, such as mg and g.

illustrations.caption: The seven SI base quantities
illustrations.description: Quantity, unit, symbol and typical instrument.

illustrations.caption: Base quantities as building blocks
illustrations.description: Seven blocks labelled with the base quantities, with derived quantities built on top.

workedExamples.problem: Name the SI base quantity and unit used to measure (a) the time of a race (b) the temperature of a room (c) the mass of a book.
steps: (b) Thermodynamic temperature, kelvin (K); in practice thermometers also show degrees Celsius.
workedExamples.answer: (a) time, s (b) temperature, K (c) mass, kg

workedExamples.problem: Convert 27 degrees Celsius to kelvin.
Which of these are SI base units: newton, kilogram, joule, second, ampere, watt?
steps: Newton, joule and watt are derived units.

realWorldApplications: Medicine and pharmacy: dosing by mass and amount of substance.
Weather and climate: temperature measured accurately in kelvin or Celsius.
Electrical safety: current in amperes decides the size of fuses and cables.
Science and navigation: time standards from atomic clocks keep GPS accurate.
commonMistakes: Listing newton, joule or watt as base units.
Confusing mass (kg) and weight (N).
Forgetting to convert Celsius to kelvin by adding 273.
Thinking the litre is the SI unit of volume (it is m^3).
summary: There are seven fundamental quantities with SI base units.
Length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, luminous intensity cd.
All other quantities and units are derived.

concepts.title: Derived quantities and their units
learningObjectives: Define derived quantities and derived units
Derive the SI unit of a derived quantity from its defining formula
Know the names and symbols of the common derived units
Express derived units in terms of base units

keyTerms.definition: A quantity obtained by combining base quantities through multiplication or division.
The unit of a derived quantity, expressed in base units.
The unit of force: 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2.
The unit of energy and work: 1 J = 1 N m.
The unit of pressure: 1 Pa = 1 N m^-2.
The unit of power: 1 W = 1 J s^-1.

concepts.definition: A derived quantity is formed from the fundamental quantities by multiplication or division, and its unit is found by substituting the units of the quantities in its defining formula.
explanation: Most quantities in physics are derived. Speed combines length and time. Density combines mass and volume. Force combines mass and acceleration. To find the unit of a derived quantity, take its defining formula and replace each quantity by its unit.

Area = length × width, so the unit is m × m = m^2. Volume = length × width × height, so the unit is m^3. Speed (velocity) = distance/time, so the unit is m/s or m s^-1. Acceleration = change in velocity/time, so the unit is (m/s)/s = m s^-2. Density = mass/volume, so the unit is kg/m^3 or kg m^-3.

Force. By Newton's second law, force = mass × acceleration, so the unit is kg × m s^-2 = kg m s^-2. This combination is given its own name, the newton (N). So 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2. A newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

Work and energy. Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, so the unit is N × m = kg m^2 s^-2 = joule (J). Power = work/time, so the unit is J/s = kg m^2 s^-3 = watt (W). Pressure = force/area, so the unit is N/m^2 = kg m^-1 s^-2 = pascal (Pa).

Other common derived units. Frequency: the number of cycles per second, unit hertz (Hz) = s^-1. Momentum = mass × velocity, unit kg m s^-1. Electric charge = current × time, unit coulomb (C) = A s. Potential difference = energy/charge, unit volt (V) = J/C. Resistance = voltage/current, unit ohm (Ω) = V/A.

Why bother naming derived units? Names such as newton and joule are short, honour scientists (Isaac Newton, James Joule, Blaise Pascal, James Watt, Heinrich Hertz, Alessandro Volta, Georg Ohm) and make equations easier to read. But you must be able to convert them back to base units, which is how unit-checking works.
A useful check: the unit of both sides of a physical equation must be the same. If you calculate a speed and the unit comes out as m^2/s, something has gone wrong.

workedExamples.problem: Derive the SI unit of density.
steps: Unit of mass: kg. Unit of volume: m^3.
Unit of density = kg/m^3 = kg m^-3.

workedExamples.problem: Express the pascal in base units.
steps: 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2, so Pa = kg m s^-2 / m^2 = kg m^-1 s^-2.

workedExamples.problem: Show that the joule equals kg m^2 s^-2.

realWorldApplications: Engineering: working with force, pressure and power units in design.
Daily life: electricity bills use kilowatt-hours (power × time).
Medicine: blood pressure in pascals or mmHg.
Science: checking that formulas have consistent units prevents mistakes.
commonMistakes: Giving the unit of density as kg/m instead of kg/m^3.
Forgetting to square or cube the length unit for area and volume.
Mixing up newton (force) and joule (energy).
Using g or cm in one place and kg or m in another without converting.
summary: Derived units come from formulas using base units.
Both sides of an equation must have the same unit.

concepts.title: SI prefixes and unit conversions
learningObjectives: Use common SI prefixes (kilo, centi, milli, micro, mega, giga, nano)
Convert lengths, masses and times between units
Convert areas, volumes and densities, using powers of conversion factors
Convert speeds between km/h and m/s

keyTerms.definition: A word added in front of a unit to indicate a power of ten, such as kilo = 1 000.
A ratio equal to 1 that changes a quantity from one unit to another.

concepts.definition: SI prefixes multiply a unit by a power of ten. To convert between units, multiply by a conversion factor equal to 1, remembering that area conversion factors are squared and volume conversion factors are cubed.
explanation: Prefixes avoid awkward numbers. Instead of writing 5 000 m we write 5 km; instead of 0.002 s we write 2 ms. The most common prefixes: giga (G) = 10^9, mega (M) = 10^6, kilo (k) = 10^3, hecto (h) = 10^2, deci (d) = 10^-1, centi (c) = 10^-2, milli (m) = 10^-3, micro (μ) = 10^-6, nano (n) = 10^-9.

Simple conversions. 250 cm = 250 × 10^-2 m = 2.5 m. 5 km = 5 × 10^3 m = 5 000 m. 450 g = 0.45 kg. 3 hours = 3 × 3 600 s = 10 800 s. 2 000 mg = 2 g. The idea: substitute the prefix by its value and multiply.

Areas and volumes. Careful: 1 cm = 10^-2 m, so 1 cm^2 = (10^-2 m)^2 = 10^-4 m^2 and 1 cm^3 = (10^-2 m)^3 = 10^-6 m^3. It is a very common error to use 10^-2 for area and volume as well. For instance, 5 000 cm^2 = 5 000 × 10^-4 m^2 = 0.5 m^2, and 2 500 cm^3 = 2.5 × 10^-3 m^3.

Density. 2.5 g/cm^3 = 2.5 × (10^-3 kg)/(10^-6 m^3) = 2.5 × 10^3 kg/m^3 = 2 500 kg/m^3. A shortcut worth remembering: to convert g/cm^3 to kg/m^3, multiply by 1 000. Water has density 1 g/cm^3 = 1 000 kg/m^3.
Speed. To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 1 000/3 600 = 5/18. Therefore 36 km/h = 36 × 5/18 = 10 m/s, and 72 km/h = 20 m/s. To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5 = 3.6.

Method: write the quantity, multiply by the conversion factor written so that the unwanted unit cancels, and check that the answer is sensible (centimetres to metres should give a smaller number). 1 L = 1 000 cm^3 = 1 dm^3 and 1 m^3 = 1 000 L.
Always give the answer in the unit asked for, and use standard form for very large or small values: 0.000 004 m = 4 × 10^-6 m = 4 μm.

workedExamples.problem: Convert (a) 250 cm to m (b) 450 g to kg (c) 3 hours to seconds.
Convert 5 000 cm^2 to m^2 and 2 500 cm^3 to m^3.
Convert (a) 72 km/h to m/s (b) 2.5 g/cm^3 to kg/m^3.

realWorldApplications: Road safety: speed limits in km/h versus physics calculations in m/s.
Medicine: converting between mg, g and μg for doses.
Construction and tiling: floor areas in cm^2 and m^2.
Computing and electronics: kilo-, mega- and gigabytes; nanometre technology.
commonMistakes: Using 10^-2 for area and 10^-6 for length conversions.
Dividing instead of multiplying (or the reverse) by the conversion factor.
Forgetting that 1 L = 1 000 cm^3.
Mixing units inside one calculation.
summary: Prefixes are powers of ten: k = 10^3, c = 10^-2, m = 10^-3, μ = 10^-6.
Area factor is squared and volume factor is cubed.
km/h to m/s: × 5/18; g/cm^3 to kg/m^3: × 1 000.
Check that the size of the answer is sensible.

concepts.title: Measurement of volume
learningObjectives: Calculate the volume of regular solids from their dimensions
Measure the volume of liquids with a measuring cylinder, pipette and burette
Find the volume of an irregular solid by displacement
Read a meniscus correctly and avoid parallax error

keyTerms.definition: The amount of space occupied by a substance.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube.
A reading error caused by viewing a scale from an angle.
Finding the volume of an object by the amount of water it pushes aside.

concepts.definition: Volume is the space an object occupies. Its SI unit is the cubic metre (m^3). Common units: 1 cm^3 = 1 mL and 1 litre = 1 000 cm^3 = 1 dm^3.
explanation: Regular solids. If the shape is regular, calculate volume from measured lengths. Cuboid: V = l × w × h. Cube: V = a^3. Cylinder: V = πr^2 h. Sphere: V = (4/3)πr^3. Cone: V = (1/3)πr^2 h. Always use the same unit for all lengths.

Liquids: use graduated containers. A measuring cylinder measures any volume up to its capacity (for example 100 cm^3) with precision depending on the scale. A pipette delivers one fixed volume (for example 25 cm^3) very accurately. A burette delivers variable volumes, which you read before and after (the difference is the volume delivered). A volumetric flask holds one exact volume.

Reading a measuring cylinder. Place it on a flat surface. Bring your eye to the level of the liquid surface to avoid parallax error. Water forms a concave meniscus (curving up at the edges), so read the bottom of the curve. For mercury, which forms a convex meniscus, read the top. Note the smallest division on the scale (the least count) and estimate to half a division if you can.

Irregular solids: displacement method. A stone's volume cannot be found by a formula. Pour water into a measuring cylinder and record the level (V1). Tie the stone to a thread, lower it carefully in so it is fully covered, and record the new level (V2). Volume of stone = V2 - V1. Example: 40 cm^3 rising to 65 cm^3 means the stone has volume 25 cm^3. For larger objects use a eureka (displacement) can: the water that overflows is collected in a measuring cylinder and its volume equals the volume of the object.
Floating objects. For an object that floats (a cork), tie a sinker (a heavy stone) to it. Find the volume of the sinker alone, then of sinker plus cork, and subtract.
Unit relationships. 1 m^3 = 1 000 000 cm^3 = 1 000 L. 1 L = 1 000 cm^3 = 1 000 mL. So 1 mL = 1 cm^3. A tank 2 m × 1.5 m × 0.8 m has volume 2.4 m^3 = 2 400 L.
Precision tip: choose the smallest measuring cylinder that can hold the liquid, because it has the smallest divisions and gives the most accurate reading.

illustrations.caption: Volume formulas for regular shapes
illustrations.description: Choose the formula that matches the shape.

illustrations.caption: Displacement method
illustrations.description: Two measuring cylinders: before and after lowering a stone; the water level rises from 40 to 65 cm^3.

workedExamples.problem: A cylinder has radius 2 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume. (Take π = 3.14)
A stone raises the water level in a measuring cylinder from 38 cm^3 to 52 cm^3. Find its volume.
steps: Volume of stone = final level - initial level.

workedExamples.problem: A rectangular tank is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 0.8 m high. How many litres of water can it hold when full?

realWorldApplications: Cooking and medicine: measuring liquids accurately.
Water supply: tank and pipeline capacity in litres and cubic metres.
Industry: filling containers with exact volumes.
Laboratories: using burettes and pipettes in chemistry experiments.
commonMistakes: Reading the top of the meniscus for water.
Viewing the scale from above or below (parallax).
Mixing cm and m in one formula.
Using the formula for the wrong shape.
Forgetting that 1 mL = 1 cm^3.
summary: Regular solids: use formulas with consistent units.
Liquids: measuring cylinder, pipette, burette; read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Irregular solids: displacement, V2 - V1.

concepts.title: Dimensions and dimensional analysis
learningObjectives: Define the dimensions of a physical quantity using L, M and T
Find the dimensions of common derived quantities
Use the principle of homogeneity to check equations
Use dimensional analysis to derive a formula up to a constant and to convert units
State the limitations of dimensional analysis

keyTerms.definition: The way a quantity depends on the base quantities, written with [L] for length, [M] for mass and [T] for time.
A quantity with no dimensions, such as a ratio or a pure number.
In a correct physical equation, every term has the same dimensions.

concepts.definition: The dimensions of a quantity show how it is built from length [L], mass [M] and time [T]. In any correct physical equation, all terms have the same dimensions (principle of homogeneity).
explanation: Dimension describes the nature of a quantity, not its units. A distance can be in metres or kilometres but it always has the dimension of length, [L]. Speed always has dimensions length divided by time: [L T^-1]. We write dimensions inside square brackets.

Finding dimensions. Replace each quantity by its dimension in the defining formula. Area = [L]^2 = [L^2]. Volume = [L^3]. Speed = [L]/[T] = [L T^-1]. Acceleration = [L T^-1]/[T] = [L T^-2]. Force = mass × acceleration = [M L T^-2]. Work and energy = force × distance = [M L^2 T^-2]. Power = energy/time = [M L^2 T^-3]. Pressure = force/area = [M L^-1 T^-2]. Density = mass/volume = [M L^-3]. Frequency = [T^-1]. Pure numbers and angles (in radians) are dimensionless.

Principle of homogeneity. You can only add or subtract quantities with the same dimensions: it makes no sense to add a length to a time. So in a correct equation, every term must have the same dimensions on both sides. This lets us test formulas. Check v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Dimensions of v^2: [L^2 T^-2]. u^2: [L^2 T^-2]. as: [L T^-2][L] = [L^2 T^-2]. All terms agree, so the equation is dimensionally consistent. Check s = ut + (1/2)at^2: s is [L]; ut = [L T^-1][T] = [L]; at^2 = [L T^-2][T^2] = [L]. Consistent.

Deriving a formula (up to a constant). Suppose the period T of a simple pendulum might depend on its length l, mass m and the acceleration due to gravity g. Assume T = k l^a g^b m^c where k is a number. Dimensions: [T] = [L]^a [L T^-2]^b [M]^c = [L^(a+b) T^(-2b) M^c]. Compare powers. Mass: c = 0, so the period does not depend on mass. Time: -2b = 1, so b = -1/2. Length: a + b = 0, so a = 1/2. Therefore T = k √(l/g). Experiment shows k = 2π.
Converting units. Dimensions can help convert units. For example, force has dimension [M L T^-2], so 1 dyne (g cm s^-2) = 10^-3 kg × 10^-2 m s^-2 = 10^-5 N.

Limitations. Dimensional analysis cannot find pure numbers (such as 1/2 or 2π), cannot tell you whether an equation is physically correct (only dimensionally consistent), and cannot handle functions like sin or exp. For example s = ut + at^2 is dimensionally consistent but physically wrong because the factor 1/2 is missing. It also fails if a quantity depends on a sum of several terms, or on more than three base quantities.
So: dimensional analysis is a quick screening test. If an equation fails, it is definitely wrong. If it passes, it may still be wrong.

workedExamples.problem: Show that v = fλ (speed = frequency × wavelength) is dimensionally consistent.
steps: Both sides have the same dimensions.

workedExamples.problem: Check whether pressure P = ρgh is dimensionally correct.
steps: ρgh = [M L^-3][L T^-2][L] = [M L^-1 T^-2]. Same as pressure.

workedExamples.problem: Derive the formula for the period of a pendulum T = k l^a g^b by dimensions.

realWorldApplications: Engineering: quickly checking formulas in design calculations.
Physics research: guessing how quantities relate before doing detailed theory.
Model testing: scaling aircraft or ship models uses dimensionless numbers.
Examinations: checking whether an answer's unit is right.
commonMistakes: Confusing dimensions with units.
Adding numbers to dimensionally different quantities.
Believing a dimensionally correct equation is guaranteed correct.
Forgetting that pure numbers (1/2, 2π) cannot be found by dimensions.
summary: Dimensions use [M], [L], [T] and show how a quantity is built.
Correct equations are homogeneous.
Dimensional analysis checks formulas and finds relations up to a constant.
It cannot find pure numbers and cannot prove an equation is correct.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Position, Distance and Displacement
topics.overview: Describes where things are and how far they move: reference points and frames, distance versus displacement, accurate measurement of length with the metre rule, vernier calipers and micrometer, displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, and average speed, velocity and acceleration.

concepts.title: Position and frames of reference
learningObjectives: Define position and explain why a reference point is needed
Describe position on a straight line using positive and negative signs
Describe position in a plane using coordinates
Explain how motion depends on the frame of reference

keyTerms.definition: The location of an object relative to a chosen reference point (origin).
The point from which positions are measured.
A reference point together with directions (axes) and a clock, used to describe position and motion.
Motion described with respect to another moving or stationary object.

concepts.definition: The position of an object is its location relative to a reference point. A frame of reference is the reference point plus a set of directions (and a clock) used to describe where something is and how it moves.
explanation: If someone asks, 'Where is the school?', a useful answer is 'It is 2 km east of the market'. The words 'east of the market' fix a reference point (the market), a direction (east) and a distance (2 km). Without a reference point, 'two kilometres' means nothing. Physics always begins by choosing a reference point.

Position on a straight line. Choose an origin (O) and decide which direction is positive. Then each position is a signed number. On a straight road, let the junction be the origin and east be positive. A shop 400 m east of the junction is at +400 m. A school 250 m west of the junction is at -250 m. The sign tells the direction; the number tells the distance from the origin.

Position in a plane. For motion on a flat surface, use two perpendicular directions, x (east-west) and y (north-south), crossing at the origin. A point is written as an ordered pair (x, y). A position of (3, 4) metres means 3 m along x and 4 m along y from the origin. Its straight-line distance from the origin is √(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 m, by Pythagoras.

Choosing the origin is a free decision. You can place it anywhere convenient; the positions change, but the distance and direction between two objects do not. For example, if the shop is at +400 m and the school at -250 m, the shop is 650 m from the school whichever origin you use.

Frame of reference. Position and motion depend on the observer. A passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving at the bus's speed relative to the road. A person on the road sees the passenger move; a person in the bus does not. Neither is wrong; they use different frames of reference. In most school problems the frame of reference is the ground (the Earth) unless stated otherwise.

Relative motion. If two cars travel in the same direction at 30 m/s and 20 m/s, then relative to the slower car the faster one moves at 10 m/s. If they approach each other, the relative speed is the sum, 50 m/s. Relative motion is used to describe overtaking and collisions.

illustrations.caption: Position on a number line
illustrations.description: A straight road with the junction as origin; a school at -250 m, a shop at +400 m.

illustrations.caption: Same objects, different origins
illustrations.description: Positions change when the origin changes; separations do not.

workedExamples.problem: On a straight road, east is positive and the origin is the junction. A shop is 400 m east and a school 250 m west of the junction. Give their positions and the distance between them.
A point has coordinates (6, 8) m. How far is it from the origin?
A bus travels east at 20 m/s. A passenger walks forward inside the bus at 1 m/s. What is the passenger's speed relative to the ground and relative to the bus?
steps: Relative to the ground: 20 + 1 = 21 m/s (same direction).
workedExamples.answer: 1 m/s relative to the bus; 21 m/s relative to the ground

realWorldApplications: GPS and maps: every position is given relative to a coordinate system (latitude and longitude).
Sport: positions on a field, track or court.
Navigation: ships and aircraft use bearings and distances from known reference points.
Engineering and surveying: drawings use an origin and axes.
commonMistakes: Giving a position without a reference point.
Forgetting the sign (direction) on a straight line.
Thinking a passenger on a bus is 'at rest' for every observer.
Mixing up distance from the origin with position.
summary: Position is measured relative to a reference point.
On a line: signed number; in a plane: (x, y).
Frame of reference = origin + axes + clock.
Motion is relative to the observer's frame.

concepts.title: Distance and displacement
learningObjectives: Define distance and displacement and state which is scalar and which is a vector
Calculate distance and displacement for journeys in straight lines and in two dimensions
Explain why displacement can be zero while distance is not
Calculate distance and displacement for motion on a circle

keyTerms.definition: The total length of the path travelled. It is a scalar (size only) and never negative.
The straight-line change in position from start to finish, with direction. It is a vector.
A quantity with magnitude only.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction.

concepts.definition: Distance is the total path length travelled (a scalar). Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the starting point to the end point, in a stated direction (a vector). Both are measured in metres in SI.
explanation: Imagine walking 3 km east and then 4 km north. Your odometer (like a car's distance counter) records 3 + 4 = 7 km. That is the distance travelled: the length of the path you followed. But if you ask 'how far am I from where I started?' the answer is the straight line from start to finish. By Pythagoras, √(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 km. That is the magnitude of your displacement. Displacement also needs a direction: 5 km at an angle of tan^-1(4/3) = 53.1° north of east (a bearing of about 037°).

Key differences. Distance depends on the path; displacement depends only on the start and end points. Distance is always positive or zero; displacement can be positive, negative or zero. Distance has no direction; displacement does. Magnitude of displacement is never greater than the distance travelled, and they are equal only for motion in a straight line without turning back.

Displacement in one dimension. Along a straight line with a sign convention, displacement = final position - initial position. If a car goes from +100 m to +400 m, its displacement is +300 m. If it then returns to +250 m, its displacement for the whole trip is 250 - 100 = +150 m, but the distance is 300 + 150 = 450 m.

Round trips. If you walk around a block and return to your start, your displacement is zero, because the final position is the same as the initial position, even though the distance may be 800 m. Likewise one complete lap of a 400 m track gives distance 400 m and displacement 0.

Circular motion. A runner on a circular track of radius r who completes half a lap travels a distance equal to half the circumference: πr. The displacement is the straight line across the diameter: 2r. For r = 50 m, the distance is π × 50 ≈ 157 m and the displacement is 100 m.

Describing a vector. To fully give a displacement, state magnitude and direction, for example '100 m due north' or '5 km on a bearing of 037°'. In one dimension, a sign is enough: +3 m (east) or -3 m (west).

Notation. Displacement is often written s (or d or Δx). It is a vector, so when you add displacements you must account for directions: 3 km east followed by 3 km west gives total displacement 0, not 6 km.

illustrations.caption: Distance versus displacement
illustrations.description: A right-angled path east then north: path length 7 km, straight-line displacement 5 km.

rows: can be zero for a trip?

workedExamples.problem: A boy walks 3 km east and then 4 km north. Find the distance travelled and the magnitude of his displacement.
steps: Direction: tan θ = 4/3, so θ = 53.1° north of east.
workedExamples.answer: Distance 7 km; displacement 5 km at 53.1° north of east

workedExamples.problem: A man walks 6 m north, then 8 m east, then 6 m south. Find his distance and displacement.
steps: North and south cancel (+6 - 6 = 0). Only the 8 m east remains.

workedExamples.problem: A runner completes half a lap of a circular track of radius 50 m. Find the distance and the displacement. (π = 3.14)
steps: Distance = half the circumference = πr = 3.14 × 50 = 157 m.

realWorldApplications: Sport: a marathon runner's distance is 42 km, but displacement from start to finish may be much smaller if the route loops.
Navigation: pilots and ship captains use displacement to plot direct routes.
Taxis and delivery: the distance on the meter versus the straight-line distance between places.
Robotics: path planning uses displacement vectors.
commonMistakes: Treating displacement as the same as distance.
Forgetting that displacement needs a direction.
Adding opposite displacements as if they were distances.
Saying displacement can be larger than distance (it cannot).
summary: Distance: total path length, scalar, never negative.
Displacement: straight-line change in position with direction, vector.
Round trip: displacement = 0.
Magnitude of displacement is at most the distance travelled.

concepts.title: Measuring length: metre rule, vernier calipers and micrometer screw gauge
learningObjectives: Use a metre rule correctly and avoid parallax error
Explain the principle of the vernier scale and read vernier calipers
Explain the principle of the micrometer screw gauge and read it
Identify and correct for zero error
Choose the right instrument for a given measurement

keyTerms.definition: The smallest value an instrument can measure directly.
An instrument with a sliding scale that measures lengths to 0.1 mm (0.01 cm).
An instrument using a precise screw to measure small lengths to 0.01 mm.
The reading an instrument gives when it should read zero.
The distance the screw advances in one complete turn.

concepts.definition: Different instruments measure length to different precisions: metre rule 1 mm, vernier calipers 0.1 mm (0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm. The reading is the main-scale reading plus the secondary-scale reading multiplied by the least count, corrected for any zero error.
explanation: Choosing an instrument. A tape measure suits the length of a room, a metre rule suits objects up to 1 m (to the nearest millimetre), vernier calipers suit small objects such as the diameter of a test tube, and a micrometer screw gauge suits very small thicknesses such as the diameter of a wire or a sheet of paper.

Metre rule. The smallest division is 1 mm (0.1 cm). Place the zero mark at one end of the object, avoid using the worn end of the rule, and view the scale directly above the mark. Looking from an angle gives parallax error, which makes the reading too big or too small. Estimate to the nearest 0.5 mm if possible.

Vernier calipers. A vernier caliper has a main scale (marked in mm) and a sliding vernier scale. On a standard 0.1 mm vernier, 10 vernier divisions span 9 mm on the main scale, so each vernier division is 0.9 mm, 0.1 mm shorter than a main-scale division. The least count is 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. To read: (1) read the main scale at the zero of the vernier (the whole mm, to the left of the zero mark); (2) find which vernier division lines up exactly with a main-scale division; (3) multiply that division number by 0.01 cm and add. Example: main scale reads 2.3 cm and the 4th vernier division lines up: reading = 2.3 + 4 × 0.01 = 2.34 cm.

Micrometer screw gauge. It has a fixed sleeve (marked in mm and half-mm) and a rotating thimble with 50 divisions. The screw has a pitch of 0.5 mm, so one full turn of the thimble moves the spindle 0.5 mm, and each thimble division represents 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. The least count is 0.01 mm. To read: (1) read the sleeve (mm and half-mm visible); (2) read the thimble division level with the reference line; (3) reading = sleeve + thimble × 0.01 mm. Example: sleeve 5.5 mm, thimble 28: 5.5 + 0.28 = 5.78 mm. Always use the ratchet so that the pressure is the same each time.

Zero error. Close the jaws or spindle fully and read the scale. If it does not read zero there is a zero error. A positive zero error (the instrument reads, say, +0.02 mm when closed) means every reading is too large, so subtract the error. A negative zero error (it reads -0.03 mm) means every reading is too small, so add 0.03 mm. In symbols: true reading = observed reading - zero error (use the sign). Example: observed 4.37 mm with zero error +0.02 mm: true reading = 4.35 mm.

Improving accuracy. Take several readings and find the average; measure thick objects in different positions; for a thin wire, wrap many turns closely side by side and divide the total width by the number of turns; check for zero error before every use.
Choose precision to match the task. Measuring a 20 m playground with a micrometer is unnecessary; measuring a wire's thickness with a metre rule is useless.

rows: diameter of a tube or ball

illustrations.caption: Reading a vernier caliper
illustrations.description: Main scale showing 2.3 cm with the 4th vernier mark aligned: reading 2.34 cm.

illustrations.caption: Reading a micrometer screw gauge
illustrations.description: Sleeve showing 5.5 mm and thimble reading 28: reading 5.78 mm.

workedExamples.problem: A vernier caliper shows 2.3 cm on the main scale and the 4th vernier division coincides with a main-scale mark. Find the reading. If the zero error is +0.02 cm, find the true reading.
steps: True reading = observed - zero error = 2.34 - 0.02 = 2.32 cm.

workedExamples.problem: A micrometer shows 5.5 mm on the sleeve and 28 on the thimble. The zero error is -0.03 mm. Find the true thickness.
Find the least count of a micrometer whose screw has pitch 0.5 mm and whose thimble has 50 divisions.
steps: Least count = pitch / number of thimble divisions.

realWorldApplications: Engineering and machining: measuring parts to a fraction of a millimetre.
Medicine: measuring thickness of instruments and tubes.
Manufacturing: quality checks on wire, sheets and pipes.
Laboratory work: accurate diameters of spheres and wires.
commonMistakes: Ignoring zero error, or adding it when it should be subtracted.
Reading the vernier at the wrong coincident mark.
Applying too much pressure on the micrometer (use the ratchet).
Parallax error when reading a metre rule.
Forgetting the half-millimetre mark on the micrometer sleeve.
summary: Metre rule 1 mm; vernier 0.1 mm (0.01 cm); micrometer 0.01 mm.
Vernier reading = main scale + (coinciding division × 0.01 cm).
Micrometer reading = sleeve + (thimble × 0.01 mm).
True reading = observed reading - zero error.

concepts.title: Displacement-time graphs
learningObjectives: Draw and interpret displacement-time graphs
Find velocity from the gradient of a displacement-time graph
Recognise a body at rest, moving at constant velocity and moving back
Find distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity from a graph

keyTerms.definition: A graph with time on the horizontal axis and displacement on the vertical axis.
Vertical change divided by horizontal change; on this graph it equals velocity.
Constant velocity (equal displacements in equal times).

concepts.definition: On a displacement-time graph, the gradient (slope) of the line equals the velocity. gradient = change in displacement ÷ change in time = velocity.
explanation: A displacement-time graph is a picture of a journey. Time goes along the horizontal axis, and displacement from the start (with sign) goes up the vertical axis. By reading the graph you can tell where the body is at any time and how fast it is moving.

Gradient equals velocity. Take two points on a straight section: (t1, s1) and (t2, s2). The velocity is (s2 - s1)/(t2 - t1). If the points are (2 s, 6 m) and (6 s, 18 m), then velocity = (18 - 6)/(6 - 2) = 12/4 = 3 m/s.

Types of line. A straight line sloping upwards: constant velocity in the positive direction (a steeper line means a greater speed). A horizontal line: displacement does not change, so velocity is zero (the body is at rest). A straight line sloping downwards: constant negative velocity (moving back towards the start). A curve: velocity is changing, meaning acceleration. A curve getting steeper means speeding up; getting flatter means slowing down.
Instantaneous velocity from a curve. For a curved graph, the velocity at an instant is the gradient of the tangent (a straight line touching the curve at that point).

Example journey. A body moves from 0 to 20 m in 0 to 10 s (velocity 20/10 = 2 m/s), then stays at 20 m from 10 s to 20 s (velocity 0), then returns to 0 from 20 s to 30 s (velocity -20/10 = -2 m/s). Total distance = 20 + 20 = 40 m. Final displacement = 0. Average speed = 40/30 = 1.33 m/s. Average velocity = 0/30 = 0.

Notes: the graph shows displacement, not distance. The line can go down; distance never decreases. A displacement-time graph never goes backwards in time. Two bodies' lines meet where they are at the same place at the same time.
Always label axes with quantity and unit, choose a sensible scale, use a pencil and a ruler for straight sections, and use a large triangle when finding the gradient to reduce error.

illustrations.caption: Displacement-time graph of a journey
illustrations.description: Rise to 20 m in 10 s, flat for 10 s, then return to 0 in 10 s.

workedExamples.problem: A displacement-time graph passes through (2 s, 6 m) and (6 s, 18 m). Find the velocity.
A body moves 0 to 20 m in 10 s, rests for 10 s, then returns to its start in 10 s. Find the velocity in each stage, the total distance, the final displacement, and the average speed.
workedExamples.answer: 2 m/s, 0, -2 m/s; distance 40 m; displacement 0; average speed 1.33 m/s

workedExamples.problem: What does a horizontal section of a displacement-time graph tell you?
steps: Displacement does not change as time passes.
The gradient is zero, so velocity is zero.

realWorldApplications: Sports analysis: tracking an athlete's position over time.
Traffic engineering: studying vehicle movement and stops.
Aviation and ship tracking.
Experiments: ticker-tape and motion sensors produce displacement-time data.
commonMistakes: Reading the height of the graph as speed (it is displacement).
Reading a horizontal line as 'moving at constant speed' (it means at rest).
Using time differences or displacement differences from the wrong points.
Forgetting units when finding gradient.
summary: Gradient of a displacement-time graph = velocity.
Horizontal line = at rest; downward slope = negative velocity.
Curve = changing velocity; tangent gives instantaneous velocity.

concepts.title: Velocity-time graphs
learningObjectives: Interpret velocity-time graphs
Find acceleration from the gradient
Find displacement from the area under the graph
Describe constant velocity, acceleration and deceleration from the graph shape
Solve multi-stage journey problems
prerequisiteNotes: Area of triangles, rectangles and trapezia

keyTerms.definition: A graph of velocity (vertical) against time (horizontal).
The rate of change of velocity: change in velocity ÷ time taken.
Negative acceleration; the body slows down.

concepts.definition: On a velocity-time graph, the gradient equals acceleration and the area under the graph equals displacement.
explanation: A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes with time. Because acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, the gradient of the graph is acceleration: a = (v2 - v1)/(t2 - t1). And since displacement = velocity × time, the area between the line and the time axis is the displacement.

Shapes. A horizontal line: constant velocity, so acceleration is zero. A straight line sloping upwards: constant acceleration (positive gradient). A straight line sloping downwards: constant deceleration (negative gradient). A line on the time axis: at rest. A curve: changing acceleration.

Finding acceleration. For a line from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (10 s, 20 m/s), a = (20 - 0)/(10 - 0) = 2 m/s^2. For a line from (30 s, 20 m/s) to (35 s, 0 m/s), a = (0 - 20)/5 = -4 m/s^2. The negative sign means velocity decreases.

Finding displacement (area). For a rectangle, area = base × height = time × velocity. For a triangle, area = (1/2) × base × height. For a trapezium, area = (1/2)(sum of parallel sides) × width. Areas below the time axis (negative velocity) count as negative displacement.

Worked journey. A car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s, travels at 20 m/s for 20 s, then brakes to rest in 5 s. The graph has three parts. Part 1 (triangle): area = (1/2) × 10 × 20 = 100 m, acceleration 2 m/s^2. Part 2 (rectangle): area = 20 × 20 = 400 m, acceleration 0. Part 3 (triangle): area = (1/2) × 5 × 20 = 50 m, acceleration -4 m/s^2. Total distance = 100 + 400 + 50 = 550 m. Total time = 35 s. Average speed = 550/35 = 15.7 m/s.

Distance versus displacement from the graph: if the velocity stays positive, the area gives both. If the velocity becomes negative, the area below the axis is subtracted from the area above for displacement but added for distance.

Check your answer: if your graph shows negative velocity the body is moving in the opposite direction, and units must match: m/s on the vertical axis and s on the horizontal axis gives m for area and m/s^2 for gradient.

illustrations.caption: Velocity-time graph of a car journey
illustrations.description: Three stages: acceleration, constant velocity, braking.

workedExamples.problem: A car accelerates uniformly from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s. Find its acceleration and the distance travelled.
A car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s, travels at 20 m/s for 20 s, then brakes to rest in 5 s. Find the total distance and average speed.
From a velocity-time graph, a bus slows from 15 m/s to 0 in 6 s. Find the acceleration and braking distance.

realWorldApplications: Road safety: estimating braking distance from deceleration.
Aviation: take-off run and landing distance calculations.
Vehicle testing: accelerometers produce velocity-time data.
Sports: training analysis of a sprinter's acceleration.
commonMistakes: Using the graph height as distance.
Forgetting the 1/2 in the area of a triangle.
Ignoring negative acceleration and signs.
Confusing the slope of a velocity-time graph (acceleration) with that of a displacement-time graph (velocity).
summary: Gradient = acceleration; area = displacement.
Horizontal line: constant velocity.
Negative gradient: deceleration.
Triangle area = (1/2) base × height; trapezium = (1/2)(a + b) × width.

concepts.title: Average speed, average velocity and acceleration problems
learningObjectives: Define average speed, average velocity and instantaneous speed
Calculate average speed for journeys with several stages
Explain why average speed for equal distances is not the arithmetic mean of speeds
Calculate average acceleration

keyTerms.definition: Distance travelled per unit time (scalar).
Displacement per unit time (vector).
Total distance divided by total time.
Total displacement divided by total time.
The speed at one particular moment.

concepts.definition: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. Average acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken. SI units: m/s, m/s, m/s^2.
explanation: A car's speedometer shows instantaneous speed, the speed at that moment. But a journey includes speeding up, slowing down and stops, so we often use the average. Average speed = total distance/total time. If you travel 120 km in 2 hours, your average speed is 60 km/h, even if you sometimes drove faster or slower.
Average velocity uses displacement: average velocity = total displacement/total time. For a round trip the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero even though the average speed is not.

Common mistake: averaging the speeds. If you drive 60 km at 30 km/h and then 60 km at 60 km/h, the average speed is NOT (30 + 60)/2 = 45 km/h. Compute the times: 60/30 = 2 h and 60/60 = 1 h. The total distance is 120 km and the total time is 3 h, so the average speed is 120/3 = 40 km/h. More time is spent at the slower speed, so the average is closer to 30 than to 60.
For two equal distances d at speeds v1 and v2, average speed = 2 v1 v2/(v1 + v2). Check: 2 × 30 × 60/(90) = 3 600/90 = 40 km/h.
Unit conversion. Convert to consistent units before calculating. 90 km/h = 90 × 1 000 m/3 600 s = 25 m/s. 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s ≈ 0.278 m/s.

Average acceleration. If a car's velocity changes from u (initial) to v (final) in time t, average acceleration a = (v - u)/t. A car going from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s: a = 20/8 = 2.5 m/s^2. A negative result means the body is slowing down (deceleration).

Using the graph: for uniform acceleration, v = u + at, and average velocity = (u + v)/2. Distance = average velocity × time = (u + v)t/2. These ideas lead to the equations of motion in the next chapters.
Strategy for problems: write what is given and what is asked; convert units; select the right formula; substitute with units; check whether the answer is sensible.

workedExamples.problem: A car travels 60 km at 30 km/h and then 60 km at 60 km/h. Find the average speed.
steps: Total distance = 120 km. Total time = 3 h.

workedExamples.problem: A girl runs 400 m around a track and returns to her start in 80 s. Find her average speed and average velocity.
steps: Displacement = 0 (she returns to the start), so average velocity = 0.

workedExamples.problem: A car increases its velocity from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s. Find the average acceleration and the distance covered.
Convert 90 km/h to m/s.

realWorldApplications: Travel planning: estimating arrival time from average speed.
Athletics: race pace and training.
Road safety and speed cameras that measure average speed between two points.
Aviation and shipping: fuel and schedules.
commonMistakes: Averaging two speeds instead of using total distance and total time.
Forgetting to convert minutes and hours to seconds.
Calling average speed zero for a round trip (it is average velocity that is zero).
Using displacement for speed.
summary: Average speed = total distance/total time.
Average velocity = total displacement/total time.
a = (v - u)/t.
Equal distances at different speeds: use total distance and total time.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Time, Mass and Weight
topics.overview: Explains how time is measured and what clocks need: units of time, timing devices from sundials to atomic clocks, the simple pendulum and its period, ticker-tape analysis of motion, and the difference between mass and weight with W = mg.

concepts.title: The concept of time and its units
learningObjectives: Distinguish a time interval from an instant of time
State the SI unit of time and convert between seconds, minutes, hours, days and years
Explain how the second is defined today
Use prefixes for small and large times

keyTerms.definition: The duration between two events (for example 20 s).
A particular moment, such as 10:30 a.m.
The SI unit of time.
A clock that keeps time using the extremely regular vibrations of atoms such as caesium.

concepts.definition: Time is the duration of events and the interval between them. Its SI unit is the second (s). In physics we usually measure time intervals, the difference between two instants.
explanation: Everything that happens takes time. A race starts at one instant and ends at another; the difference is the time interval, which is the quantity physics measures. A clock reading such as 10:30 a.m. gives an instant, while '45 minutes' gives an interval.

Units. The SI unit of time is the second (s). Other units: 1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 60 min = 3 600 s; 1 day = 24 h = 86 400 s; 1 year (365 days) = 31 536 000 s, about 3.15 × 10^7 s. When using formulas such as speed = distance/time in SI units, convert the time into seconds.

Small and large times. Use prefixes: 1 millisecond (ms) = 10^-3 s, 1 microsecond (μs) = 10^-6 s, 1 nanosecond (ns) = 10^-9 s. Large spans are written in standard form: the age of the Earth is about 4.5 billion years, or about 1.4 × 10^17 s.

How is the second defined? Originally it was 1/86 400 of a mean solar day (based on the Earth's rotation), but the Earth's rotation is not perfectly regular. Today the second is defined from the vibrations of caesium-133 atoms: it is the time taken for 9 192 631 770 periods of a particular microwave radiation emitted by those atoms. Atomic clocks based on this lose less than a second in millions of years, and they keep the clocks in GPS satellites synchronised.

Why time matters. Time appears in speed, acceleration, frequency, power and many other quantities. To measure it we need a regularly repeating event: the swing of a pendulum, the vibration of a quartz crystal, the rotation of the Earth. You will see how such events are used to build clocks later in this chapter.
Time is a scalar quantity: it has size only, no direction. Intervals are never negative when we describe how long something lasted.

Accuracy and precision. A stop clock that reads to 0.1 s is more precise than a wall clock that reads to 1 s. Human reaction time, about 0.2 s, limits how accurately we can start and stop a stopwatch, so we time many repetitions (for example 20 oscillations) and divide.

illustrations.caption: Instant versus interval
illustrations.description: A time line showing two instants and the interval between them.

workedExamples.problem: Convert (a) 2.5 hours to seconds (b) 45 minutes to seconds (c) 0.25 ms to seconds.
A race starts at 3:15:20 and ends at 3:17:05. Find the time interval in seconds.
steps: Subtract 15 s because 3:17:05 is 15 s earlier than 3:17:20: 120 - 15 = 105 s.

workedExamples.problem: How many seconds are there in one day?

realWorldApplications: Sport: timing races to hundredths of a second.
Transport: timetables and schedules.
GPS and phones: nanosecond timing from atomic clocks gives location accuracy.
Medicine: recording pulse and breathing rates per minute.
commonMistakes: Confusing an instant with an interval.
Forgetting to convert minutes or hours to seconds in formulas.
Using 100 seconds per minute.
Writing a time without units.
summary: Time interval = difference between two instants.
SI unit: the second; 1 h = 3 600 s; 1 day = 86 400 s.
Second defined by caesium atomic vibrations.
Time is a scalar.

concepts.title: Time-measuring devices: from sundials to atomic clocks
learningObjectives: Name and describe natural and man-made time-measuring devices
Explain the repetitive event each device relies on
Compare their accuracy and convenience
Choose a suitable timing device for a given experiment

keyTerms.definition: An event that repeats at regular intervals, used to measure time.
A device that starts and stops to measure a time interval directly.
A clock controlled by the vibrations of a quartz crystal.

concepts.definition: Every clock uses a repetitive event that occurs at regular intervals and a way of counting those events. Examples: the Sun's motion (sundial), flowing water or sand, a swinging pendulum, a vibrating quartz crystal and vibrating atoms.
explanation: Natural time keepers. People first measured time using the Sun (day and night), the Moon (months) and the seasons (years). Heartbeat and pulse are natural but not accurate, since they change with activity.
Sundial. A pointer (gnomon) casts a shadow that moves round as the Sun appears to move. The position of the shadow shows the time. It works only in sunshine and is not very accurate.

Water clock (clepsydra) and hour glass (sand clock). Water or sand flows at a steady rate through a narrow opening, so the amount that has flowed shows how much time has passed. They were used before mechanical clocks and are still used for fixed intervals such as an egg timer. Their accuracy is limited because the flow rate depends on how full the container is.
Candle and incense clocks burn at a fairly steady rate with markings on the candle, but are affected by draughts.

Pendulum clock. The regular swing of a pendulum controls the movement of gears. It was a major advance in accuracy in the 17th century and is still used in grandfather clocks, but it must stay still and needs winding.
Mechanical watch. A balance wheel and hairspring oscillate regularly, driven by a coiled spring. They are portable but need winding and are affected by temperature and position.

Quartz clock and watch. A tiny quartz crystal in an electric circuit vibrates at a very stable frequency of 32 768 Hz. Electronic circuits halve this frequency 15 times (2^15 = 32 768) to produce one pulse per second. Quartz watches typically gain or lose only seconds per month and are cheap.
Atomic clock. It counts the vibrations of caesium atoms and is the most accurate timekeeper, used for the world's time standard and GPS.

Stop clock and stopwatch. For laboratory use, a stop clock (analogue or digital) measures time intervals directly to 0.1 s or 0.01 s. Human reaction time of about 0.2 s causes errors when starting and stopping, so time several repeats and average. The ticker-tape timer, studied next, records time automatically as a series of dots.

illustrations.caption: Timekeeping through history
illustrations.description: A strip showing sundial, hour glass, pendulum clock, quartz watch and atomic clock.

workedExamples.problem: Name the repetitive event used in (a) a pendulum clock (b) a quartz watch (c) an atomic clock.
steps: (b) Vibration of a quartz crystal at 32 768 Hz.
workedExamples.answer: (a) pendulum swing (b) quartz vibration (c) atomic vibration

workedExamples.problem: Why is an hour glass not very accurate?
steps: Sand flows steadily, but the rate changes slightly as the amount in the top changes.
It also measures only a fixed interval and must be turned over.
workedExamples.answer: The flow rate changes and it only measures one fixed interval.

workedExamples.problem: A quartz crystal vibrates 32 768 times a second. How many times must the frequency be halved to give one pulse per second?

realWorldApplications: Sport: electronic timing with start sensors and finish cameras.
Computers and phones: quartz clocks keep time between network updates.
Navigation: GPS uses atomic clocks on satellites.
Cooking and laboratory work: timers and stop clocks.
commonMistakes: Thinking all clocks work in the same way.
Using a pulse as an accurate timer.
Ignoring reaction time with a stopwatch.
Believing sundials work at night or in cloudy weather.
summary: Every clock needs a regular repeating event plus a counter.
Devices: sundial, water clock, hour glass, pendulum, mechanical, quartz, atomic.
Accuracy improves from natural events to atomic clocks.
Reaction time limits stopwatch accuracy.

concepts.title: The simple pendulum: period, frequency and g
learningObjectives: Define oscillation, amplitude, period and frequency
State the factors that affect the period of a simple pendulum
Use T = 2π√(l/g) and f = 1/T
Describe an experiment to investigate the pendulum and find g from a graph
Explain sources of error and how to reduce them

keyTerms.definition: A small heavy bob hung from a light, inextensible string fixed at the top.
One complete to-and-fro swing (back to the same point moving the same way).
The maximum displacement from the rest (equilibrium) position.
The time for one complete oscillation, in seconds.
The number of oscillations per second, in hertz (Hz): f = 1/T.
The distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob.

concepts.definition: For small swings, the period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(l/g), where l is its length and g the acceleration due to gravity. Frequency f = 1/T. The period depends on length and g, not on the mass of the bob or (for small angles) the amplitude.
explanation: A simple pendulum is a small bob swinging on a string. One oscillation is a full to-and-fro movement: from the extreme left, to the extreme right, and back to the left. The time for one oscillation is the period T. The frequency f is how many oscillations occur each second: f = 1/T. If T = 2 s then f = 0.5 Hz.

Measuring the period accurately. A single swing is too fast to time precisely. Instead time n oscillations (say n = 20) and divide: T = t/n. If 20 oscillations take 40 s, then T = 2.0 s. Start timing as the bob passes the centre (the fastest point) and count 'zero' as it passes first. Time at least twice and average.

What affects the period? (1) Length: the longer the pendulum, the longer the period. T is proportional to the square root of l, so doubling the length multiplies T by √2 (about 1.41), not 2. (2) The value of g: the pendulum swings more slowly where gravity is weaker (for example on the Moon or on top of a high mountain). (3) Mass of the bob: no effect. (4) Amplitude: for small angles (up to about 10°), no effect; large swings make the period slightly longer.

The formula. T = 2π√(l/g). Squaring both sides gives T^2 = (4π^2/g) l. So a graph of T^2 (vertical) against l (horizontal) is a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π^2/g. Therefore g = 4π^2/gradient. This is how g can be measured in the laboratory.
Example. A pendulum is 0.64 m long and its period is 1.6 s. Then g = 4π^2 l/T^2 = 4 × 9.87 × 0.64/(1.6)^2 = 25.27/2.56 = 9.87 m/s^2, close to the accepted value of 9.8 m/s^2.

Experiment (finding g). Set up a pendulum with a small dense bob on a long thread clamped between two blocks so the pivot is fixed. Measure the length from the clamp to the centre of the bob. Displace the bob by a small angle and release it. Time 20 oscillations, repeat and average. Calculate T. Change the length (for example 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, 1.00 m) and repeat. Plot T^2 against l and find the gradient.

Sources of error and improvements. Parallax when judging the centre of the swing: use a fiducial marker (pointer) at the centre. Large amplitude: keep below 10°. Timing error: time many oscillations. Swinging in a circle or an ellipse: release without pushing. Measuring length wrongly: measure to the centre of the bob, not the bottom. String stretching or loose clamp: use a thin inextensible thread and a firm clamp.
Dimensional check. T = 2π√(l/g): [l/g] = [L]/[L T^-2] = [T^2], so √(l/g) has dimension [T]. Good: it matches the period.

illustrations.caption: The simple pendulum
illustrations.description: A bob on a string swinging between two extreme positions with the centre position marked.

workedExamples.problem: Twenty oscillations of a pendulum take 40 s. Find the period and the frequency.
A pendulum of length 0.64 m has a period of 1.6 s. Calculate g.
What length of pendulum has a period of 2.0 s? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
A pendulum's length is increased from 0.25 m to 1.0 m. By what factor does the period change?
steps: Length is multiplied by 4, so T is multiplied by √4 = 2.

realWorldApplications: Clocks: grandfather clocks use a pendulum.
Geophysics: pendulums measure g and detect changes in gravity (for example to locate oil and minerals).
Seismology: pendulum-type seismographs detect earthquakes.
Playground swings and amusement rides follow the same physics.
commonMistakes: Measuring the length to the bottom of the bob instead of its centre.
Timing one swing only.
Using large angles.
Believing a heavier bob changes the period.
Forgetting that T^2, not T, is proportional to l.
summary: T = time for one oscillation; f = 1/T.
T = 2π√(l/g): depends on l and g, not mass or small amplitude.
T^2 against l is a straight line with gradient 4π^2/g.
Time many oscillations and average.

concepts.title: Ticker-tape timer, repetitive events and building a clock
learningObjectives: Explain how a ticker-tape timer works and its time interval
Interpret a ticker tape to describe uniform velocity, acceleration and deceleration
Calculate velocity and acceleration from a ticker tape
Describe the requirements for a device that measures time

keyTerms.definition: A device with a vibrating arm that makes dots on a paper tape at equal time intervals.
The distance between successive dots; it shows how far the tape moved in that time.
One dot, 1/50 s apart when the timer runs on 50 Hz mains.

concepts.definition: A ticker-tape timer powered by 50 Hz alternating current makes 50 dots per second, one dot every 0.02 s. The distance between dots shows the speed of the tape: close dots mean slow motion, wide spacing means fast motion.
explanation: The ticker-tape timer is a simple device for studying motion in the laboratory. A thin paper tape is pulled through the timer and attached to a trolley. A small arm vibrates up and down 50 times each second (the frequency of the mains supply), hitting carbon paper to print a dot on the tape. So successive dots are 1/50 = 0.02 s apart. A series of 10 spaces takes 10 × 0.02 = 0.2 s, called a 'ten-tick' interval.

Reading the tape. If the dots are equally spaced, the trolley moved at constant velocity. If the spacing increases steadily, the trolley is accelerating. If it decreases, the trolley is decelerating. A tape with widely spaced dots shows high speed; closely spaced dots show slow motion.

Calculating velocity. Cut the tape into pieces of ten spaces (time 0.2 s each). The velocity for each piece is length of piece/0.2 s. For a piece 4.0 cm long: v = 0.040 m/0.2 s = 0.20 m/s. For one 8.0 cm long: v = 0.080/0.2 = 0.40 m/s.

Calculating acceleration. Because each piece represents the average velocity during its 0.2 s, the change in velocity between successive pieces took 0.2 s. For the pieces above: a = (0.40 - 0.20)/0.2 = 1.0 m/s^2. If the lengths of successive ten-tick strips increase by the same amount each time (4, 8, 12, 16 cm), the acceleration is uniform. A neat method is to stick the strips side by side on a graph sheet to form a velocity-time (step) graph: the heights of the strips are proportional to velocity.
If the mains frequency were different, the dot interval would change. At 60 Hz the dot interval is 1/60 s. Always use T = 1/f for the timer.

Constructing a timing device. A simple clock needs (1) a regularly repeating process (pendulum, water drip, vibration), (2) a way to count the repetitions, and (3) a display. For example, a water clock drips at a steady rate; count drips or measure volume collected. A pendulum clock counts swings with a gear train. A good timer should have a steady period, be little affected by temperature, vibration and friction, and give readings that are easy to read.
Why mains frequency matters. In Nigeria the supply is 50 Hz, so the timer prints 50 dots per second. If the mains supply is unstable the frequency drifts slightly and the timer's accuracy changes.

illustrations.caption: Ticker tape examples
illustrations.description: Three tapes: constant spacing, increasing spacing, decreasing spacing.

workedExamples.problem: A ticker-tape timer uses 50 Hz mains. What is the time between dots, and how long do 10 spaces take?
A ten-tick strip is 4.0 cm long and the next is 8.0 cm long. Find the velocities and the acceleration.
steps: Time between the middle of the strips = 0.2 s.

workedExamples.problem: Strips of ten spaces measure 3.0 cm, 3.0 cm, 3.0 cm. What is the motion and the velocity?
steps: Equal lengths mean equal distances in equal times.

realWorldApplications: Physics laboratory: studying acceleration of trolleys and falling objects.
Early motion studies in schools and physics education.
Understanding data-logger and motion-sensor technology, which does the same thing electronically.
Developing timing devices based on regular repeating events.
commonMistakes: Using 0.1 s as the time between dots (it is 0.02 s at 50 Hz).
Forgetting to convert cm to m.
Counting dots instead of spaces for a ten-tick strip.
Using the time of a strip as the time between strips when the strips overlap.
summary: At 50 Hz, the dot interval is 0.02 s; ten spaces = 0.2 s.
Equal spacing: constant velocity; growing spacing: acceleration.
v = strip length / 0.2 s; a = change in v / 0.2 s.
A clock needs a regular repeating event, a counter and a display.

concepts.title: Mass and weight
learningObjectives: Define mass and weight and state their SI units
Explain the difference between mass and weight
Use W = mg to calculate weight, mass or g
Explain why weight varies with location but mass does not
Describe instruments that measure mass and weight

keyTerms.definition: The amount of matter in a body, measured in kilograms (a scalar that does not change with place).
The gravitational force acting on a body, measured in newtons (a vector pointing towards the centre of the Earth).
The acceleration of a freely falling body; about 9.8 m/s^2 on the Earth's surface (often taken as 10 m/s^2 in calculations).
The force of gravity per kilogram: g in N/kg (numerically equal to 9.8).
The sensation of having no weight, as in free fall or orbit.

concepts.definition: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body (SI unit kg). Weight is the force of gravity on that mass: W = mg (SI unit newton, N). Mass is constant everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.
explanation: Mass. The mass of a body is the quantity of matter it contains. It is measured in kilograms. Your mass is the same on Earth, on the Moon and in space. It is a scalar and is also a measure of inertia (how hard it is to change the body's motion).

Weight. Weight is the force with which the Earth (or another planet) pulls a body towards its centre. It is measured in newtons (N). Weight is a force, so it is a vector pointing downwards. Weight = mass × acceleration due to gravity: W = mg. On Earth g is about 9.8 m/s^2 (or 9.8 N/kg), usually rounded to 10 m/s^2 in calculations. Always use the value of g the question gives.

Worked idea. A 5 kg bag has weight W = 5 × 10 = 50 N (using g = 10 m/s^2) or 49 N (using g = 9.8). On the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s^2, so the same bag weighs only 5 × 1.6 = 8 N. The bag has not lost any matter: its mass is still 5 kg. Only its weight has changed.

Why does g vary? Gravitational pull depends on the mass of the planet and the distance from its centre. At the poles (closer to the centre) g is slightly higher, about 9.83 m/s^2, and at the equator slightly lower, about 9.78 m/s^2. On high mountains g is slightly less. On the Moon it is about one-sixth of Earth's value; on Jupiter it is about 25 m/s^2.

Measuring mass and weight. Mass is measured with a beam (lever) balance or an electronic balance, by comparing with standard masses. A beam balance gives the same reading anywhere, because the unknown and standard masses are both affected equally by gravity. Weight is measured with a spring balance (newton meter): the extension of the spring is proportional to the pull. A spring balance would read less on the Moon.

Kilograms are not newtons. Bathroom scales are spring balances calibrated in kilograms, so they show mass assuming Earth's gravity. Moved to the Moon they would read about one-sixth of the value even though your mass has not changed.

Weightlessness. Astronauts in orbit appear weightless because they and the spacecraft are in free fall together: there is nothing pushing up on them, so they do not feel their weight. Gravity is still acting; the Earth's pull at the height of the International Space Station is almost the same as at the surface.
Summary of differences: mass is a scalar in kg that is constant everywhere; weight is a vector (force) in N that depends on g and is measured with a spring balance.

workedExamples.problem: Find the weight of a 5 kg bag on Earth (g = 10 m/s^2) and on the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s^2).
steps: The mass of 5 kg is the same in both places.
workedExamples.answer: 50 N on Earth; 8 N on the Moon; mass unchanged

workedExamples.problem: A body weighs 245 N on Earth (g = 9.8 m/s^2). Find its mass.
An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg. What is her weight on the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s^2) and what is her mass there?
A spring balance reads 120 N for a stone on Earth (g = 10 m/s^2). What will it read on the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s^2)?

realWorldApplications: Engineering: structures are designed to carry weights; lifts and cranes use force ratings in newtons.
Space exploration: astronauts' weights differ on the Moon and Mars; spacecraft design uses mass and weight carefully.
Shopping and trade: scales used for goods measure mass (kg).
Medicine: weight-based doses use body mass.
commonMistakes: Saying 'weight in kilograms'. Weight is in newtons; mass is in kilograms.
Saying mass changes on the Moon.
Using W = m/g instead of W = mg.
Believing astronauts in orbit have no gravity acting on them.
summary: Mass: matter in a body, kg, constant.
Weight: force of gravity, N, W = mg.
g is about 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth and 1.6 m/s^2 on the Moon.
Beam balance measures mass; spring balance measures weight.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Introduction to Chemistry
topics.overview: Introduces chemistry: what it is and its branches, chemistry in daily life, the scientific method, the uses and harmful effects of chemistry, careers, and the safety rules, hazard symbols and apparatus used in the laboratory.

concepts.title: What is chemistry? Meaning and branches
learningObjectives: Define chemistry
Explain why chemistry is called the central science
Name and describe the main branches of chemistry
Link everyday observations to chemical ideas
prerequisiteNotes: Basic science from junior secondary school

keyTerms.definition: The branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter, and the energy changes that go with them.
Anything that has mass and occupies space.
A kind of matter with a definite composition, such as water or iron.
A process in which substances change into new substances.

concepts.definition: Chemistry is the science that studies matter: what it is made of (composition), how it is arranged (structure), how it behaves (properties) and how it changes into other substances (reactions), including the energy changes involved.
explanation: Wherever you look, there is chemistry. Wood burns into ash, smoke and gases. Iron turns to red-brown rust. Milk turns sour. A cooking pot's metal handle does not melt, but the margarine inside does. Chemistry asks: what are these materials made of, why do they behave as they do, and how can we change them into more useful things?

Four big questions. (1) Composition: what substances (elements and compounds) is a material made of? Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. (2) Structure: how are the particles arranged? Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon but arranged differently, so one is hard and the other soft. (3) Properties: what is it like (colour, hardness, melting point, reactivity)? (4) Changes: how does it change into other substances, how fast, and with what energy changes?

Why is chemistry called the 'central science'? Physics explains the energy and forces behind chemical change; biology depends on the chemical reactions in living cells; geology depends on the chemistry of rocks and minerals; medicine and agriculture depend on chemicals such as drugs and fertilisers. Chemistry connects them all.

Branches. Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds (fuels, plastics, drugs, foods). Inorganic chemistry studies all other elements and compounds (metals, salts, acids). Physical chemistry studies the rules behind chemical change (energy, rates, equilibrium). Analytical chemistry finds out what substances are present and how much (quality control, forensic tests). Biochemistry studies the chemistry of living things (proteins, enzymes, DNA). Industrial chemistry applies chemistry to large-scale production (cement, fertilisers, petroleum products, soap). Environmental chemistry studies pollution and its control. Nuclear chemistry studies radioactivity and nuclear reactions.

Chemistry and the scientific method. Like physics, chemistry relies on careful observation, measurement and experiment. A chemist forms a hypothesis, tests it, records results with units, and draws conclusions based on evidence.

A note on terms. A 'chemical' is simply a substance, either natural or man-made. Water, salt, sugar and oxygen are all chemicals. The word 'chemical-free' is not scientifically meaningful, because all matter is made of chemicals.

concepts.title: Chemistry in our daily life

concepts.definition: Chemistry is part of everyday life: in cooking, cleaning, farming, health, transport, communication and the materials around us. Many everyday changes are chemical reactions.
explanation: Food and cooking. Cooking is chemistry: heating an egg changes its proteins permanently; baking powder reacts to release carbon dioxide that makes cakes rise; fermentation turns sugary palm sap into palm wine and cassava into garri (fermentation and roasting also help remove harmful cyanide compounds from cassava). Salt, sugar and vinegar preserve food by stopping the growth of microbes.

Cleaning. Soap is made by reacting palm oil or other fats with an alkali (such as potash from burnt wood ash) in a reaction called saponification, which is how traditional black soap is made. Soap and detergents help water remove grease because one end of their molecules attracts water and the other attracts oil. Bleach and disinfectants destroy germs by chemical reactions.

Health. Medicines are chemicals designed to act on the body: paracetamol for pain, antibiotics against bacteria, oral rehydration salts for dehydration, chlorine for water purification. Soap and hand sanitisers (containing alcohol) kill microbes. NAFDAC tests food and drugs to protect public health.

Agriculture. Fertilisers (compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) feed crops; pesticides and herbicides protect them; lime (calcium compounds) reduces soil acidity. Misuse can pollute water and harm health, so correct use matters.

Energy and transport. Fuels such as petrol, diesel, kerosene and cooking gas are produced from crude oil by chemical processes. Burning them releases heat that drives engines. Batteries in phones and cars store chemical energy and release it as electricity.

Materials. Metals, glass, cement, ceramics, plastics, paints and textiles come from chemical processes. Cement is made by heating limestone and clay. Rusting (iron slowly combining with oxygen and water) is a chemical reaction that damages metal.

Distillation in local industry. Local gin (ogogoro) is made by distilling fermented palm wine. Distillation separates a mixture by boiling and condensing, a physical separation method you will study in the next chapter.
Observing chemistry around you. Learn to ask: Is a new substance formed? Does the change involve heat, light, gas or colour change? Such questions help you decide if a change is chemical.

concepts.title: The scientific method in chemistry
learningObjectives: List the steps of the scientific method
Design a fair test with independent, dependent and controlled variables
Distinguish observation from inference
Record and present experimental data clearly
Write a simple laboratory report
prerequisiteNotes: Scientific method in physics (Physics Chapter 1) helpful

keyTerms.definition: Information gathered with the senses or instruments (for example, 'the solution turned blue').
A conclusion drawn from observations ('the solution contains copper ions').
A testable explanation or prediction.
A factor that can change in an experiment.
A comparison experiment in which the factor being tested is left out or unchanged.

concepts.definition: The scientific method is a systematic way of finding answers: observe, ask a question, form a hypothesis, test it with a fair experiment, record and analyse results, conclude and report. Results must be repeatable.
explanation: Chemists use a logical approach. Steps: (1) Observe and ask a question; (2) form a hypothesis; (3) plan a fair experiment; (4) carry it out safely and record observations and measurements; (5) analyse the results; (6) draw a conclusion; (7) communicate the results.

Example. Question: does the temperature of water affect how quickly sugar dissolves? Hypothesis: sugar dissolves faster in hotter water. Variables: independent (what you change) is the water temperature (20, 40, 60, 80 °C); dependent (what you measure) is the time taken for 5 g of sugar to dissolve; controlled (kept the same) variables are the volume of water, the mass and type of sugar, the amount of stirring and the container.

Collecting data. Use appropriate apparatus (thermometer, stopwatch, balance), take repeated readings, record in a neat table with units and column headings, and note qualitative observations (colour, gas, smell, precipitate). Observations are what you actually see; do not write conclusions such as 'a reaction occurred' in the observation column.
Observation versus inference. Observation: 'a white solid formed when the two clear solutions were mixed.' Inference: 'an insoluble compound (a precipitate) was formed.' Always keep these separate.

Controls and repeats. A control tests the experiment's baseline: for example, to test if a fertiliser helps plants grow, grow some plants without fertiliser under the same conditions. Repeat the experiment at least three times and take an average to reduce random errors.

Analysis and conclusion. Plot a graph where useful (time against temperature). State whether the data support or reject the hypothesis, and mention sources of error. A conclusion must come from the data collected.

Laboratory report format: title, aim, apparatus and materials, procedure, results (table and graph), calculations, conclusion, sources of error and precautions. Write in the past tense and in your own words.
Safety is part of the method: wear safety goggles and protective clothing, follow your teacher's instructions, never taste chemicals, and dispose of waste correctly.

rows: volume of water, mass of sugar, stirring, container

concepts.title: Uses of chemistry in society

keyTerms.definition: A large molecule made of many repeating units, such as nylon and polythene.
