A substance burned to produce thrust in rockets.

concepts.definition: Chemistry provides food, clothing, housing materials, medicines, fuels and transport materials, and contributes to defence and space exploration.
explanation: Food. Fertilisers increase crop yields; pesticides and herbicides protect crops; preservatives and refrigeration keep food from spoiling; food additives improve taste, colour and nutrition (vitamin A added to cooking oil, iodine added to salt). Food science relies on chemistry.

Clothing. Natural fibres (cotton, wool, silk) are treated with dyes and finishing chemicals. Synthetic fibres such as nylon, polyester and rayon are made in chemical industries from petroleum products. Chemistry also produces detergents, bleaches and stain removers.

Housing. Cement, concrete, bricks, glass, paint, roofing sheets (aluminium and iron alloys), plastics, pipes and tiles all depend on chemistry. Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. Wood preservatives and paints protect buildings from decay and corrosion.

Medicine. Chemists discover and manufacture drugs: antibiotics fight bacterial infections, anaesthetics allow surgery, antimalarials treat malaria, vaccines prevent diseases. Antiseptics and disinfectants prevent infection. Medical devices use polymers and metals that are safe in the body.

Transport. Fuels (petrol, diesel, aviation fuel) power vehicles. Tyres are made from rubber and synthetic polymers; car bodies from steel and aluminium alloys; batteries store electricity; catalytic converters reduce exhaust pollution; lubricants reduce friction in engines.

Military. Chemistry produces explosives, propellants, and protective materials. Armour and materials for equipment are developed by chemists. Chemical and biological weapons are banned by international agreements because they cause suffering to people.

Space science. Rocket fuels and oxidisers provide thrust. Lightweight alloys and heat-resistant ceramics protect spacecraft. Life-support systems purify air and water. Solar cells are made of chemically prepared semiconductors.
Communications and technology. Semiconductors, optical fibres, batteries, liquid crystal displays and printed circuits are all products of chemistry.
Energy. Chemistry supports energy production through fuels and cleaner technologies such as fuel cells, solar panels and biofuels.

rocket fuels, heat shields, lightweight alloys

concepts.title: Adverse effects of chemistry: corrosion, pollution and drug abuse
learningObjectives: Define corrosion and describe its effects and prevention
Explain the types of pollution (air, water, soil, noise) and their causes and effects
Describe drug abuse and its consequences
Suggest ways of reducing harmful effects of chemicals

keyTerms.definition: The gradual destruction of metals by chemical reaction with their surroundings (for example rusting of iron).
The release of harmful substances into the environment.
A substance that harms the environment or living things.
Use of drugs for non-medical purposes or in harmful amounts.
Designing products and processes that reduce hazards and waste.

concepts.definition: Chemistry has many benefits but can cause harm through corrosion of metals, pollution of air, water and soil, and abuse of drugs. Understanding the causes helps us prevent the damage.
explanation: Corrosion. Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen and water. Rust is a flaky, reddish-brown hydrated iron(III) oxide that weakens iron structures. Corrosion damages bridges, pipelines, roofing sheets, cars and ships and costs billions of naira each year. Prevention: painting, oiling or greasing, galvanising (coating with zinc), plating with another metal, using alloys such as stainless steel, and sacrificial protection (attaching a more reactive metal such as magnesium or zinc).

Air pollution. Sources: burning fuels in vehicles and generators (carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, soot), gas flaring in oil production, burning refuse, industrial smoke. Effects: breathing problems, acid rain (sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain, damaging buildings, crops and water bodies), global warming from greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, and depletion of the ozone layer by CFCs.

Water pollution. Sources: oil spills, industrial effluents, sewage, plastics, fertiliser and pesticide runoff, mining waste. Effects: killing fish and other aquatic life, spreading diseases such as cholera and typhoid, making water unfit to drink, and destroying livelihoods of fishing communities. Oil spills in the Niger Delta are a well-known example.

Soil pollution. Sources: pesticides, fertiliser overuse, oil spills, dumping of refuse, mining and industrial waste. Effects: reduced soil fertility, poisoning of crops and groundwater, and harm to organisms in the soil.
Noise and other pollution. Loud machinery and generators cause hearing loss and stress. Radioactive waste and heavy metals (lead, mercury) cause long-term health effects.

Drug abuse. Drugs can heal when used correctly, but abuse of drugs such as opioids (codeine and tramadol misuse), cocaine, cannabis, alcohol and tobacco harms the body and mind. Effects include addiction, damage to the liver, lungs, heart and brain, mental illness, accidents, crime and family breakdown. The Nigerian National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) combats illegal drugs. Always use medicines as prescribed, never share prescription drugs, and seek help from health workers if there is dependence.

Reducing harm. Use clean energy and efficient engines, treat waste before release, recycle and reuse materials, avoid single-use plastics, use fertilisers and pesticides correctly, protect metals from corrosion, enforce environmental laws, educate the public about drug abuse and encourage green chemistry.

concepts.definition: Chemistry opens careers in medicine and pharmacy, engineering, agriculture, food science, environmental science, the oil and gas industry, forensic science, teaching, research and many other fields.
explanation: Health. Pharmacists prepare medicines and advise on their safe use. Medical laboratory scientists analyse blood, urine and other samples. Doctors, nurses and dentists use chemistry to understand drugs and the body. Pharmaceutical researchers develop new medicines and vaccines.

Engineering and industry. Chemical engineers design plants for refining petroleum, producing fertilisers, cement, paints, soap and food. Petroleum engineers and process technologists work in oil and gas. Materials scientists create alloys, plastics and ceramics. Metallurgists extract and refine metals.

Agriculture and food. Agricultural chemists study soil and fertilisers; food scientists and nutritionists test food quality; brewers and bakers use fermentation chemistry. NAFDAC analysts check that foods and drugs meet safety standards.
Environment. Environmental scientists test air, water and soil for pollutants; water treatment chemists make water safe to drink; waste managers design recycling systems.
Law and security. Forensic scientists analyse fingerprints, drugs and explosives for the police and courts; customs and drug-control officers use chemical tests to detect illegal substances.
Education and research. Chemistry teachers and lecturers train future scientists; research chemists work in universities and laboratories on new materials, energy and medicines.

Other careers. Cosmetic chemists develop soaps, creams and perfumes; textile technologists work with dyes and fibres; quality-control chemists work in factories; science journalists and consultants communicate and apply chemical knowledge.

Planning. University courses linked to chemistry include Chemistry, Industrial Chemistry, Biochemistry, Pharmacy, Medicine, Chemical Engineering, Petroleum Engineering, Food Science, Agriculture, Environmental Science and Medical Laboratory Science. These usually require chemistry plus mathematics, physics or biology at senior secondary level; check specific admission requirements early.

concepts.title: Laboratory safety, hazard symbols and common apparatus
learningObjectives: State and follow basic laboratory safety rules

keyTerms.definition: Something that can cause harm.

A ventilated enclosure that removes toxic gases and vapours.
Immediate help given to an injured person before professional medical help arrives.

concepts.definition: Chemistry practical work is safe when rules are followed. Wear protective equipment, know the hazard symbols, handle apparatus correctly, and report all accidents to the teacher immediately.
explanation: Basic safety rules. (1) Listen to and follow your teacher's instructions. (2) Wear a laboratory coat and safety goggles; tie back long hair. (3) Never eat, drink or taste anything in the laboratory. (4) Do not run or play. (5) Read labels carefully; never use unlabelled containers. (6) Never smell chemicals directly; waft the vapour gently towards your nose. (7) Point the mouth of a heated test tube away from yourself and others. (8) Keep flammable liquids away from flames. (9) Wash your hands after every practical. (10) Report breakages, spills and injuries at once.

Hazard symbols. A red diamond or square with a picture warns of danger: flammable (flame), corrosive (liquid eating a hand and a metal), toxic or poisonous (skull and crossbones), harmful or irritant (exclamation mark), oxidising (circle with a flame above it), explosive (exploding bomb), health hazard (human figure with star on chest) and hazardous to the environment (dead tree and fish). Treat any container with a hazard symbol with extra caution.

Heating safely. Use a Bunsen burner only with the teacher's permission. A luminous (yellow) flame is cooler and sooty; a non-luminous (blue) flame with the air hole open is hotter and cleaner. Heat test tubes with a holder and shake gently; never heat a closed container.

Handling chemicals. Pour from the side opposite the label to protect it. Add acid to water slowly, never water to acid, to avoid spitting. Do not return unused chemicals to stock bottles. Dispose of waste as directed, since some chemicals must not go down the sink.

First aid. Chemical in the eye: rinse immediately with plenty of clean water for at least 10 minutes and seek medical help. Acid or alkali on skin: wash with plenty of water. Burn from heat: cool under running cold water for at least 10 minutes. Cut: apply pressure and cover. Inhaled fumes: move to fresh air. Fire: use a fire blanket or sand for small fires; never use water on oil or electrical fires; evacuate if the fire is large.

Common apparatus. Beaker: holding and heating liquids. Conical flask: titrations and mixing. Measuring cylinder: approximate volumes. Pipette: accurate fixed volumes. Burette: delivering variable volumes in titration. Funnel and filter paper: filtration. Evaporating dish: evaporating solutions. Bunsen burner, tripod stand and wire gauze: heating. Test tubes and boiling tubes: small reactions. Spatula: handling small amounts of solids. Thermometer: measuring temperature. Retort stand with clamp: holding apparatus. Condenser and round-bottom flask: distillation. Crucible: heating solids strongly. Wash bottle: rinsing with distilled water. Gas jar: collecting gases.
Good practice. Read the procedure fully before starting, set up apparatus carefully, keep the workspace clean and tidy, record observations immediately, and clean apparatus at the end.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Matter and Separation Techniques
topics.overview: Studies what matter is and how it behaves: states of matter, physical and chemical properties and changes, elements, compounds and mixtures, the main methods of separating mixtures (filtration, evaporation, crystallisation, distillation, separating funnel, sublimation, chromatography) and how purity is judged.

concepts.title: Matter and the states of matter
learningObjectives: Define matter and give examples
Describe the three states of matter in terms of particle arrangement, movement and properties
Name the changes of state and the energy changes involved
Explain a heating curve for a pure substance

keyTerms.definition: Anything that has mass and occupies space.
A very small piece of matter: an atom, molecule or ion.
The form in which matter exists: solid, liquid or gas.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid boils and changes to gas throughout.

concepts.definition: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It exists mainly in three states: solid, liquid and gas, which differ in how closely the particles are packed and how freely they move.
explanation: Everything around us is matter: a stone, water, air, wood, your body. Light and heat are not matter because they have no mass and take up no space. All matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion, and the state depends on how strongly the particles attract each other and how fast they move.

Solids. Particles are packed closely in a regular, fixed pattern and can only vibrate about fixed positions. So a solid has a definite shape and volume, is very difficult to compress and does not flow. Liquids. Particles are close but can slide past one another. A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container, flows, and is almost incompressible. Gases. Particles are far apart and move rapidly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape or volume, fills its container, is easily compressed and has low density.

Changes of state. Melting: solid to liquid (heat absorbed). Freezing: liquid to solid (heat released). Boiling/evaporation (vaporisation): liquid to gas (heat absorbed). Condensation: gas to liquid (heat released). Sublimation: solid directly to gas (for example iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice) and the reverse is also called sublimation (or deposition). When heat is supplied the particles gain energy and move faster, overcoming attractions between them.

Heating curve. When a solid is heated steadily, its temperature rises until it reaches the melting point. Then the temperature stays constant while the solid melts, because the heat is used to break the attractions between particles (latent heat) rather than to raise temperature. After all the solid has melted, the temperature of the liquid rises until the boiling point. It stays constant again during boiling, and then the gas temperature rises. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure.

Evaporation versus boiling. Evaporation takes place at the surface of a liquid at any temperature below boiling point, and it cools the liquid (which is why sweating cools you and wet clothes dry). Boiling takes place throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, when bubbles of vapour form inside it.
Plasma. At extremely high temperatures, as in the Sun and lightning, gases become plasma, sometimes called the fourth state of matter, in which atoms lose electrons.

Diffusion. Particles move randomly and spread out from high concentration to low concentration: perfume spreads across a room; a drop of ink spreads in water; faster in gases than in liquids, and fastest at higher temperatures. This is evidence that matter is made of moving particles.

illustrations.description: Arrows between solid, liquid and gas labelled melting, freezing, boiling, condensation and sublimation.

illustrations.caption: Heating curve of water
illustrations.description: Temperature rising, flat at 0 degrees C (melting), rising, flat at 100 degrees C (boiling), rising.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why a gas can be compressed but a solid cannot.

workedExamples.answer: Gas particles are far apart; solid particles are already close together

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the temperature of boiling water stays at 100 °C although heat is still being supplied.
steps: The heat energy is used to overcome the attractions between the particles so that the liquid changes to gas.
It is not used to raise the temperature until all of the liquid has changed state.
workedExamples.answer: The heat is used for the change of state (latent heat), not to raise the temperature

workedExamples.problem: Name the change of state in each: (a) wet clothes drying (b) dew forming on grass at night (c) iodine crystals turning directly to vapour.
steps: (a) Liquid to gas at the surface: evaporation.

realWorldApplications: Cooking: boiling, steaming and freezing food.
Refrigerators and air conditioners work by evaporation and condensation of a refrigerant.
Weather: evaporation, condensation and rainfall.
Industry: liquefying gases such as oxygen and cooking gas for storage.
commonMistakes: Saying heat is matter (heat is energy).
Thinking particles in solids do not move.
Believing temperature keeps rising during melting or boiling.
Confusing evaporation (any temperature, surface) with boiling (fixed temperature, throughout).
summary: Matter has mass and occupies space.
Solids: fixed shape and volume; liquids: fixed volume, no fixed shape; gases: neither.
Changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation.
Temperature stays constant during a change of state.

concepts.title: Properties of matter: physical and chemical
learningObjectives: Distinguish physical properties from chemical properties
List common physical properties and how they are measured
Calculate density
Distinguish intensive from extensive properties

keyTerms.definition: A property that can be observed or measured without changing the substance into a new substance.
A property that describes how a substance reacts or changes into a new substance.
Mass per unit volume: density = mass/volume.
Able to be hammered into sheets.
Able to be drawn into wires.

concepts.definition: Physical properties (colour, density, melting point, solubility, conductivity) can be observed without changing the substance. Chemical properties (flammability, reactivity, rusting) describe how a substance changes into new substances.
explanation: To identify a substance and decide how to use it, chemists use its properties. Properties are of two main kinds: physical and chemical.

Physical properties include: state at room temperature, colour, odour, taste (never taste in the laboratory), density, melting point, boiling point, solubility in water, hardness, malleability, ductility, electrical and thermal conductivity, magnetism and lustre (shine). Measuring them does not change what the substance is. For example, copper is reddish-brown, a good conductor, malleable and ductile, which is why it is used for electric wire.

Density. Density = mass ÷ volume. Its SI unit is kg/m^3 but g/cm^3 is common in the laboratory. If an object has mass 156 g and volume 20 cm^3, its density is 156/20 = 7.8 g/cm^3 (about that of iron). Water has density 1.0 g/cm^3 (1 000 kg/m^3). Objects less dense than water float; denser ones sink.

Chemical properties describe the way a substance reacts or changes into other substances: whether it burns (flammability), reacts with acids, rusts, reacts with water, tarnishes, decomposes on heating or acts as an oxidising agent. For example, magnesium burns with a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide, while gold does not burn or tarnish, which is why gold jewellery stays shiny.

Intensive and extensive properties. Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of substance, such as density, colour and melting point. Extensive properties depend on the amount, such as mass and volume. One gram or one kilogram of pure iron has the same density, but different masses.

Using properties to separate and choose materials. Differences in properties allow separation: magnetism (iron from sulphur), solubility (salt from sand), boiling point (ethanol from water). Choose materials by properties: copper for wire (conductor, ductile), plastic for handles (insulator), aluminium for aircraft (low density, strong).
Identify a substance by a set of properties. Many substances look alike (sugar and salt), but their melting points and solubilities differ. A single property is rarely enough; use several.

illustrations.caption: Uses of materials from their properties

workedExamples.problem: Find the density of a metal block of mass 156 g and volume 20 cm^3.
Classify each as physical or chemical property: (a) melting point of lead (b) iron rusts (c) copper conducts electricity (d) petrol burns.
steps: (a) Physical: can be measured without changing the lead.

workedExamples.problem: A solid has mass 50 g and density 2.5 g/cm^3. Find its volume.

realWorldApplications: Construction: choosing materials by strength, density and corrosion resistance.
Jewellery: gold and platinum are chosen because they do not tarnish.
Electrical engineering: copper and aluminium wires, plastic insulation.
Food and pharmacy: using properties such as solubility to dissolve and administer drugs.
commonMistakes: Treating colour change as a physical property when it comes from a reaction.
Mixing up mass and density.
Forgetting units in density.
Thinking a single property is enough to identify a substance.
summary: Physical properties can be seen or measured without forming new substances.
Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts.
Density = mass/volume.
Intensive properties do not depend on amount; extensive properties do.

concepts.title: Types of change: physical and chemical
learningObjectives: Define physical and chemical changes
List evidence of a chemical change
Classify everyday changes
Explain the energy changes in exothermic and endothermic processes

keyTerms.definition: A change in which no new substance is formed; usually easy to reverse.
A change in which one or more new substances are formed; usually difficult to reverse.
A change that releases heat.
A change that absorbs heat.
A change that can be undone.

concepts.definition: In a physical change no new substance is formed (only state, shape or size changes). In a chemical change new substances with different properties are formed.
explanation: Matter can change in two broad ways. In a physical change, the substance stays the same chemically: melting ice gives water, dissolving sugar gives a sugar solution, breaking a stick leaves wood, and boiling water gives steam. The particles themselves are not changed, and most physical changes can easily be reversed (freeze the water to get ice, evaporate the solution to recover the sugar).

In a chemical change (chemical reaction), the particles are rearranged to form new substances with different properties. Burning wood forms ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour; iron rusts to form iron(III) oxide; milk turns sour; an egg cooks; magnesium burns to form magnesium oxide. These changes are generally permanent: you cannot get the original substance back simply by cooling or drying.

Evidence of chemical change: (1) a new substance forms, with different properties (colour, odour, taste); (2) a gas is given off (bubbling); (3) an insoluble solid (precipitate) forms when solutions are mixed; (4) heat or light is given out or taken in; (5) a permanent colour change. One sign alone may not be enough; for example, bubbles also appear when water boils (a physical change), so the question is whether a NEW substance is formed.

Energy changes. Chemical changes involve energy. Exothermic reactions give out heat (burning, respiration, neutralisation), so the surroundings get warmer. Endothermic reactions take in heat (photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate in water, thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate), so the surroundings get cooler. Physical changes also involve energy: melting and evaporation are endothermic, freezing and condensation are exothermic.

Reversible chemical changes exist. Heating blue copper(II) sulphate crystals drives off water of crystallisation, leaving a white powder; adding water turns it blue again. So 'chemical changes are never reversible' is not completely true. A better statement: chemical changes are difficult to reverse and need a chemical process.

Conservation of mass. In any chemical or physical change the total mass stays the same. When a candle burns, the gases produced are lost to the air, so the candle appears to lose mass; if all products were collected the mass would be unchanged. This is the law of conservation of mass you will study in Chapter 4.
Decision guide: ask 'is a new substance formed?' If yes, chemical; if no, physical.

rows: photosynthesis, ammonium nitrate dissolving, heating limestone

workedExamples.problem: Classify as physical or chemical change: (a) tearing paper (b) burning paper (c) dissolving salt in water (d) souring of milk.
Bubbles appear when water is boiled and also when magnesium is added to acid. Which is a chemical change and why?
steps: Boiling water: bubbles are water vapour; the substance is still water: physical.
Magnesium and acid: bubbles are hydrogen gas, a new substance: chemical.
workedExamples.answer: Magnesium with acid; a new gas is formed

workedExamples.problem: Heating blue copper(II) sulphate crystals produces a white powder; adding water restores the blue colour. Is this a physical or chemical change? Explain.
steps: Heating removes water of crystallisation to form a new substance (anhydrous copper(II) sulphate) with different properties.
It is a reversible chemical change.

realWorldApplications: Cooking: baking and frying are chemical changes.
Fuels: burning is an exothermic chemical change giving usable heat.
Cold packs: use endothermic dissolving to cool injuries.
Industry: understanding changes helps control reactions.
commonMistakes: Thinking that bubbles always mean a chemical change.
Believing all chemical changes are irreversible.
Calling dissolving a chemical change.
Ignoring energy changes.
summary: Physical change: no new substance; chemical change: new substance formed.
Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, heat or light, new substance.
Exothermic releases heat; endothermic absorbs heat.
Mass is conserved in all changes.

concepts.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
learningObjectives: Define element, compound and mixture
Compare compounds and mixtures
Classify elements as metals, non-metals and metalloids
Distinguish homogeneous from heterogeneous mixtures and name types of mixtures (solution, suspension, colloid, alloy)

keyTerms.definition: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means; it contains only one kind of atom.
A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Two or more substances physically mixed, not chemically combined.
A mixture with uniform composition throughout (a solution).
A mixture with visibly different parts.

concepts.definition: An element contains one kind of atom. A compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio and has properties different from its elements. A mixture is a physical combination of substances that keep their own properties.
explanation: Elements. There are 118 known elements, about 90 of which occur naturally. Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, iron, copper, gold, sulphur. Each is made of one kind of atom and is represented by a symbol (H, O, C, Fe, Cu, Au, S). Elements are classified as metals (shiny, malleable, ductile, good conductors, usually solids at room temperature), non-metals (dull, brittle if solid, poor conductors, many are gases) and metalloids (boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium), which have properties between the two. Mercury is a liquid metal; bromine is a liquid non-metal.

Compounds. A compound forms when elements combine chemically. Water (H2O) is hydrogen and oxygen in the fixed mass ratio 1:8; carbon dioxide is carbon and oxygen in the ratio 3:8. A compound has a fixed composition and its properties are completely different from those of its elements: sodium is a soft reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, but sodium chloride (table salt) is a harmless white crystalline solid. A compound can be broken down only by chemical methods such as electrolysis or heating, not by physical methods.

Mixtures. A mixture has no fixed composition (you can mix any amounts), the components keep their own properties, and they can be separated by physical methods. Air is a mixture of gases (about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% others); sea water is a mixture of water and salts; crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons.

Iron and sulphur demonstration. A mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder (any proportion) can be separated by a magnet; each keeps its own properties; adding dilute hydrochloric acid gives hydrogen from the iron. If the mixture is heated strongly, a chemical change happens and iron(II) sulphide forms, a dark compound that is not magnetic and with acid gives hydrogen sulphide (smells like rotten eggs). The compound cannot be separated by a magnet.

Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures. In a homogeneous mixture the composition is uniform and the parts cannot be seen separately: salt solution, air, brass, vinegar. In a heterogeneous mixture the parts are visible: sand and water, oil and water, soil, granite.

Types of mixtures. A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent (sugar in water). A suspension contains insoluble particles that settle on standing (muddy water, chalk in water). A colloid has particles of intermediate size that do not settle (milk, fog, smoke, paint, gelatin). An emulsion is a colloid of two immiscible liquids (milk, mayonnaise). An alloy is a solid solution of metals, for example brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin) and steel (iron and carbon).

How to classify a substance. Can it be separated by physical methods? Then it is a mixture. If not, can it be broken down chemically into simpler substances? Then it is a compound. If not, it is an element.

rows: uniform, particles very small, do not settle

workedExamples.problem: Classify each as an element, compound or mixture: (a) sea water (b) sodium chloride (c) oxygen (d) air (e) carbon dioxide.
steps: (b) Sodium and chlorine combined in a fixed ratio: compound.

workedExamples.problem: A mixture of iron filings and sulphur is heated and a dark solid forms that is not attracted by a magnet. Explain.
steps: Heating caused a chemical reaction between the iron and sulphur.
A new compound, iron(II) sulphide, formed, with different properties from either element.
workedExamples.answer: A compound formed, so the magnet no longer separates it

workedExamples.problem: State three differences between a compound and a mixture.
steps: Compounds have a fixed composition; mixtures vary.
Components of compounds are chemically combined; mixtures are physical.
Compounds are separated chemically; mixtures by physical methods.
workedExamples.answer: Fixed composition, chemical bonding, chemical separation

realWorldApplications: Air is a mixture used for breathing and industry.
Alloys: steel for construction, brass for taps, bronze for statues.
Pharmacy: solutions, suspensions and emulsions as medicines.
Food: milk (colloid), mayonnaise (emulsion), vinegar (solution).
commonMistakes: Calling air or sea water a compound.
Saying a mixture must be 50-50.
Thinking compounds keep the properties of their elements.
Assuming all metals are solid (mercury is liquid).
summary: Element: one kind of atom. Compound: elements chemically combined in fixed ratio. Mixture: physical combination.
Mixtures keep component properties and are separated physically.
Metals, non-metals and metalloids.
Solutions, suspensions, colloids and alloys.

concepts.title: Separation techniques (1): sieving, decantation, filtration, evaporation and crystallisation
learningObjectives: Explain the principle behind each separation method
Choose a suitable method for a given mixture
Describe the apparatus and procedure for filtration, evaporation and crystallisation
Explain terms such as residue, filtrate, solute, solvent and saturated solution

keyTerms.definition: The solid left on the filter paper.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper.
A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
The substance that dissolves.
The liquid in which a solute dissolves.

concepts.definition: Mixtures are separated by physical methods that use differences in properties such as particle size, density, solubility, boiling point or magnetism. The choice depends on the type of mixture.
explanation: Why separate? Raw materials are mixtures; to get useful pure substances we separate them: salt from sea water, clean water from mud, oil from crude oil. Each method uses a difference in physical properties.

Sieving. Separates solid particles of different sizes using a sieve. Examples: removing stones from sand, separating gari or flour from lumps, separating coarse and fine sand on a building site. Winnowing separates light chaff from heavier grain by wind.
Magnetic separation. A magnet picks out magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) from non-magnetic ones. Used to separate iron filings from sulphur or sand, and iron scrap from other waste.

Decantation. Pouring off a liquid from a solid that has settled. The mixture is left to stand so the denser solid settles. For example separating muddy water after sedimentation, or tea leaves from tea. It is quick but incomplete because some liquid remains with the solid.

Filtration. Separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper and a funnel. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate and the solid left behind is the residue. For example separating sand from water, or chalk powder from a suspension. Filtration cannot separate dissolved substances because the particles are small enough to pass through the paper.

Evaporation. Heating a solution until the liquid turns to vapour and leaves the dissolved solid behind. Used to obtain salt from sea water in salt pans. It is suitable only if you want the solid, not the liquid, and the solid does not decompose on heating.

Crystallisation. Used when a solid decomposes on strong heating, or when you want large pure crystals. Evaporate some solvent until the solution is saturated (test by dipping a clean glass rod and seeing crystals form as it cools), then allow it to cool slowly. Crystals form because solubility decreases as temperature falls. Filter off the crystals, wash with a little cold distilled water, and dry between filter papers. Used for sugar, copper(II) sulphate and many salts.

Separating salt and sand. Add water; salt dissolves and sand does not. Filter: sand is the residue and salt solution is the filtrate. Evaporate the filtrate to obtain the salt. This combines dissolving, filtration and evaporation.

Choosing the method: insoluble solid + liquid: filtration or decantation; dissolved solid + liquid, solid wanted: evaporation or crystallisation; solids of different sizes: sieving; magnetic + non-magnetic solids: magnet.

illustrations.caption: Separation methods and what they use
Filtration
illustrations.description: Funnel with filter paper in a conical flask; residue on the paper, filtrate below.

workedExamples.problem: Describe how to obtain dry salt from a mixture of salt and sand.
steps: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt.
Filter: sand remains as the residue; salt solution is the filtrate.
Heat the filtrate in an evaporating dish until the water has evaporated (or crystallise), leaving dry salt.

workedExamples.problem: Why is crystallisation used to obtain copper(II) sulphate crystals instead of evaporating to dryness?
steps: Evaporating to dryness may decompose the crystals and removes their water of crystallisation.
Crystallisation gives pure crystals as the saturated solution cools.
workedExamples.answer: To avoid decomposition and obtain pure, well-formed crystals

workedExamples.problem: Which separation method would you use to separate (a) iron filings from sand (b) chalk from water (c) a mixture of stones and gari?

realWorldApplications: Salt production from sea water.
Water purification: sedimentation, decantation and filtration.
Kitchen: sieving flour, straining tea or soup.
Mining: magnetic separation of iron ore and sieving of sand and gravel.
commonMistakes: Trying to separate dissolved salt by filtration.
Confusing residue and filtrate.
Evaporating to dryness for substances that decompose or have water of crystallisation.
Using too much solvent when crystallising.
summary: Choose the method according to the property that differs.
Filtration: insoluble solid from liquid; residue stays on paper.
Evaporation: dissolved solid; crystallisation: pure crystals from a saturated solution.
Sieving: size; magnet: magnetic materials.

concepts.title: Separation techniques (2): distillation, fractional distillation, separating funnel, sublimation and precipitation
learningObjectives: Describe simple distillation and what it separates
Explain fractional distillation and its applications (crude oil, air, ethanol and water)
Use a separating funnel to separate immiscible liquids
Separate mixtures using sublimation
Explain precipitation as a way to remove ions
prerequisiteNotes: Boiling point and states of matter (2.1)

keyTerms.definition: A process of heating a liquid to vapour and condensing it back to liquid to separate it from dissolved solids or other liquids.
The liquid collected after condensation.
Distillation that separates liquids with different boiling points using a fractionating column.
Unable to mix, forming separate layers (oil and water).
Able to mix completely (ethanol and water).
An insoluble solid formed in a solution during a reaction.

concepts.definition: Distillation separates a liquid from a dissolved solid or from other liquids by boiling and condensing. Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points. A separating funnel separates immiscible liquids. Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour.
explanation: Simple distillation. Used to get a pure liquid from a solution. The solution is heated in a flask. The solvent boils off as vapour, passes into a Liebig condenser (cold water flows in at the bottom and out at the top), and condenses into pure liquid collected in a receiver. The dissolved solid stays behind. Example: obtaining distilled water from salty water. A thermometer at the vapour outlet shows the boiling point of the distillate (100 °C for water). Anti-bumping granules prevent violent boiling.

Fractional distillation. When two or more liquids are miscible and have different boiling points, a fractionating column (packed with glass beads or rings) is placed between the flask and the condenser. Vapours rise and repeatedly condense and re-evaporate on the packing; the more volatile liquid (lower boiling point) reaches the top first. Ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (100 °C) can be separated this way: ethanol distils first at about 78 °C.

Applications. Crude oil is separated in a refinery by fractional distillation into fractions of different boiling ranges: refinery gas (LPG), petrol (gasoline), naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, fuel oil and bitumen (the residue). Liquid air is fractionally distilled to give nitrogen (b.p. -196 °C), argon (-186 °C) and oxygen (-183 °C). Local gin (ogogoro) and spirits are produced by distilling fermented liquids.

Separating funnel. For immiscible liquids that form two layers, such as oil and water or kerosene and water. Pour the mixture into the funnel and let it settle; the denser liquid forms the lower layer. Open the tap to run off the lower layer into a beaker, close it when the boundary reaches the tap, and collect the upper liquid separately. Also used to extract substances with a solvent.

Sublimation. Used for mixtures in which only one solid sublimes. Example: ammonium chloride sublimes when heated; sodium chloride does not. Heat the mixture in an evaporating dish covered by an inverted funnel with cotton wool in the stem. Ammonium chloride vapour rises and solidifies on the cooler funnel walls, leaving sodium chloride in the dish. Iodine and naphthalene also sublime.

Precipitation. Mixing two solutions can form an insoluble solid, the precipitate, which can then be filtered. For example silver nitrate solution mixed with sodium chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride; water softening with sodium carbonate removes calcium ions as insoluble calcium carbonate.

Selecting the method. Pure solvent from solution: distillation. Liquids with close boiling points that mix: fractional distillation. Liquids that do not mix: separating funnel. Solid that sublimes: sublimation. Ions in solution that form insoluble compounds: precipitation then filtration. Many separations combine two or more methods.

illustrations.caption: Simple distillation apparatus
illustrations.description: Flask heated, thermometer at the neck, Liebig condenser with water in at the bottom and out at the top, receiver.

illustrations.caption: Fractional distillation of crude oil
illustrations.description: A tall column hotter at the bottom, cooler at the top, with fractions drawn off at different heights.

workedExamples.problem: Describe how to obtain pure water from salty water.
steps: Heat the salty water in a distillation flask.
Water boils and the vapour passes into a condenser, where it cools and condenses.
Collect pure distilled water; salt remains in the flask.

workedExamples.problem: Why is fractional distillation used instead of simple distillation to separate ethanol and water?
steps: Both are liquids and miscible, with boiling points that are fairly close (78 °C and 100 °C).
The fractionating column gives repeated condensation and evaporation, giving better separation.
workedExamples.answer: Fractional distillation separates liquids with different but close boiling points

workedExamples.problem: Describe how to separate sodium chloride from ammonium chloride.
steps: Heat the mixture in an evaporating dish covered with an inverted funnel.
Ammonium chloride sublimes and recondenses on the funnel; sodium chloride remains in the dish.

realWorldApplications: Petroleum refineries: petrol, kerosene and diesel from crude oil.
Production of distilled water for laboratories and car batteries.
Beverage industry: spirits.
Air separation plants: oxygen for hospitals and welding; nitrogen for food packing.
commonMistakes: Using simple distillation for liquids with close boiling points.
Connecting cooling water the wrong way (it must enter at the bottom).
Heating a closed system.
Forgetting that the thermometer bulb must be at the vapour outlet.
summary: Distillation: boil and condense to get a liquid from a solution.
Fractional distillation: separate miscible liquids by boiling point.
Separating funnel: immiscible liquids.
Sublimation: solid goes directly to vapour.
Precipitation then filtration removes ions.

concepts.title: Chromatography and Rf values
learningObjectives: Explain how paper chromatography separates substances
Carry out and interpret a paper chromatogram
Calculate Rf values and use them to identify substances
Give applications of chromatography

keyTerms.definition: A method of separating substances in a mixture by their different rates of movement through a stationary phase carried by a moving solvent.
The material that does not move (the paper).
The solvent that moves up the paper.
The farthest point reached by the solvent.
The ratio of the distance moved by a substance to the distance moved by the solvent front.

concepts.definition: In paper chromatography, substances in a mixture travel up the paper at different speeds depending on how soluble they are in the solvent and how strongly they are attracted to the paper. Rf = distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent front.
explanation: Chromatography is used to separate very small amounts of mixtures, such as the coloured dyes in ink or food colouring. The name comes from the Greek for 'colour writing'.

Method. (1) Draw a pencil line (not ink!) about 2 cm above the bottom of a strip of chromatography paper. (2) Place a small spot of the mixture on the line; add reference spots of known substances beside it. (3) Stand the paper in a beaker with a little solvent (water or ethanol), making sure the solvent level is BELOW the pencil line. (4) Let the solvent rise by capillary action. (5) Remove the paper before the solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front. (6) Dry and observe the spots (colourless spots may need to be sprayed with a locating agent or viewed under ultraviolet light).

Why do substances separate? The solvent carries the substances upwards. A substance that is very soluble in the solvent and only weakly attracted to the paper travels far; one that is less soluble or strongly attracted to the paper moves little. Each substance in a mixture has its own balance, so they form separate spots at different heights.

Interpreting a chromatogram. The number of spots shows the minimum number of substances in the mixture. A pure substance gives a single spot. Matching spots at the same height with those of known substances shows what is present. The spot that moves farthest is the most soluble in that solvent.

Rf value. Measure the distance from the baseline to the centre of the spot (d) and from the baseline to the solvent front (D). Then Rf = d/D. Rf is always between 0 and 1 and has no units. If a spot moved 3.2 cm and the solvent front moved 8.0 cm, Rf = 3.2/8.0 = 0.40. For a given solvent and paper under the same conditions, a substance always has the same Rf, so Rf values help to identify substances.
Why use pencil, not ink? Pencil graphite does not dissolve in the solvent, but ink contains dyes that would run and interfere with the results.

Uses. Testing food colours and additives; identifying dyes in forensic work; detecting drugs and banned substances in sport; monitoring pollutants in water; checking purity of chemicals and medicines; analysing plant pigments (chlorophyll, carotene). Other types: thin-layer chromatography (TLC), column chromatography and gas chromatography, which work on the same principle.

illustrations.caption: Paper chromatogram
illustrations.description: A paper strip with baseline and spots at different heights, solvent front marked.

workedExamples.problem: In a chromatography experiment a spot moved 3.2 cm and the solvent front moved 8.0 cm. Calculate Rf.
steps: Rf = distance moved by spot/distance moved by solvent front.

workedExamples.problem: A chromatogram of ink shows three spots. What does it tell you about the ink?
steps: Each spot is a different substance (dye).
The ink contains at least three dyes; it is a mixture.
workedExamples.answer: It is a mixture of at least three substances

workedExamples.problem: A pure substance has Rf = 0.35. If the solvent front moves 12 cm, how far will the spot have moved?

realWorldApplications: Forensic science: identifying inks, dyes and drugs.
Food industry: checking colourings and additives.
Anti-doping tests in sport.
Environmental testing: finding pollutants in water.
commonMistakes: Drawing the baseline in ink.
Putting the solvent above the baseline, which washes the sample away.
Measuring from the bottom of the paper instead of the baseline.
Using different solvents when comparing Rf values.
summary: Chromatography separates mixtures by different rates of movement in a solvent.
Use pencil; solvent must be below the baseline.
Rf = distance by spot ÷ distance by solvent front (no units, less than 1).
One spot suggests a pure substance.

concepts.title: Pure and impure substances and criteria for purity
learningObjectives: Define pure and impure substances
Explain how melting and boiling points show purity
Describe the effect of impurities on melting and boiling points
Describe other tests for purity and why purity matters

keyTerms.definition: A single element or compound with a fixed composition and fixed properties.
A substance contaminated with other substances (a mixture).
The range of temperatures over which a substance melts.
An unwanted substance mixed with the main substance.

concepts.definition: A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point and boiling point and gives a single spot in chromatography. Impurities lower the melting point, raise the boiling point and make the change happen over a range of temperatures.
explanation: In everyday language 'pure water' may mean clean water, but in chemistry a pure substance contains only one substance, either one element or one compound. Distilled water is nearly pure. Tap water, sea water, air and bottled 'pure water' are mixtures (they contain dissolved salts and gases).

Criteria for purity. (1) Melting point: a pure solid melts at a sharp, fixed temperature (pure ice melts at 0 °C; naphthalene at about 80 °C). An impure solid melts over a range and at a LOWER temperature. (2) Boiling point: a pure liquid boils at a fixed temperature at a given pressure (water at 100 °C; ethanol at about 78 °C). Impurities raise the boiling point and make it vary during boiling. (3) Chromatography: a pure substance gives one spot. (4) Density and refractive index: pure substances have fixed values. (5) Appearance and other tests (clear and colourless where expected).

Why do impurities change melting and boiling points? Impurity particles interfere with the regular arrangement of the pure substance's particles, so less energy is needed to break the solid pattern, giving a lower melting point. In a solution, the dissolved particles reduce the tendency of the solvent to escape as vapour, so a higher temperature is needed to boil. Common examples: salt water freezes below 0 °C and boils above 100 °C; adding salt to ice lowers its melting point (used in cooling ice cream mixtures and in cold countries to melt ice on roads).

How to test purity of a solid in the laboratory. Heat a small sample in a melting point tube in an oil bath with a thermometer. Record the temperature at which melting starts and ends. If the range is narrow (about 1 °C) and matches the known value, the sample is probably pure.

Why does purity matter? Medicines must be pure to be safe and effective; impurities may be toxic. Food must be free from harmful contamination; drinking water must meet purity standards; electronic components need highly pure silicon; chemical reactions give predictable products only if reagents are pure. NAFDAC checks the purity of food and drugs in Nigeria.

Methods used to purify substances: filtration, crystallisation, distillation, fractional distillation, sublimation and chromatography, depending on the impurity and the substance. Recrystallisation (dissolve in hot solvent, filter, cool, collect crystals) is a common method for solids.
Remember that 'pure' is relative. No substance is 100% pure; we describe purity as a percentage (for example 99.9% pure).

illustrations.caption: Effect of salt on water
illustrations.description: Impurity changes the freezing and boiling points.

workedExamples.problem: A solid melts between 74 °C and 78 °C. The pure compound is known to melt sharply at 80 °C. What can you say about the sample?
steps: The melting point is lower than the pure value and occurs over a range.
Both indicate that the sample is impure.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why salt is added to ice in making ice cream or cooling drinks.
steps: Salt lowers the melting point of ice, so the ice melts below 0 °C.
The melting ice absorbs heat from the mixture, making it colder than 0 °C.
workedExamples.answer: Salt lowers the melting point, so the ice-salt mixture can reach temperatures below 0 °C

workedExamples.problem: Which is a pure substance: sea water, distilled water, air or soil?
steps: Sea water, air and soil are mixtures.

realWorldApplications: Pharmacy: purity tests for drugs.
Food safety: checking additives and contaminants.
Water supply: testing drinking water standards.
Electronics and chemical industry: high-purity materials.
commonMistakes: Calling bottled or tap water 'pure' in the chemical sense.
Saying impurities raise the melting point (they lower it).
Saying impurities lower the boiling point (they raise it).
Using only one test to prove purity.
summary: Pure substances have fixed melting and boiling points.
Impurities lower melting point and raise boiling point, and spread them over a range.
Chromatography: one spot means pure.
Purity matters for health, safety and industry.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Particulate Nature of Matter
topics.overview: Explores what matter is made of: the history of the atom, atoms, molecules and ions, Dalton's theory and its modifications, the modern atomic model, the subatomic particles, atomic number, mass number and isotopes, relative atomic and molecular masses, and percentage composition calculations.

concepts.title: History of the atom: from Democritus to the quantum model
learningObjectives: Outline the development of atomic models from Democritus to the modern model
State the key experiment and conclusion of Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr and Chadwick
Explain Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment and its observations
Explain why scientific models change over time

keyTerms.definition: The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A negatively charged particle that moves around the nucleus.
A positively charged particle (helium nucleus) given off by some radioactive substances.
A simplified representation used to explain observations; models are improved when new evidence appears.

concepts.definition: The idea of the atom has changed over 2 400 years: from indivisible solid particles (Democritus, Dalton), to a sphere with electrons embedded (Thomson), to a tiny nucleus with orbiting electrons (Rutherford, Bohr), to the modern quantum-mechanical model with electron clouds.
explanation: Democritus (about 400 BC). The Greek philosopher Democritus suggested that matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles which he called atomos (meaning 'cannot be cut'). He had no experiments to prove it; it was a philosophical idea. Aristotle disagreed and the idea was neglected for about 2 000 years.

John Dalton (1803 to 1808). The English schoolteacher and chemist Dalton revived the atom as a scientific theory to explain chemical laws. He pictured atoms as tiny, solid, indivisible spheres, with atoms of the same element identical and those of different elements different. Dalton's atom is sometimes called the 'billiard ball' model.

J. J. Thomson (1897). Thomson studied cathode rays (beams in a vacuum tube) and showed that they are streams of very light, negatively charged particles, now called electrons, which are present in all atoms. Since atoms are neutral overall, he proposed the 'plum pudding' model: a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it like currants in a pudding. So atoms were divisible after all.

Ernest Rutherford (1909 to 1911). Rutherford's team (Geiger and Marsden) fired a beam of positively charged alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil and detected where they went. Observations: most alpha particles passed straight through; some were deflected through small angles; a very few (about 1 in 8 000) bounced back. Conclusions: most of the atom is empty space (so most particles passed through); the atom has a very small, dense, positively charged centre, the nucleus (which deflected or repelled the positive alpha particles); the electrons are outside the nucleus. The nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller than the atom. This 'nuclear model' replaced the plum pudding model.

Niels Bohr (1913). Bohr proposed that electrons move round the nucleus in fixed circular paths called energy levels or shells, each with a definite energy, and that electrons give out or take in energy only when they jump between levels. This explained the coloured lines in the spectrum of hydrogen. The idea of electron shells is the basis of the electronic configurations you will study.

James Chadwick (1932). Chadwick discovered the neutron, a particle with about the same mass as the proton but no charge, inside the nucleus. This explained why atoms are heavier than the total mass of their protons and why isotopes exist. Earlier, Goldstein (1886) found positive rays, and Rutherford identified the proton as the hydrogen nucleus (about 1919).

The quantum-mechanical model (1920s). Schrodinger, Heisenberg and others showed that electrons do not follow exact orbits; we can only describe the probability of finding an electron in a region of space called an orbital, which forms an electron cloud around the nucleus. This is the modern atomic model.

Why models change. Each model explained the evidence available at the time. When new experiments gave results that the old model could not explain, scientists improved or replaced the model. This is how science progresses.

rows: atoms as solid indivisible spheres; atomic theory
nucleus discovered by gold foil experiment
nucleus is small, dense and positively charged

illustrations.caption: Atomic models
illustrations.description: Four panels: Dalton sphere, Thomson plum pudding, Rutherford nuclear model, Bohr shell model.

workedExamples.problem: In Rutherford's experiment most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What did this show?
steps: Most particles did not meet anything solid.
So most of the atom is empty space.
workedExamples.answer: Most of the atom is empty space

workedExamples.problem: Why did a few alpha particles bounce back?
steps: They were repelled by a small, dense, positively charged region, the nucleus.
workedExamples.answer: The nucleus is small, dense and positive

workedExamples.problem: What did Chadwick discover and why was it important?
steps: He discovered the neutron: a neutral particle in the nucleus with mass similar to a proton.
It explained the extra mass of atoms and the existence of isotopes.

realWorldApplications: Nuclear energy and medicine (radiotherapy, imaging) rely on nuclear structure.
Electronics: quantum models led to transistors and lasers.
Chemistry: electron shells explain bonding and the periodic table.
Understanding of how scientific theories are tested and improved.
commonMistakes: Saying Democritus proved the atom (it was an idea, not an experiment).
Mixing up the models of Thomson and Rutherford.
Thinking the nucleus fills most of the atom.
Believing the electron orbits are fixed paths in the modern model.
summary: Democritus: atomos; Dalton: solid sphere; Thomson: electron; Rutherford: nucleus; Bohr: energy levels; Chadwick: neutron; quantum model: electron cloud.
Gold foil: most pass through, few deflect, very few bounce back.
Models are improved by new evidence.

concepts.title: Atoms, molecules and ions
learningObjectives: Define atom, molecule and ion
Distinguish monatomic, diatomic and polyatomic molecules
Explain how ions form (cations and anions)
Give examples of simple and polyatomic ions
Distinguish molecules from ionic lattices

keyTerms.definition: A group of two or more atoms bonded together (covalently) that acts as a unit.
The number of atoms in one molecule of an element or compound.
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electric charge.
A positive ion (formed by loss of electrons).
A negative ion (formed by gain of electrons).
An ion made of several atoms bonded together, carrying one overall charge (for example SO4^2-).

concepts.definition: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together. An ion is a charged atom or group of atoms formed by loss or gain of electrons.
explanation: Atoms. The atom is the basic unit of an element. Atoms of metals such as iron (Fe), copper (Cu) and sodium (Na), and of carbon (C), exist as continuous structures, and we use the symbol to represent them. Atoms of noble gases, such as helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar), exist alone and are described as monatomic.

Molecules. A molecule forms when atoms share electrons. Molecules of elements: hydrogen H2, nitrogen N2, oxygen O2, fluorine F2, chlorine Cl2, bromine Br2 and iodine I2 are diatomic (two atoms); ozone O3 is triatomic; phosphorus P4 has four atoms; sulphur S8 has eight. Molecules of compounds contain atoms of different elements: water H2O, carbon dioxide CO2, ammonia NH3, methane CH4, glucose C6H12O6. The number of atoms in a molecule is its atomicity.

Reading formulae. In H2O the small 2 after H means two atoms of hydrogen; no number means one atom of oxygen. In 3H2O the big 3 means three molecules of water, with six H atoms and three O atoms in total.

Ions. An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons (+) and electrons (-). If it loses electrons it becomes positive; if it gains electrons it becomes negative. A sodium atom (11 protons, 11 electrons) loses one electron to become Na+ (11 protons, 10 electrons). A chlorine atom (17 protons, 17 electrons) gains one electron to become Cl- (17 protons, 18 electrons). Metals tend to form cations (Na+, Mg^2+, Al^3+); non-metals tend to form anions (Cl-, O^2-, S^2-).
Polyatomic ions. Some ions consist of groups of atoms: ammonium NH4+, hydroxide OH-, nitrate NO3-, carbonate CO3^2-, sulphate SO4^2-, phosphate PO4^3-. The charge belongs to the whole group.

Ionic compounds. Oppositely charged ions attract strongly and arrange themselves in a regular giant lattice, for example sodium chloride. There are no separate molecules in an ionic compound, so its formula (NaCl) shows only the simplest ratio of ions and is called a formula unit.
Comparing the three. An atom is neutral; a molecule is neutral and made of bonded atoms; an ion carries a charge. Charge is written as a superscript after the symbol: Na+, Mg^2+, Cl-, O^2-.

Particles are extremely small: a water molecule is about 0.3 nm across, and a drop of water contains billions of billions of molecules. The movement of these particles explains diffusion, dissolving and changes of state.

workedExamples.problem: How many atoms of each element are in one molecule of H2SO4? What is the atomicity?
steps: Two H atoms, one S atom and four O atoms.

workedExamples.problem: Describe how a magnesium atom forms Mg^2+.
steps: A magnesium atom has 12 protons and 12 electrons.
It loses two electrons, leaving 12 protons and 10 electrons, so the charge is +2.

workedExamples.problem: State the number of atoms of each element in 3Ca(OH)2.
steps: Each Ca(OH)2 has 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H.
For 3 units: 3 Ca, 6 O and 6 H.

realWorldApplications: Medicine and biology: ions such as Na+ and K+ carry signals in nerves.
Water treatment: ions control hardness.
Batteries and electrolysis rely on moving ions.
Food: table salt is an ionic compound; sugar is made of molecules.
commonMistakes: Saying ionic compounds are made of molecules.
Confusing the small subscript with the large coefficient.
Writing charges as subscripts.
Thinking an ion has a different number of protons than the atom (protons stay the same).
summary: Atom: neutral basic unit of an element.
Molecule: two or more atoms bonded; atomicity is the number of atoms in it.
Ion: charged particle formed by electron loss (cation) or gain (anion).
Ionic compounds form lattices.

concepts.title: Dalton's atomic theory and its modifications
learningObjectives: State the postulates of Dalton's atomic theory
Explain how the theory accounted for the laws of chemical combination
State the modifications made to the theory in the light of later discoveries
Judge which parts of the theory remain valid

keyTerms.definition: A basic assumption of a theory.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Atoms of different elements with the same mass number.
A substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.

concepts.definition: Dalton's atomic theory (1803-1808): matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical; atoms of different elements differ; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; and atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions.
explanation: Dalton's five postulates. (1) All matter is made up of very small particles called atoms. (2) Atoms of the same element are identical in mass, size and properties. (3) Atoms of different elements have different masses and properties. (4) Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds. (5) Atoms cannot be created, destroyed or changed into atoms of another element in a chemical reaction; a chemical reaction is only a rearrangement of atoms.

What the theory explained. Postulate 5 explains the law of conservation of mass: if atoms are only rearranged, the total mass must stay the same. Postulates 3 and 4 explain the law of definite proportions: a compound always contains the same elements in the same mass ratio because atoms combine in fixed numbers. Postulate 4 also predicted the law of multiple proportions, for example carbon forms CO and CO2, in which the masses of oxygen combining with a fixed mass of carbon are in the ratio 1:2.

Modifications. Later discoveries showed that parts of the theory need correcting. (1) Atoms are NOT indivisible: they contain protons, neutrons and electrons. (2) Atoms of the same element are not all identical in mass: isotopes exist (chlorine-35 and chlorine-37). (3) Atoms of different elements can have the same mass: isobars such as argon-40 and calcium-40. (4) Atoms can be changed from one element to another in nuclear reactions such as radioactive decay and nuclear fission, so postulate 5 holds only for chemical reactions. (5) Atoms of the same element are not all identical in other respects (for example ions of an element differ from atoms).

What remains valid. Matter is made of atoms; atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties (although atoms of an element share the same number of protons); atoms combine in fixed ratios (with some exceptions in non-stoichiometric compounds); and in chemical reactions atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so mass and atoms are conserved.

Scientific theories develop. Dalton's theory was an excellent starting point: it explained known laws and made predictions. New evidence (from electrons, radioactivity and mass spectrometers) required improvements. The modern atomic theory builds on Dalton's work.
Exam tip: state the postulate, then its correction clearly, for example 'Postulate: atoms of the same element are identical. Modification: isotopes of the same element have different masses.'

rows: atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons
atoms of an element are identical in mass
atoms of different elements have different masses
isobars (different elements, same mass number) exist
atoms cannot be changed into other atoms
possible in nuclear reactions (radioactivity, fission, fusion)
atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios
true for most small molecules; exceptions exist

workedExamples.problem: State two postulates of Dalton's theory that are no longer fully accepted, with the reason.
steps: Atoms are indivisible: they contain subatomic particles.
Atoms of the same element are identical: isotopes differ in mass.
workedExamples.answer: Indivisibility and identical atoms; corrected by subatomic particles and isotopes

workedExamples.problem: Use Dalton's theory to explain the law of conservation of mass.
steps: In a chemical reaction atoms are only rearranged.
Since no atoms are created or destroyed, the total mass before equals the total mass after.
workedExamples.answer: Atoms are conserved, so mass is conserved

workedExamples.problem: Chlorine has isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37. Which postulate does this contradict?
steps: Postulate 2: atoms of an element are identical in mass.
Isotopes of chlorine have different masses.
workedExamples.answer: The postulate that atoms of the same element are identical

realWorldApplications: Foundation of modern chemistry and chemical equations.
Helps to explain why reactions follow fixed ratios in industry.
Teaches how scientists improve theories using evidence.
Nuclear technology shows where the original theory fails.
commonMistakes: Saying Dalton's theory is wrong; it was largely correct and has been refined.
Mixing isotopes with isobars.
Forgetting that postulate 5 applies only to chemical reactions.
Not giving both the postulate and the modification.
summary: Five postulates: atoms, identical for an element, different for different elements, fixed whole-number ratios, rearranged in reactions.
Modifications: subatomic particles, isotopes, isobars, nuclear reactions.
Theory supports conservation of mass and definite proportions.

concepts.title: The modern atomic theory
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of the atom according to modern theory
Explain electron shells (energy levels) and orbitals
State the maximum number of electrons in the first four shells
Explain why atoms are mostly empty space

keyTerms.definition: A region around the nucleus where electrons of a certain energy are found.
A region of space where an electron is most likely to be found.
Electrons in the outermost shell, which take part in bonding.
The three-dimensional region around the nucleus where electrons are found.

concepts.definition: According to modern atomic theory, an atom consists of a very small, dense nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons moving in energy levels (shells) as a cloud. Most of the atom's volume is empty space, and the number of protons determines the element.
explanation: Structure of the atom. At the centre is the nucleus, which contains protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral). It holds almost all of the atom's mass, but is tiny: its diameter is about 10^-15 m compared with 10^-10 m for the whole atom, so the atom is about 100 000 times wider than its nucleus. If the nucleus were a pea, the atom would be as large as a stadium. Outside the nucleus are electrons (negative), which are very light and move rapidly in the space around it.

Energy levels. Electrons are arranged in shells (energy levels) numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 ... outward from the nucleus. Shell 1 is nearest and has the lowest energy. The maximum number of electrons in shell n is 2n^2: shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 18, shell 4 holds 32. For the first 20 elements, shell 3 is treated as holding 8 before shell 4 begins to fill, giving the pattern 2, 8, 8, 2 (for calcium, 2, 8, 8, 2).

Examples of electron arrangements. Hydrogen (1 electron): 1. Carbon (6): 2, 4. Oxygen (8): 2, 6. Sodium (11): 2, 8, 1. Chlorine (17): 2, 8, 7. Calcium (20): 2, 8, 8, 2. The outermost electrons, the valence electrons, decide how the atom reacts. You will study this further in the chapter on chemical combination.

Orbitals. In the modern quantum-mechanical model, we cannot say exactly where an electron is at any moment; we can only give the probability of finding it. A region where this probability is high is an orbital. Shells are made of sub-shells (s, p, d, f) which contain orbitals; an s orbital is spherical and a p orbital is dumb-bell shaped, and each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons.

Key points of the modern theory: (1) the atom is mostly empty space; (2) the nucleus is small, dense and positively charged; (3) the number of protons (the atomic number) defines the element; (4) a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons; (5) electrons occupy energy levels and orbitals; (6) atoms of an element can have different numbers of neutrons (isotopes).
Why is the atom mostly empty? The electrons are far from the nucleus compared with the nucleus' size. That is why most alpha particles passed straight through gold foil.

The model explains chemical behaviour. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and therefore similar properties. Metals tend to lose electrons, non-metals to gain or share them.

illustrations.caption: Atom with shells
illustrations.description: Nucleus with protons and neutrons, surrounded by shells with electrons (sodium: 2, 8, 1).

workedExamples.problem: Write the electron arrangement of (a) oxygen (atomic number 8) (b) sodium (11) (c) calcium (20).
How many valence electrons do (a) chlorine (2, 8, 7) and (b) magnesium (2, 8, 2) have?
steps: Valence electrons are in the outermost shell.

workedExamples.problem: An atom has a diameter of 1 × 10^-10 m and its nucleus a diameter of 1 × 10^-15 m. How many times wider is the atom?

realWorldApplications: Chemistry: predicting how elements react from their electrons.
Electronics: movement of electrons in semiconductors.
Spectroscopy: electrons moving between levels produce light of specific colours (neon signs, fireworks).
Medicine: imaging and radiotherapy.
commonMistakes: Thinking electrons orbit like planets on fixed paths.
Forgetting the 2, 8, 8, 2 pattern for the first 20 elements.
Counting inner electrons as valence electrons.
Believing the nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume.
summary: Atom = tiny dense nucleus (protons + neutrons) + electrons in shells.
Atom is mostly empty space.
Shell capacity 2, 8, 18, 32 (2n^2); first 20 elements: 2, 8, 8, 2.
Valence electrons control chemical behaviour.

concepts.title: Constituents of the atom: protons, neutrons and electrons
learningObjectives: State the relative mass and charge of the proton, neutron and electron
Describe where each particle is found
Explain why atoms are electrically neutral
Calculate numbers of subatomic particles in atoms and ions

keyTerms.definition: A positively charged particle in the nucleus; relative mass 1, charge +1.
An uncharged particle in the nucleus; relative mass 1, charge 0.
A negatively charged particle outside the nucleus; relative mass about 1/1840, charge -1.
A particle in the nucleus (a proton or a neutron).
A unit of mass equal to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

concepts.definition: An atom contains three kinds of subatomic particles: protons (+1, mass 1), neutrons (0, mass 1) and electrons (-1, mass about 1/1840). Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside it.
explanation: Protons. Found in the nucleus, carry a positive charge (+1 in relative units, 1.6 × 10^-19 coulomb) and have a relative mass of 1 (actually 1.67 × 10^-27 kg). The number of protons is the atomic number and identifies the element: every atom with 6 protons is carbon.

Neutrons. Found in the nucleus; they carry no charge; their mass is almost the same as a proton's (relative mass 1). Neutrons help to hold the nucleus together. Hydrogen-1 has no neutrons; most other atoms have at least as many neutrons as protons.

Electrons. Found in shells outside the nucleus; they carry a negative charge (-1) and are extremely light, about 1/1840 of a proton's mass (9.11 × 10^-31 kg). In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges cancel and the atom has no overall charge.
Where the mass is. Because electrons are so light, almost all the mass of an atom (more than 99.9%) is in the nucleus, which is why atomic mass is calculated from protons plus neutrons only.

Calculations. Atomic number Z = number of protons. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = A - Z. For a neutral atom, electrons = Z. For an ion: electrons = Z - charge. Examples: sodium atom (Z = 11, A = 23): 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons. Na+ ion: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 10 electrons. Chloride ion Cl- (Z = 17, A = 35): 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons.
Charge of an ion. Charge = protons - electrons. For aluminium ion Al^3+ (Z = 13): electrons = 13 - 3 = 10. For sulphide S^2- (Z = 16): electrons = 16 + 2 = 18.

Comparing the three: proton and neutron have equal mass but only the proton is charged; the electron has far less mass than either. The number of protons never changes in a chemical reaction; only electrons are gained, lost or shared.

illustrations.caption: Particles in some atoms and ions

workedExamples.problem: An atom has atomic number 19 and mass number 39. Find the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Find the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the Al^3+ ion (Z = 13, A = 27).
Why is an atom electrically neutral?
steps: The number of protons (positive) equals the number of electrons (negative).
workedExamples.answer: Equal numbers of protons and electrons

realWorldApplications: Chemistry: reactions involve electrons; the number of protons identifies elements.
Electricity: moving electrons form an electric current.
Medicine and nuclear energy: changes in the nucleus.
Understanding ions in batteries and body fluids.
commonMistakes: Thinking electrons contribute much to mass.
Mixing up atomic number and mass number.
Forgetting to adjust electrons for ions.
Believing the number of protons changes when an ion forms.
summary: Proton: +1, mass 1, nucleus. Neutron: 0, mass 1, nucleus. Electron: -1, mass 1/1840, shells.
Neutrons = A - Z.
Neutral atom: electrons = protons.
Ion: electrons = Z - charge.

concepts.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
learningObjectives: Define atomic number and mass number
Write and interpret nuclide notation
Define isotopes and give examples
Explain that isotopes have identical chemical properties but different physical properties
Describe uses of radioactive isotopes

keyTerms.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).
An atom characterised by its atomic number and mass number.
An unstable isotope that gives off radiation.

concepts.definition: Atomic number Z = number of protons. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. An atom is written ^A_Z X. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).
explanation: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons and defines the element. All carbon atoms have Z = 6. Mass number (A) is the number of protons plus neutrons. The number of neutrons is A - Z. Notation: the symbol with the mass number at the top left and the atomic number at the bottom left, for example ^35_17 Cl for chlorine with 17 protons and 35 - 17 = 18 neutrons. The element can also be written as chlorine-35.

Isotopes. Chlorine atoms all have 17 protons, but some have 18 neutrons (chlorine-35) and some 20 neutrons (chlorine-37). These are isotopes of chlorine. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (1 proton, 0 neutrons), deuterium (1 proton, 1 neutron) and tritium (1 proton, 2 neutrons). Carbon has isotopes carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14. Isotopes of an element occupy the same position in the periodic table (the name means 'same place').

Properties. Isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons, so they have the same chemical properties (they react in the same way). They differ in mass, so physical properties that depend on mass, such as density, melting point, boiling point and rate of diffusion, differ slightly.

Natural abundance. Most elements occur naturally as mixtures of isotopes in fixed proportions: chlorine is about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, which is why its relative atomic mass is about 35.5 and not a whole number.

Radioisotopes and their uses. Some isotopes are unstable and give off radiation.
