Uses: carbon-14 for radiocarbon dating of ancient wood, bones and fabrics; iodine-131 for diagnosing and treating thyroid disease; cobalt-60 for treating cancer and sterilising medical equipment; uranium-235 as nuclear fuel; tracers in medicine, industry and agriculture; detecting leaks in pipes; and smoke detectors (americium-241). Safe handling and disposal are essential because radiation can damage living cells.

Examples to calculate. Iron-56 (Z = 26): 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons. Uranium-235 (Z = 92): 92 protons, 143 neutrons. Carbon-14 (Z = 6): 6 protons, 8 neutrons. Isotopes of oxygen ^16_8 O, ^17_8 O and ^18_8 O have 8, 9 and 10 neutrons respectively.
Do not confuse isotopes with isobars (same mass number, different elements: argon-40 and calcium-40), or with isotones (same number of neutrons, different protons).

rows: diagnosis and treatment of thyroid disease

illustrations.caption: Nuclide notation
illustrations.description: The symbol of chlorine with mass number 35 at top left and atomic number 17 at bottom left.

workedExamples.problem: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ^35_17 Cl and ^37_17 Cl. Are they isotopes?
steps: Same atomic number, different mass number: they are isotopes.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why isotopes have the same chemical properties.
steps: Chemical properties depend on the number and arrangement of electrons.
Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they react in the same way.

workedExamples.problem: Carbon-14 has atomic number 6. Find the number of neutrons and name one use of this isotope.
steps: Carbon-14 is used for radiocarbon dating.
workedExamples.answer: 8 neutrons; used for dating ancient objects

realWorldApplications: Archaeology: radiocarbon dating of ancient remains.
Medicine: radioisotopes diagnose and treat diseases.
Industry: tracers detect pipe leaks and measure thickness.
Energy: uranium-235 in nuclear reactors.
commonMistakes: Saying isotopes have different numbers of protons.
Saying isotopes have different chemical properties.
Confusing mass number with atomic mass.
Mixing up isotopes and isobars.
summary: Z = protons; A = protons + neutrons; neutrons = A - Z.
Isotopes: same Z, different A.
Same chemical properties; slightly different physical properties.
Radioisotopes have many useful applications but need careful handling.

concepts.title: Relative atomic mass
learningObjectives: Define relative atomic mass using the carbon-12 scale
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances
Find abundance from relative atomic mass
Explain why relative atomic masses are often not whole numbers

keyTerms.definition: The average mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12 the mass of an atom of carbon-12 (taking isotopes and their abundances into account).
The scale in which an atom of carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12 units.
The percentage of each isotope in a natural sample of the element.

concepts.definition: Relative atomic mass Ar = (average mass of one atom of the element) ÷ (1/12 × mass of one atom of carbon-12). It is a weighted average of the masses of the isotopes: Ar = Σ (isotope mass × % abundance)/100. It has no units.
explanation: The mass of a single atom is far too small to handle (a carbon atom is about 2 × 10^-26 kg). So chemists compare atomic masses with a standard. The standard chosen is the carbon-12 atom, assigned a mass of exactly 12 units (atomic mass units, u). One atomic mass unit is 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

Definition. The relative atomic mass of an element is the average mass of an atom of the element, compared with one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Because it is a ratio, it has no units. Examples: Ar of hydrogen is about 1, carbon 12, nitrogen 14, oxygen 16, sodium 23, magnesium 24, aluminium 27, sulphur 32, chlorine 35.5, calcium 40, iron 56, copper 63.5 (often used as 64), zinc 65.

Why non-whole numbers? Most elements are mixtures of isotopes, and the relative atomic mass is the weighted average. Chlorine: 75% of atoms are chlorine-35 and 25% are chlorine-37. Ar = (75 × 35 + 25 × 37)/100 = (2 625 + 925)/100 = 35.5. No individual chlorine atom has mass 35.5; it is the average.
Calculation method. For each isotope, multiply the mass number by its percentage abundance. Add the results and divide by 100. If abundances are given as fractions, add the products directly.

Working backwards. If an element has two isotopes of masses 10 and 11 and Ar = 10.8, let the abundance of the heavier isotope be x%. Then (10 × (100 - x) + 11 × x)/100 = 10.8, so 1 000 + x = 1 080 and x = 80. So the abundances are 20% and 80%.
Measuring Ar. Mass spectrometers measure the masses and abundances of isotopes accurately; they separate ions by mass in a magnetic field.

In calculations, use the values of Ar given in the question or on the data sheet; for WAEC and NECO, values such as H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, Mg = 24, Al = 27, S = 32, Cl = 35.5, K = 39, Ca = 40, Fe = 56, Cu = 64 and Zn = 65 are typically provided.

illustrations.caption: Relative atomic masses of common elements

workedExamples.problem: Chlorine has two isotopes: chlorine-35 (75%) and chlorine-37 (25%). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
Magnesium contains 79% of ^24Mg, 10% of ^25Mg and 11% of ^26Mg. Calculate Ar.
An element has two isotopes of masses 10 and 11 and Ar = 10.8. Find the percentage of the heavier isotope.
steps: Let the heavier isotope be x%; the lighter is (100 - x)%.

realWorldApplications: Chemistry calculations: Ar is used in every mole and mass calculation.
Mass spectrometry: forensic labs, pharmaceutical analysis.
Geology: isotopic ratios date rocks.
Industry: formula masses of reagents for production.
commonMistakes: Calculating a simple average of the mass numbers instead of a weighted one.
Forgetting to divide by 100.
Giving units (u) to a relative quantity.
Thinking an actual atom has the non-integer mass.
summary: Ar compares the average atomic mass with 1/12 of carbon-12.
Ar = Σ (mass × % abundance)/100.
Non-whole values result from isotopic mixtures.
Ar has no units.

concepts.title: Relative molecular mass and formula mass
learningObjectives: Define relative molecular mass and relative formula mass
Calculate Mr for molecules and formula units, including brackets and water of crystallisation
Interpret formulae with subscripts and coefficients

keyTerms.definition: The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in one molecule.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula unit of an ionic compound.
Water molecules that are part of a crystal structure, as in CuSO4.5H2O.

concepts.definition: Relative molecular mass (Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecule. For ionic compounds the same calculation gives the relative formula mass. Mr has no units.
explanation: Definition. Mr compares the mass of a molecule with 1/12 of the mass of carbon-12. To calculate it, add the Ar of every atom in the formula. Use the formula's subscripts to count the atoms.

Water, H2O: 2 × 1 + 16 = 18. Carbon dioxide, CO2: 12 + 2 × 16 = 44. Ammonia, NH3: 14 + 3 × 1 = 17. Sulphuric acid, H2SO4: 2 × 1 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 98. Sodium hydroxide, NaOH: 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Glucose, C6H12O6: 6 × 12 + 12 × 1 + 6 × 16 = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180.

Brackets. A subscript outside a bracket multiplies everything inside. Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74. Ammonium sulphate, (NH4)2SO4: 2 × (14 + 4) + 32 + 4 × 16 = 36 + 32 + 64 = 132. Aluminium sulphate, Al2(SO4)3: 2 × 27 + 3 × (32 + 64) = 54 + 288 = 342.

Water of crystallisation. In a hydrated salt such as CuSO4.5H2O, the dot means 'combined with'. The mass of the water is included. Mr (CuSO4.5H2O) = 64 + 32 + 64 + 5 × 18 = 160 + 90 = 250 (taking Cu = 64). Also Na2CO3.10H2O: 2 × 23 + 12 + 48 + 10 × 18 = 106 + 180 = 286; MgSO4.7H2O: 24 + 32 + 64 + 7 × 18 = 120 + 126 = 246.

Formula mass for ionic compounds. NaCl is not made of molecules, so we speak of its relative formula mass: 23 + 35.5 = 58.5. In school the term 'relative molecular mass' is often used for both; use the term the question uses.

Reading formulae. Subscripts are inside the formula (the 2 in H2O); coefficients are in front and count whole molecules or formula units (the 3 in 3H2O). Mass of 3H2O = 3 × 18 = 54. Coefficients do not change the Mr of one molecule.
Why Mr is useful. It converts between mass and number of moles (n = m/M), and is used to calculate percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulae, and quantities in reactions.

Common errors: forgetting to multiply the atoms inside brackets, forgetting the water of crystallisation, mixing up the Ar of elements with similar symbols (for example Co cobalt and CO carbon monoxide), and adding atomic numbers instead of relative atomic masses.

illustrations.caption: Relative molecular and formula masses
illustrations.description: Using Ar: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, Ca 40, Cu 64.

workedExamples.problem: Calculate the relative molecular mass of (a) H2SO4 (b) Ca(OH)2 (c) (NH4)2SO4. (H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32, Ca = 40)
Calculate the relative formula mass of CuSO4.5H2O. (Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
Calculate the relative formula mass of aluminium sulphate, Al2(SO4)3. (Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16)

realWorldApplications: Pharmacy and medicine: calculating doses by moles of drug.
Industry: calculating reagent quantities.
Agriculture: calculating nitrogen content of fertilisers.
Laboratories: making solutions of exact concentrations.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the subscript outside brackets.
Leaving out the water of crystallisation.
Using atomic numbers instead of relative atomic masses.
Adding the coefficient into the Mr of one molecule.
summary: Mr = sum of Ar of all atoms in the formula.
Brackets multiply everything inside.
Include water of crystallisation in hydrated salts.
Mr has no units; ionic compounds have formula mass.

concepts.title: Percentage composition by mass
learningObjectives: Calculate the percentage by mass of an element in a compound
Calculate the mass of an element in a given mass of a compound
Compare compounds (such as fertilisers) by percentage composition
Calculate the percentage of water of crystallisation

keyTerms.definition: The percentage by mass of each element in a compound.
The percentage of the sample that is the stated compound.

concepts.definition: Percentage of an element in a compound = (number of atoms × Ar of the element ÷ Mr of the compound) × 100.
explanation: The composition of a compound can be given as the percentage by mass of each element. It is the same for every sample of the compound (law of definite proportions).

Method. (1) Write the formula and calculate Mr. (2) Find the total mass of the element in one formula (number of atoms × Ar). (3) Divide by Mr and multiply by 100. Example, water H2O (Mr = 18): H = 2/18 × 100 = 11.1%; O = 16/18 × 100 = 88.9%. The percentages must add to 100.

Mass of an element in a given mass. Mass of element = % of element × mass of compound. Ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3 (Mr = 80) has nitrogen 28/80 = 35%. In 50 kg of ammonium nitrate, nitrogen = 0.35 × 50 = 17.5 kg. Iron(III) oxide Fe2O3 (Mr = 160): Fe = 112/160 = 70%; in 400 kg of the oxide there is 0.70 × 400 = 280 kg of iron.

Comparing fertilisers. A farmer wants the most nitrogen per kilogram. Urea CO(NH2)2 (Mr = 60): N = 28/60 = 46.7%. Ammonium nitrate: 35%. Ammonium sulphate (NH4)2SO4 (Mr = 132): N = 28/132 = 21.2%. Urea has the highest nitrogen content.

Water of crystallisation. In CuSO4.5H2O (Mr = 250), the water makes up 90/250 × 100 = 36% of the mass. In MgSO4.7H2O (Mr = 246), the water is 126/246 × 100 = 51.2%. When the crystals are heated, the mass lost corresponds to this water.
Percentage purity. If a sample of calcium carbonate contains 90% pure CaCO3, then 100 g of the sample has 90 g of CaCO3. Percentage purity = (mass of pure compound/mass of sample) × 100.
Check: the percentages of all elements in a compound must add to 100% (allowing for rounding). If they do not, recheck the Mr.

illustrations.caption: Nitrogen in fertilisers
illustrations.description: Higher % means more nitrogen per kg.

workedExamples.problem: Calculate the percentage by mass of (a) hydrogen and (b) oxygen in water. (H = 1, O = 16)
Find the mass of nitrogen in 50 kg of ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3. (H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)
Calculate the percentage of water of crystallisation in CuSO4.5H2O. (Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
Which contains more nitrogen by mass: urea CO(NH2)2 or ammonium sulphate (NH4)2SO4? (C = 12, N = 14, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)

realWorldApplications: Agriculture: choosing the most economical fertiliser.
Mining and metallurgy: the percentage of metal in an ore decides if mining it is worthwhile (haematite is 70% iron).
Food and nutrition labelling.
Quality control in pharmacy and industry.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply Ar by the number of atoms.
Using the wrong Mr (for example forgetting brackets).
Giving percentages that do not add up to 100.
Dividing by the mass of the sample instead of Mr.
summary: % of element = (n × Ar/Mr) × 100.
Mass of element = % × mass of compound.
Percentages of all elements add to 100.
Water of crystallisation percentage = (mass of water/Mr) × 100.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Symbols, Formulae and Equations
topics.overview: Gives chemistry its language: symbols of elements, valency and chemical formulae, systematic (IUPAC) naming, empirical and molecular formulae, the laws of chemical combination, chemical equations and how to balance them, and an introduction to calculations from equations using the mole.

concepts.title: Chemical symbols
learningObjectives: State the rules for writing chemical symbols
Write the symbols of the first twenty elements and other common elements
Explain the origin of symbols derived from Latin names
State what a symbol represents

keyTerms.definition: One or two letters that stand for an element.
The number of protons in the atom of an element.
The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles.

concepts.definition: A chemical symbol is a short way of writing the name of an element. It is one capital letter or a capital letter followed by a small letter. For example C (carbon), Ca (calcium), Cl (chlorine).
explanation: Chemists all over the world use the same symbols, so a chemical formula written in Nigeria is understood in Japan or Brazil. In ancient times alchemists used drawings; Berzelius (1813) suggested using letters from the names of the elements, which is the system used today.

Rules. (1) The symbol is the first letter of the name, written as a capital: H (hydrogen), C (carbon), N (nitrogen), O (oxygen), S (sulphur), P (phosphorus), K (potassium after the Latin kalium), I (iodine). (2) When several elements start with the same letter, a second small letter is added: Ca (calcium), Cl (chlorine), Cu (copper), Co (cobalt), Cr (chromium). (3) The second letter is always lower case: Co is cobalt, but CO is carbon monoxide (carbon and oxygen). This difference matters!

Symbols from Latin names. Some symbols come from the Latin names: sodium Na (natrium), potassium K (kalium), iron Fe (ferrum), copper Cu (cuprum), silver Ag (argentum), gold Au (aurum), lead Pb (plumbum), tin Sn (stannum), mercury Hg (hydrargyrum), antimony Sb (stibium), tungsten W (wolfram).

The first twenty elements, in order of atomic number: 1 H hydrogen, 2 He helium, 3 Li lithium, 4 Be beryllium, 5 B boron, 6 C carbon, 7 N nitrogen, 8 O oxygen, 9 F fluorine, 10 Ne neon, 11 Na sodium, 12 Mg magnesium, 13 Al aluminium, 14 Si silicon, 15 P phosphorus, 16 S sulphur, 17 Cl chlorine, 18 Ar argon, 19 K potassium, 20 Ca calcium. A useful way to learn them is in groups of ten and with a rhyme or story.
Other common elements: Mn manganese, Cr chromium, Ni nickel, Co cobalt, Zn zinc, Br bromine, Ba barium, Pb lead, Sn tin, Ag silver, Au gold, Hg mercury, I iodine.

What does a symbol represent? (1) The name of the element. (2) One atom of the element. (3) One mole of atoms of the element (6.02 × 10^23 atoms). (4) The relative atomic mass of the element (for example O represents 16). Written with a number in front, the symbol shows a number of atoms: 3C means three carbon atoms.

Symbols and formulae. Symbols combine to make formulae: H2O means two atoms of hydrogen and one of oxygen. Symbols with a charge (Na+, Cl-) show ions. Some elements exist as molecules (O2, N2, Cl2), so the formula of the element is not the same as its symbol.
Writing correctly: capital first letter, small second letter, no full stops; Cl not CL or cl; Co is not CO; Ca is not CA.

workedExamples.problem: Write the symbols of (a) magnesium (b) sodium (c) chlorine (d) phosphorus (e) potassium.
steps: Use capital then small letter, and Latin origin when needed.
(a) Mg (b) Na (from natrium) (c) Cl (d) P (e) K (from kalium).

workedExamples.problem: Explain the difference between Co and CO.
steps: Co (capital C, small o) is the symbol for the element cobalt.
CO (two capitals) is carbon (C) and oxygen (O): the compound carbon monoxide.
workedExamples.answer: Co is cobalt; CO is carbon monoxide

workedExamples.problem: What does the symbol Ca represent?
steps: One atom of calcium, or a mole of calcium atoms, with relative atomic mass 40.
workedExamples.answer: The element calcium, one atom (or one mole) of it

realWorldApplications: International communication: every chemistry book and label uses the same symbols.
Chemical formulae and equations are written using symbols.
The periodic table is organised by symbols.
Safety labels, packaging and medicine labels.
commonMistakes: Writing two capital letters for a one-element symbol (CO for cobalt).
Forgetting Latin symbols (using S for sodium or I for iron).
Writing CA, cl or other wrong cases.
Confusing the symbol of an element with the formula of its molecule.
summary: Symbol: one capital letter, or a capital plus a small letter.
Latin-derived: Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Pb, Sn, Hg.
Symbol means the element, one atom, one mole, and its Ar.
Learn the first 20 elements.

concepts.title: Chemical formulae and valency
learningObjectives: Explain what a chemical formula shows
Define valency and charge of ions
Use a table of valencies and radicals
Distinguish between molecular and ionic compounds

keyTerms.definition: A way of showing the symbols and number of atoms or ions of each element in a compound.
The combining power of an atom or ion: the number of electrons it loses, gains or shares when it forms a compound.
A group of atoms that behaves as a single charged unit, such as SO4^2-.
A small number written below and after a symbol to show how many atoms.

concepts.definition: A chemical formula shows the elements in a compound and the number of atoms (or ions) of each in the simplest unit. The valency of an element is its combining power, equal to the number of electrons it loses, gains or shares.
explanation: A formula is a short way of describing a compound. H2O tells us that a molecule of water has two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen. CO2 has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. For ionic compounds the formula shows the simplest ratio of ions: NaCl means one Na+ ion for every Cl- ion; MgCl2 means one Mg^2+ for every two Cl- ions.

Valency. Atoms combine to achieve a stable outer shell, usually 8 electrons (2 for the first shell). They do this by losing, gaining or sharing electrons. The valency tells how many electrons are involved. Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses 1 electron, so its valency is 1 and it forms Na+. Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains 1 electron, so its valency is 1 and it forms Cl-. Oxygen (2, 6) gains 2 electrons: valency 2 (O^2-). Magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses 2: valency 2 (Mg^2+). Aluminium (2, 8, 3) loses 3: valency 3 (Al^3+).

Group patterns: Group 1 metals (Li, Na, K): valency 1; Group 2 (Mg, Ca, Ba): 2; Aluminium: 3; Group 7 non-metals (F, Cl, Br, I): 1; Group 6 non-metals (O, S): 2; Nitrogen (as nitride): 3; Hydrogen: 1. Some elements have more than one valency: iron (2 or 3), copper (1 or 2), lead (2 or 4), mercury (1 or 2).

Radicals (polyatomic ions). These groups keep together in reactions and carry one charge: ammonium NH4+ (1+), hydroxide OH- (1-), nitrate NO3- (1-), hydrogencarbonate HCO3- (1-), permanganate MnO4- (1-), carbonate CO3^2- (2-), sulphate SO4^2- (2-), sulphite SO3^2- (2-), phosphate PO4^3- (3-). Learn this table; it is essential.

Molecular and ionic compounds. In covalent (molecular) compounds, atoms share electrons: the formula shows the atoms in each molecule (H2O, NH3, CH4, CO2). In ionic compounds, ions are held in a lattice: the formula shows the ratio of ions (NaCl, CaCO3). The total positive charge in an ionic compound equals the total negative charge, so the compound is neutral.

Valency in covalent compounds. In water each H shares one electron (valency 1) and O shares two (valency 2): H2O. In methane, carbon has valency 4 and hydrogen 1: CH4. In ammonia nitrogen has valency 3: NH3.
Variable valency is shown with Roman numerals in names: iron(II) is Fe^2+, iron(III) is Fe^3+, copper(I) Cu+ and copper(II) Cu^2+.
To write correct formulae you must know the symbols and valencies (or ion charges). Learn the table below by heart.

workedExamples.problem: State the valency of (a) sodium (b) calcium (c) aluminium (d) oxygen, from their electron arrangements (Na 2,8,1; Ca 2,8,8,2; Al 2,8,3; O 2,6).
Give the charge on each ion: (a) sulphate (b) nitrate (c) ammonium (d) phosphate.
What do the formulae H2O and NaCl tell you? Are both molecules?
steps: H2O: two H atoms and one O atom in a molecule: a molecular compound.
NaCl: one Na+ ion to one Cl- ion in a lattice: ionic, so there are no separate NaCl molecules.
workedExamples.answer: H2O is molecular; NaCl is ionic (formula unit)

realWorldApplications: Pharmacy: formulae of drugs give exact compositions.
Industry: ordering and mixing the correct compounds.
Medicine labels (for example sodium chloride solution, NaCl).
Chemical education and examinations.
commonMistakes: Mixing up valency with number of atoms.
Forgetting that radicals are groups with one charge.
Giving a metal a negative charge or a non-metal a positive one.
Forgetting variable valency for iron and copper.
summary: A formula shows the elements and the numbers of atoms or ions.
Valency is the combining power (electrons lost, gained or shared).
Learn the charges of common ions and radicals.
Ionic compounds are neutral overall.

concepts.title: Writing chemical formulae by the criss-cross method
learningObjectives: Write formulae for compounds from the valencies or ion charges
Use brackets for repeated radicals
Simplify formulae to the lowest ratio
Write formulae for covalent compounds

keyTerms.definition: A method of writing formulae by swapping the valency numbers of the two parts.
The simplest whole-number ratio of ions in a compound.

concepts.definition: To write a formula: write the symbols with their valencies, swap (criss-cross) the valencies to become subscripts, simplify to the lowest ratio, and use brackets around radicals when more than one is needed.
explanation: Steps. (1) Write the symbol or formula of each part, the positive part first. (2) Write the valency of each below the symbol. (3) Cross over: the valency of the first becomes the subscript of the second and vice versa. (4) Simplify if both subscripts have a common factor. (5) Leave out subscripts of 1. (6) Put brackets round a radical if its subscript is more than 1.

Example 1: sodium chloride. Na has valency 1 and Cl has valency 1. Criss-cross: Na1Cl1 gives NaCl. Example 2: magnesium chloride. Mg valency 2, Cl valency 1: Mg1Cl2 gives MgCl2. Example 3: aluminium oxide. Al valency 3, O valency 2: Al2O3. Check the charges: 2 × (3+) = 6+ and 3 × (2-) = 6-. The total is zero.

Simplifying. Magnesium oxide: Mg valency 2, O valency 2: Mg2O2, which simplifies to MgO. The ratio 2:2 is 1:1. Calcium oxide: CaO. Always check for a common factor. Be careful: only simplify when the subscripts really have a common factor and the formula is ionic; do not change molecular formulae such as H2O2.

Radicals and brackets. Calcium hydroxide: Ca^2+ and OH-: Ca(OH)2 (brackets show two hydroxide groups; without brackets Ca OH2 would suggest two H atoms). Ammonium sulphate: NH4+ and SO4^2-: (NH4)2SO4. Aluminium sulphate: Al^3+ and SO4^2-: Al2(SO4)3. Magnesium nitrate: Mg(NO3)2. Calcium phosphate: Ca^2+ and PO4^3-: Ca3(PO4)2. When the radical is needed only once, there are no brackets: sodium sulphate Na2SO4, calcium sulphate CaSO4, calcium carbonate CaCO3, sodium nitrate NaNO3.

Variable valency. Use the Roman numeral in the name. Iron(III) oxide: Fe^3+ and O^2-: Fe2O3. Iron(II) oxide: FeO. Iron(III) chloride: FeCl3. Iron(II) sulphate: FeSO4. Copper(II) oxide: CuO. Copper(I) oxide: Cu2O. Copper(II) sulphate: CuSO4.

Covalent compounds. The same idea applies to valencies: H2O (H 1, O 2), NH3 (N 3, H 1), CH4 (C 4, H 1), CO2 (carbon 4, oxygen 2: C2O4 simplifies to CO2), HCl, H2S. Many molecular formulae are learned directly.
Check your formula: the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge, and the formula must show the simplest ratio for ionic compounds.

illustrations.caption: Criss-cross method
illustrations.description: Arrows crossing from the valency of Al to the subscript of O and vice versa.

workedExamples.problem: Write the formula of aluminium sulphate.
steps: Criss-cross: Al2(SO4)3, with brackets because 3 sulphate groups are needed.

workedExamples.problem: Write the formula of calcium hydroxide and of ammonium sulphate.
Write the formula of (a) magnesium oxide (b) iron(III) oxide (c) copper(II) nitrate.
steps: (a) Mg^2+, O^2-: Mg2O2 simplifies to MgO.

realWorldApplications: Chemical industry: writing correct formulae on labels and in production plans.
Medicine and pharmacy: correct drug formulae.
Agriculture: fertiliser formulae such as (NH4)2SO4.
Laboratory work: preparing solutions of known compounds.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to simplify (writing Mg2O2).
Forgetting brackets for radicals (writing CaOH2).
Changing the radical's formula (writing Ca(O2H)2).
Using the wrong valency for variable-valency metals.
summary: Write symbols with valencies, criss-cross, simplify, bracket radicals.
Total positive charge = total negative charge.
Roman numerals show the valency of metals with more than one.
Do not change the formula of the radical itself.

concepts.title: Naming compounds using IUPAC nomenclature
learningObjectives: Name binary compounds ending in -ide
Name compounds containing oxoanions (trioxocarbonate(IV), tetraoxosulphate(VI), etc.) using IUPAC rules
Use Roman numerals (Stock numbers) for variable valency
Convert between common names and IUPAC names

keyTerms.definition: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, the body that sets rules for naming chemical compounds.
A compound made of two elements.
A negative ion containing oxygen and another element, such as carbonate.
A Roman numeral in brackets showing the oxidation state of an element, as in iron(III).

concepts.definition: IUPAC names follow rules: binary compounds end in -ide; compounds with oxygen radicals are named by the number of oxygen atoms (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra- + oxo) with the central element ending in -ate and its oxidation number in Roman numerals; metals with variable valency show it in brackets.
explanation: Why systematic names? Before IUPAC, the same compound might have different names in different places. IUPAC names tell you what elements are in the compound and the oxidation state, so the formula can be worked out from the name.

Binary compounds. Name the metal (or the first element) first, then the non-metal with its ending changed to -ide: sodium chloride (NaCl), magnesium oxide (MgO), calcium sulphide (CaS), aluminium nitride (AlN), hydrogen chloride (HCl). Special names: water (H2O), ammonia (NH3), methane (CH4).

Variable valency. If the metal can form more than one ion, give its valency in Roman numerals: FeO iron(II) oxide; Fe2O3 iron(III) oxide; FeCl2 iron(II) chloride; FeCl3 iron(III) chloride; CuO copper(II) oxide; Cu2O copper(I) oxide; PbO lead(II) oxide; PbO2 lead(IV) oxide. For non-metals that form several oxides: CO carbon(II) oxide (carbon monoxide), CO2 carbon(IV) oxide (carbon dioxide), SO2 sulphur(IV) oxide, SO3 sulphur(VI) oxide, NO2 nitrogen(IV) oxide.

Oxoanions (compounds with oxygen-containing radicals). Under the IUPAC system used in the Nigerian syllabus, the number of oxygen atoms is shown by a prefix: di-, tri-, tetra-, followed by 'oxo', then the name of the central element ending in -ate, with its oxidation number in Roman numerals. SO4^2-: tetraoxosulphate(VI); SO3^2-: trioxosulphate(IV); NO3-: trioxonitrate(V); NO2-: dioxonitrate(III); CO3^2-: trioxocarbonate(IV); PO4^3-: tetraoxophosphate(V); MnO4-: tetraoxomanganate(VII).

Compounds with these radicals. H2SO4: tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid (sulphuric acid). Na2SO4: sodium tetraoxosulphate(VI) (sodium sulphate). CuSO4: copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI). HNO3: trioxonitrate(V) acid (nitric acid). KNO3: potassium trioxonitrate(V). Na2CO3: sodium trioxocarbonate(IV). CaCO3: calcium trioxocarbonate(IV). NaHCO3: sodium hydrogentrioxocarbonate(IV). H3PO4: tetraoxophosphate(V) acid. KMnO4: potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII). (NH4)2SO4: ammonium tetraoxosulphate(VI).

Where do the Roman numerals come from? They show the oxidation state of the central atom. In SO4^2- the total charge is 2-; four oxygens contribute 4 × (-2) = -8; so sulphur must be +6, giving sulphate(VI). In NO3-: 3 × (-2) = -6; the total is -1; so nitrogen is +5: nitrate(V). In CO3^2-: -6 + x = -2 gives x = +4: carbonate(IV).

Common names remain in everyday use and in many books: sulphate, nitrate, carbonate, phosphate, permanganate, hydroxide. You should know both systems and convert between them. Note that IUPAC now recommends the spelling 'sulfur' and 'sulfate', but the Nigerian syllabus uses 'sulphur' and 'sulphate'.

Hydroxides and ammonium. NaOH sodium hydroxide; Ca(OH)2 calcium hydroxide; NH4Cl ammonium chloride; NH4OH ammonium hydroxide (aqueous ammonia). Acids: HCl hydrochloric acid, H2S hydrogen sulphide (in water, hydrosulphuric acid).

Covalent compounds with prefixes (older approach): carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, dinitrogen monoxide N2O, phosphorus pentachloride PCl5. IUPAC also accepts these, especially in introductory courses.

illustrations.caption: Oxoanions and their names
illustrations.description: Number of O atoms, central element and oxidation state.

workedExamples.problem: Name (a) KNO3 (b) Na2SO4 (c) CaCO3 using IUPAC names.
workedExamples.answer: (a) potassium trioxonitrate(V) (b) sodium tetraoxosulphate(VI) (c) calcium trioxocarbonate(IV)

workedExamples.problem: Name FeCl2, FeCl3 and Cu2O.
steps: Cu2O: copper(I) oxide (copper has charge 1+, two Cu+ for one O^2-).
workedExamples.answer: iron(II) chloride; iron(III) chloride; copper(I) oxide

workedExamples.problem: Show that the oxidation number of sulphur in SO4^2- is +6.
steps: Total charge of ion = -2, so S + (-8) = -2.
S = +6, so the name is tetraoxosulphate(VI).

realWorldApplications: Chemical labels and safety data sheets use systematic names.
Examinations use IUPAC names in questions and answers.
International trade in chemicals and scientific communication.
Understanding formulae from names and the reverse.
commonMistakes: Writing sulphate(IV) for sulphate or forgetting the Roman numeral.
Counting oxygen atoms wrongly in the prefix.
Ending names with -ate when the compound is a binary -ide.
Not using Roman numerals for iron, copper and lead.
summary: Binary compounds end in -ide.
Oxoanion: (number of O) + oxo + element-ate + (oxidation number).
Roman numeral shows the oxidation state (valency).
Know both common and IUPAC names.

concepts.title: Empirical formula and molecular formula
learningObjectives: Define empirical formula and molecular formula
Calculate the empirical formula from percentage composition or masses
Find the molecular formula from the empirical formula and relative molecular mass
Use mole ratios and rounding rules correctly
prerequisiteNotes: Relative molecular mass and percentage composition (Chapter 3)

keyTerms.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
The ratio of the amounts (in moles) of atoms combined in a compound.

concepts.definition: The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: molecular formula = (empirical formula)n, where n = relative molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.
explanation: Two formulae. Glucose has molecular formula C6H12O6 (6 C, 12 H, 6 O atoms in each molecule). Dividing all numbers by 6 gives the simplest ratio 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH2O. Ethene is C2H4 (empirical CH2); water H2O is both molecular and empirical.

Finding the empirical formula. (1) Write the mass or percentage of each element (percentages can be treated as grams in 100 g). (2) Divide each by its relative atomic mass to get the amount in moles. (3) Divide all by the smallest number to get the simplest ratio. (4) If the ratios are not whole numbers, multiply by 2, 3 or 4 to make them whole (for example 1.5 becomes 3 when multiplied by 2). (5) Write the formula.

Example 1: a compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. In 100 g: C 40 g, H 6.7 g, O 53.3 g. Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33; H = 6.7/1 = 6.7; O = 53.3/16 = 3.33. Divide by 3.33: C 1, H 2, O 1. Empirical formula CH2O. If the relative molecular mass is 180, then n = 180/30 = 6 and the molecular formula is C6H12O6.
Example 2: an iron oxide contains 70% iron and 30% oxygen. Moles: Fe = 70/56 = 1.25; O = 30/16 = 1.875. Divide by 1.25: Fe 1, O 1.5. Multiply by 2: Fe 2, O 3. Empirical formula Fe2O3.

Example 3: 2.4 g of carbon combine with 0.6 g of hydrogen. Moles: C = 2.4/12 = 0.2; H = 0.6/1 = 0.6. Ratio 1:3. Empirical formula CH3. If Mr = 30, the empirical formula mass is 15, so n = 2 and the molecular formula is C2H6.

Rounding rules. Ratios such as 1.98 or 2.03 are rounded to the nearest whole number (2). But ratios like 1.5 or 1.33 or 2.5 must be multiplied by 2 or 3, not rounded. Ratios of 0.5 need multiplying by 2. Ratios of 1.33 (or 1.25) need multiplying by 3 (or 4).

Mass of oxygen found by difference. In many experiments, the mass of oxygen is found by subtracting the mass of the metal from the mass of the oxide. Magnesium (2.4 g) burned in air gives 4.0 g of magnesium oxide, so oxygen = 1.6 g. Moles: Mg = 2.4/24 = 0.1; O = 1.6/16 = 0.1. Ratio 1:1: MgO.

Important: the empirical formula of ionic compounds is the formula (NaCl, MgO). For molecular compounds, you need the relative molecular mass to find the molecular formula. Different compounds can share an empirical formula (CH2O is the empirical formula for methanal HCHO, ethanoic acid CH3COOH and glucose).

concepts.title: Laws of chemical combination
learningObjectives: State the laws of conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions and reciprocal proportions
Explain each law with Dalton's atomic theory
Use data from experiments to illustrate each law
Do calculations that apply the laws

keyTerms.definition: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
A pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same proportions by mass.
When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.
If two elements each combine with a third, their combining masses with the third element are in the same ratio (or a simple multiple) as when they combine with each other.

concepts.definition: Four laws describe how elements combine: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton) and reciprocal proportions (Richter). Dalton's atomic theory explains all of them.
explanation: Law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier, 1789). The total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. When 24 g of magnesium burns in 16 g of oxygen, 40 g of magnesium oxide forms: 24 + 16 = 40. When a candle burns, the gases escape; if they are collected the mass is unchanged. Explanation: atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

Law of definite (constant) proportions (Proust, 1799). A compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass, regardless of source or method of preparation. Example: copper(II) oxide from two different samples. Sample A: 8.0 g of the oxide yields 6.4 g of copper, so 1.6 g of oxygen; Cu:O = 6.4:1.6 = 4:1. Sample B: 4.0 g yields 3.2 g of copper and 0.8 g of oxygen; Cu:O = 4:1. The ratio is the same. Similarly, water always has hydrogen and oxygen in mass ratio 1:8. Explanation: each compound has a fixed number of atoms of each kind.

Law of multiple proportions (Dalton, 1803). Carbon forms two oxides: carbon monoxide has 12 g of C combined with 16 g of O; carbon dioxide has 12 g of C combined with 32 g of O. For a fixed mass of carbon (12 g), the oxygen masses are 16:32 = 1:2, a simple whole-number ratio. The nitrogen oxides N2O, NO and NO2 combine 28 g of nitrogen with 16 g, 32 g and 64 g of oxygen: ratio 1:2:4. Explanation: atoms combine in small whole numbers.

Law of reciprocal proportions (Richter, 1792). Consider hydrogen, carbon and oxygen. In methane, 3 g of carbon combine with 1 g of hydrogen (C:H = 12:4 = 3:1). In carbon dioxide, 3 g of carbon combine with 8 g of oxygen (12:32 = 3:8). So 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen each combine with 3 g of carbon. The law predicts that hydrogen and oxygen combine in the ratio 1:8 (or a simple multiple), and in water they do: H:O = 2:16 = 1:8. Agreement shows the law is true.

Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes (1808) is a law about gases at the same temperature and pressure: gases react in simple whole-number ratios by volume (for example 2 volumes of hydrogen react with 1 volume of oxygen to give 2 volumes of steam). You will meet it again with the gas laws.

Applying the laws. Conservation of mass: if 10 g of calcium carbonate decomposes to give 5.6 g of calcium oxide, the carbon dioxide mass is 10 - 5.6 = 4.4 g. Definite proportions: if water has H:O = 1:8, then 36 g of water contains 4 g of hydrogen and 32 g of oxygen. Multiple proportions: if oxide X has 28 g of nitrogen with 16 g of oxygen, and oxide Y has 28 g of nitrogen with 48 g of oxygen, the ratio is 16:48 = 1:3.
These laws are the experimental basis of Dalton's atomic theory; the theory in turn explains why the laws hold.

concepts.title: Chemical equations
learningObjectives: Distinguish reactants from products
Write word equations and convert them to symbol equations
Use state symbols and reaction conditions
Interpret the information given by a balanced equation

keyTerms.definition: A substance that takes part in a reaction (on the left of the arrow).
A substance formed in a reaction (on the right).
A shorthand description of a reaction using formulae.
(s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (dissolved in water).
A number written before a formula to show how many units are involved.

concepts.definition: A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using formulae: reactants → products. A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, in agreement with the law of conservation of mass.
explanation: A chemical reaction can be described in words: 'hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water'. This is a word equation: hydrogen + oxygen → water. The arrow means 'forms' or 'yields'. To write a symbol equation we replace the names with formulae: H2 + O2 → H2O. This is called the skeleton equation. It is not yet balanced, because there are two O atoms on the left and only one on the right.

Steps for writing an equation. (1) Write a word equation. (2) Write the correct formula of each substance (the elements H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2 are diatomic; metals and carbon are written as atoms: Mg, Fe, C). (3) Balance by putting coefficients in front of formulae (see the next lesson). Never change a subscript to balance an equation, because that would change the substance.

State symbols tell the physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) in aqueous solution. Example: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g). Conditions such as heat, a catalyst or temperature may be written above the arrow: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g) with the word 'heat' over the arrow. A reversible reaction uses a double arrow.

Information from a balanced equation. 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O tells you: (1) the reactants and products; (2) the ratio of molecules (2 molecules of hydrogen to 1 of oxygen to 2 of water); (3) the ratio of moles (2 mol : 1 mol : 2 mol); (4) the ratio of gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure (2 : 1 : 2 for gases); (5) the masses involved: 2 × 2 = 4 g of H2 and 32 g of O2 give 36 g of H2O, consistent with conservation of mass.

Examples of word and symbol equations. Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide: Mg + O2 → MgO (to be balanced). Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen: Na + H2O → NaOH + H2. Calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. Zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen: Zn + HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. Methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O.

Limits of an equation. It does not show how fast the reaction occurs or what you would see. It shows only the amounts of reactants and products and the conditions you write. You still need observations for the full story (colour, gas, heat).

Types of reactions (preview): combination (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), displacement (A + BC → AC + B) and double decomposition (AB + CD → AD + CB). These are studied in detail in the Book Two chapter on types of reactions.

concepts.title: Balancing chemical equations
learningObjectives: Balance simple and complex equations by inspection
Apply a systematic strategy to balance equations with polyatomic ions
Balance combustion and redox-type equations
Check a balanced equation

keyTerms.definition: An equation with equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
Balancing by adjusting coefficients step by step by looking at the atoms.
Burning in oxygen.

concepts.definition: To balance an equation, adjust the coefficients (numbers in front of formulae) until each element has the same number of atoms on both sides. Never change a formula's subscripts.
explanation: Why balance? The law of conservation of mass says atoms are not created or destroyed, so the number of atoms of every element must be the same before and after the reaction.

Strategy. (1) Write the correct formulae. (2) Count the atoms of each element on both sides. (3) Balance metals first, then non-metals, then hydrogen and oxygen last (they usually appear in several compounds). (4) Treat polyatomic ions such as SO4^2- or OH- as one unit if they appear unchanged on both sides. (5) Use fractions if necessary and then multiply through to remove them. (6) Recount all atoms.

Example 1: H2 + O2 → H2O. Oxygen: 2 on the left, 1 on the right, so put 2 before H2O: H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Now hydrogen: 2 on the left, 4 on the right, so put 2 before H2: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Check: H 4 = 4; O 2 = 2.

Example 2: Fe + O2 → Fe2O3. Oxygen is 2 on the left and 3 on the right; the lowest common multiple is 6: 3O2 and 2Fe2O3. Then iron: 4 on the right, so 4Fe. Result: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. Check: Fe 4 = 4; O 6 = 6.

Example 3: Al + HCl → AlCl3 + H2. Chlorine: 3 on the right, so 3HCl: Al + 3HCl → AlCl3 + H2. Hydrogen: 3 on the left, 2 on the right. Use 6HCl and 3H2, then 2AlCl3 and 2Al: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2. Check: Al 2 = 2; H 6 = 6; Cl 6 = 6.

Example 4: combustion of propane, C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. Balance C: 3CO2. Balance H: 4H2O. Count oxygen: 6 + 4 = 10, so 5O2. Result: C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. Check: C 3 = 3; H 8 = 8; O 10 = 10. For hydrocarbons, balance C, then H, then O last.

Example 5: with polyatomic ions. Al2(SO4)3 + NaOH → Al(OH)3 + Na2SO4. Treat SO4 as a unit: 3 on the left, 1 on the right, so 3Na2SO4. Then Na: 6 on the right, so 6NaOH. Then Al: 2 on the left, so 2Al(OH)3. Result: Al2(SO4)3 + 6NaOH → 2Al(OH)3 + 3Na2SO4. Check OH: 6 = 6.
Example 6: Ca(OH)2 + HCl → CaCl2 + H2O. Cl: 2 on the right, so 2HCl; then H: 2 + 2 = 4 on the left, and 2 in water on the right, so 2H2O: Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + 2H2O. Check: O 2 = 2; H 4 = 4.
Fractional method for odd numbers: for example C2H6 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. C: 2CO2. H: 3H2O. O: 4 + 3 = 7, so 7/2 O2. Multiply by 2: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O. Check: C 4, H 12, O 14 on each side.
Always recount every element at the end. Add state symbols if requested. If all the coefficients have a common factor, divide to give the simplest whole numbers.

concepts.title: Calculations from chemical equations: the mole and stoichiometry
learningObjectives: Define the mole, molar mass and Avogadro's constant
Convert between mass, moles and number of particles
Use the molar volume of a gas at STP
Calculate masses and volumes of reactants and products from balanced equations
Calculate percentage yield

keyTerms.definition: The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10^23 elementary particles (Avogadro's number).
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol; numerically equal to Ar or Mr.
6.02 × 10^23 particles per mole.
The volume of one mole of any gas: 22.4 dm^3 at STP.
Standard temperature and pressure: 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa).
(actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100.

concepts.definition: n = m/M (moles = mass ÷ molar mass); number of particles = n × 6.02 × 10^23; volume of gas at STP = n × 22.4 dm^3. A balanced equation tells you the mole ratio, which lets you calculate unknown masses and volumes.
explanation: The mole. Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in huge groups called moles, in the same way that a dozen means 12. One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). The mass of one mole, the molar mass, equals the relative atomic or molecular mass in grams: carbon 12 g/mol, oxygen atoms 16 g/mol, O2 32 g/mol, water 18 g/mol, carbon dioxide 44 g/mol, NaCl 58.5 g/mol.

Key formulae. Number of moles n = mass (g) / molar mass (g/mol). Mass = n × M. Number of particles = n × 6.02 × 10^23. For gases at STP: n = volume (dm^3)/22.4. Examples: 36 g of water is 36/18 = 2 mol. 11 g of carbon dioxide is 11/44 = 0.25 mol. 0.5 mol of any substance contains 3.01 × 10^23 particles. 2 mol of NaOH has mass 2 × 40 = 80 g.

Method for stoichiometry (calculations from equations). (1) Write the balanced equation. (2) Convert the given mass or volume to moles. (3) Use the equation's mole ratio to find moles of the wanted substance. (4) Convert to mass or volume. Example 1: what mass of magnesium oxide is formed when 12 g of magnesium burns? 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Moles of Mg = 12/24 = 0.5 mol. Ratio Mg : MgO = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1, so 0.5 mol of MgO. Mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g.

Example 2: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate. CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. From 50 g of CaCO3 (Mr = 100): n = 0.5 mol. So 0.5 mol of CaO (mass 0.5 × 56 = 28 g) and 0.5 mol of CO2 (mass 0.5 × 44 = 22 g, volume 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm^3 at STP). Check: 28 + 22 = 50 g, in agreement with conservation of mass.

Example 3: gas volumes. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. From 6.5 g of zinc (Ar = 65): n(Zn) = 0.1 mol. Ratio Zn : H2 = 1 : 1, so 0.1 mol of H2, volume = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm^3 at STP. HCl needed: ratio 1 : 2, so 0.2 mol, mass 0.2 × 36.5 = 7.3 g.

Example 4: extraction of iron. Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Mass of iron from 160 kg of Fe2O3 (Mr = 160): 1 kmol of Fe2O3 gives 2 kmol of iron, i.e. 2 × 56 = 112 kg. (Mass ratios work the same in g or kg.)

Percentage yield. The theoretical yield is the mass calculated from the equation; the actual yield is what is obtained in practice. Percentage yield = (actual/theoretical) × 100. If the theoretical mass of MgO is 20 g and 16 g are collected, the yield is 16/20 × 100 = 80%. Yield is below 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions and losses during purification.

Mole and volume relationships for gases. At STP one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm^3; at room temperature and pressure (about 25 °C and 1 atm) it is about 24 dm^3. Use the value given in the question.
Setting out: always write the equation, list the molar masses, show the mole ratio and include units in every step.
